Build Production-Grade Software with Claude

Claude Code is an agent: a program that can read your codebase, run commands in your terminal, and change any file you can change. This is not a tour of its menus. It is a course on shipping real software with it. You will learn four things: how to limit what it is allowed to do, how to make it check its own work, how to keep a long session (four hours or more) on track, and how to hand the whole setup to a team so it works the same way for everyone.

How to use this course

  • It is about a tool, and it is not a feature list. Every section is built around a decision you will really have to make. Should this rule go in CLAUDE.md (a notes file Claude reads at the start of every session) or in a hook (a script that runs automatically at a fixed moment)? Should you hand this task to a helper or keep it in the main conversation? Which check lets you walk away while Claude works? The features are taught as answers to questions like these.
  • It describes the product as it stands in August and September 2026. (Sections 16 and 17 and the additions to sections 1 to 3 were checked on 2026-09-25 against the documentation and Claude Code 2.1.282.) Every flag, field name, default and limit comes from the documentation, and every shell command uses the real command-line program (the CLI).
  • It assumes you can use a terminal and have worked in a codebase with other people. You do not need any experience with agents. Some theory sits underneath the tool: what a token (the unit of text a model reads and is billed by) costs, why an agent's loop needs a rule for when to stop, and how a model really asks for a tool to be run. The AI Engineering course teaches that theory. This course names it where it matters but does not teach it again.
  • Each section follows the same order: Concept → Mechanism → Trade-off → Practice → Exercises with solutions. First the idea, then how it works inside, then what it costs you, then how to use it, and finally exercises with worked answers.

The one idea the rest of the course depends on

A language model produces text. That is all it can do. It cannot open a file or run a command by itself.

Claude Code is the program that lets that text cause real actions. It works like this:

  1. It tells the model which tools exist (read a file, edit a file, run a command, and so on).
  2. The model writes a structured request to use one of them.
  3. Claude Code decides whether to execute it.
  4. It runs the tool (or refuses) and feeds the result back to the model, which writes its next request.

The program wrapped around the model that does all this has a name: the agentic harness. Keeping this picture clear in your head is what separates people who configure the tool well from people who argue with it.

The model proposes
Reasoning, judgement, what to try next. Influenced by your prompt, your CLAUDE.md, what it just read. Never guaranteed by any of them.
The harness disposes
Permission rules, hooks, sandboxing, context management. Evaluated by code, unaffected by persuasion, and the same on turn one and turn ninety.

"Claude deleted the file" is never quite true. The model produced a request. Claude Code checked that request against your rules, and then ran it. Where that check lives, and what it refuses, is the whole of agent safety. That is why this course teaches permissions (what Claude is allowed to do) before capabilities (what it is able to do), and not the other way round.

What you are actually learning

"Using Claude Code well" is really three separate skills. People mix them up, and that is why their experiences of the tool differ so much.

Driving a session
Steering, interrupting, planning, and knowing when to throw the conversation away. The part that feels like the whole job at first and turns out to be the smallest — and the part where the most valuable habit is being quick to clear.
Engineering the context
Deciding what is in the window and what it costs. One window, filling up, degrading as it fills. Skills, subagents, MCP tool search, compaction and worktrees are all one subject wearing different clothes.
Bounding and verifying
What Claude may do, and how it proves the work is right. Permission rules, sandboxing, hooks and a check that returns a pass or a fail. This is the part that makes everything else safe to scale, and almost nobody does it first.

The course is ordered so each section can build on the ones before it.

  • Sections 1–3 explain the loop (the model asks, Claude Code acts, the result comes back), how to steer it, and the one limit that never goes away: the model can only hold so much text at once.
  • Sections 4–6 teach Claude about your project and limit what it may touch.
  • Section 7 is the turning point: a check that lets the loop finish its work on its own, without you inspecting every step.
  • Sections 8–12 are extensions: skills (saved procedures), hooks (scripts that run automatically), MCP (a standard way to connect outside systems), subagents (helpers with their own separate conversation) and plugins (a package of all of these).
  • Sections 13–15 run Claude Code without you watching: headless mode and the SDK (using it from a script or your own program), CI and automation, and cost and operations.
  • Sections 16–17 apply all of it to real work: one change taken from idea to merged pull request, then code you did not write, debugging, and sessions that have gone wrong.
  • Section 18 takes one repository from a cold start to a production setup, in the order a real project would.

A note on the ordering

That order has a bias, and it is worth naming now. It will look like caution. It is not.

The sections that make Claude more capable come after the ones that make it bounded and verifiable: limited in what it may do, and able to prove its work is right. Permissions come before skills. Verification comes before subagents. A check comes before automation.

The reason is not that independence is dangerous in general. It is that every mechanism in the second half increases the distance between you and what happens. You see less of each step. That distance is only safe when something at the far end can tell you whether the work is right.

A subagent whose output nobody checks is just a faster way to produce something that looks right. A nightly job with no check on its output can produce confident summaries built on nothing, for weeks, before anyone notices. Both appear in this course as worked examples. Both are common, and neither looks like a failure while it is happening.

A note on versions

This course names exact flags, fields, defaults, limits and model behaviour instead of hiding behind "the latest version". That is a deliberate trade. You get examples you can really run, but some details will go out of date. Three habits keep you safe as that happens.

Check what the interface says rather than what you remember. Four commands answer most questions:

  • claude --help lists every flag.
  • /hooks shows which hooks are configured and where each one came from.
  • /status names the settings files that loaded.
  • /mcp shows which MCP servers connected.

Nearly every "it stopped working" in this course is answered by one of those four in under a minute.

Treat a silent failure as the default, not the exception. Claude Code is deliberately built so that broken configuration does not stop it. It just keeps going with less. A hook that cannot start, a permission rule that matches nothing, an MCP server that failed its checks, a skill whose description was dropped because the list of skills ran out of room: in every case the session continues, quietly. That design is correct, because one broken file should not stop your work. Its consequence is that a gate you have never seen fire is a gate you have no evidence about. If you have never watched a check block something, you do not know that it works.

Re-derive anything version-dependent. Defaults move, limits change, and features leave research preview (Anthropic's label for features that are still experimental). Where this course gives a number, the number was true when it was written. The reason behind it will last longer than the number.

SECTION 1

The Agentic Loop

A coding agent is a program that uses an AI model to read, write and run code for you. Almost everything written about coding agents describes what they can do. Very little describes what they are. That gap matters. Nearly every mistake people make with Claude Code comes from a wrong picture of the machinery underneath:

  • over-specifying (dictating every step instead of stating the goal),
  • under-verifying (not giving it a way to check its own work),
  • letting a session run for four hours,
  • wondering why an instruction was ignored.

So this section builds the right picture. It covers few features and a lot of mechanism (how things work inside). Every later section argues for configuring something a certain way, and you cannot follow those arguments without knowing what is being configured.

1.1 What Claude Code Actually Is

A language model produces text. That is all it can do: given a sequence of tokens (small pieces of text), it produces more tokens. It cannot read a file, run a command, or change anything in the world.

Claude Code is the program that turns that into agency. Agency here means the ability to act. Claude Code offers the model a set of tools, each described in the request it sends. When the model writes a structured request to use one (read this path, run this command), Claude Code carries it out and feeds the result back in as more text. Then the model decides what to do next.

The way of working built on that arrangement has a name too: agentic coding. It means writing software by directing a loop that reads, edits and runs things for you, instead of typing every change yourself. The program that makes agentic coding possible also has a name, and it is what the rest of this course configures: the agentic harness. The model reasons. The harness provides everything else: the tools, the management of the context, the permission checks and the place where commands run.

Two phrases in this course follow from that split:

  • "Claude decided" means the model produced tokens that Claude Code read as a tool request.
  • "Claude Code blocked it" means the agentic harness refused to carry one out.

Everything you configure in the next fifteen sections is part of the agentic harness. None of it is part of the model.

The model proposes; the harness disposes. Every safety property in §5 descends from that sentence. "Claude deleted the file" is never quite true — the model emitted a request, and Claude Code, having checked your permission rules, ran it. Where that check lives, and what it refuses, is the whole of agent safety.

1.2 The Loop

Given a task, the work moves through three phases that blend into each other:

Gather context
Find out what is true. Search for files, read them, run a command to see what it prints, look something up.
Take action
Change something. Edit a file, create one, run a build, make a commit.
Verify results
Find out whether it worked. Run the tests, check the build, read the output. §7 is entirely about this phase, because it is the one that most often does not happen.

The loop adapts to the task. A question about the codebase may need only the first phase. A bug fix cycles through all three again and again. A refactor is mostly the third. Claude decides what each step needs from what it learned in the step before. It can chain dozens of actions and correct its course as it goes.

"Fix the failing tests" typically becomes:

1
Run the test suite to see what is failing
2
Read the error output
3
Search for the relevant source files
4
Read those files to understand the code
5
Edit the files to fix the issue
6
Run the tests again to verify

Notice what you did not have to say: which files, which test command, in what order. That is the property worth protecting: §2.1's advice to delegate (state the goal) rather than dictate (list the steps) follows directly from it. Notice also that step six only exists because the loop had something to run. Without a check, the loop ends at step five, and "done" means "looks done". That is the whole subject of §7.

You are part of the agentic loop, and that is part of the design, not a courtesy. You can interrupt at any point to redirect, add context, or ask for a different approach. Being able to course-correct in the middle of a turn is what makes a long agentic loop bearable. A wrong direction caught at the first tool call costs you one sentence. The same mistake caught eight calls later costs you those eight calls. §2.3 covers how to course-correct without throwing away work in progress.

1.3 The Tools

Tools are what make any of this agentic. Without them, the model can only reply with text. Every built-in tool falls into one of five categories, and each category is a different kind of action. The built-in tools are the base that skills, MCP and subagents all build on:

File operations
The Read tool, the Edit tool, the Write tool and NotebookEdit. The Read tool takes an optional offset and limit, so a large file need not arrive whole; the Edit tool replaces a string rather than rewriting a file; the Write tool creates or overwrites one outright, which is why it is the one that most often wants a permission rule.
Search
Glob, Grep. Find files by pattern, search content by regular expression.
Execution
Bash, PowerShell. Run any command you could run. This is the tool with the widest blast radius, and most of §5 is about bounding it.
Web
WebSearch, WebFetch. Search the web, fetch documentation, look up an error message.
Code intelligence
LSP. Type errors and warnings after edits, jump to definition, find references. Requires a code-intelligence plugin (§12), and it reduces context use by replacing file reads.

Four of them are worth knowing one by one, because how they behave shapes how Claude explores your code and how much context that costs.

The Glob tool
Finds files by pattern — **/*.ts, optionally rooted at a directory. Cheap, because it returns paths rather than contents. A search that starts with the Glob tool and reads three results costs far less than one that reads to find out what exists.
The Grep tool
Searches contents by regular expression, with an output_mode of content, files_with_matches or count. That last detail matters: the same Grep tool call can return a number, a file list, or matching lines, and the difference between them is often two orders of magnitude of context.
The Bash tool
Runs a command, with a timeout, an output limit, and the option to run in the background. The Bash tool is the one whose output most often overwhelms a context window, because a build log or a test run is a single call that can cost more than an hour of conversation.
The Task tool
Spawns a subagent (§11), taking a prompt, a description, a subagent_type and optionally a model. The Task tool is how a second context window comes into existence, which makes it the most consequential entry in the built-in tool list. It was renamed from Task to Agent, and Task(...) still works as an alias in settings and agent definitions — so both spellings appear in configuration written at different times.

Beyond those there are orchestration tools, which Claude uses to organise its own work: AskUserQuestion for asking you something, TodoWrite, Skill, ToolSearch and others. The full list is in the tools reference. What matters here is the overall shape, not the complete list.

Two properties of the built-in tools are worth noticing now, because they come back throughout the course.

  • Each tool use returns a tool result that feeds the next decision. A failed command is not an error state; it is just more input. The tool result lands in the context window exactly like any other content.
  • And the tool list itself is configurable. A deny rule that names only a tool removes that tool from the model's view entirely (§5.1). A subagent gets a shorter list (§11.2). MCP adds new tools (§10).

The built-in tools are the foundation. Four mechanisms extend them, and knowing which is which is most of the value of this course:

Skills
Extend what Claude knows — procedures and reference material, loaded on demand (§8)
MCP
Extend what Claude can reach — external services and data (§10)
Hooks
Make things happen deterministically, whether the model wanted them or not (§9)
Subagents
Move work into another context window (§11)

1.4 What Claude Can Access

Running claude in a directory gives it access to six things. Read the list as a statement about security as much as about what it can do:

Your project
Files in the directory and its subdirectories, plus anything else with your permission (§5.4).
Your terminal
Any command you could run. Build tools, git, package managers, system utilities, scripts. If you can do it from the command line, so can Claude.
Your git state
Current branch, uncommitted changes, recent commit history.
Your CLAUDE.md
Project instructions loaded at the start of every session (§4).
Auto memory
Learnings Claude saved for itself — the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md (§4.5).
Your extensions
MCP servers, skills, subagents, Chrome integration — whatever you configured.

The second row is the one to think about. "Any command you could run" is the accurate description. It is why the permission system exists and is not just a nice extra. It is also why §5 comes early in the course rather than late.

Because Claude sees the whole project, it can work across all of it: search for the relevant files, read several to understand how they fit together, make matching edits in many places, run the tests, and commit. That is the difference from an inline assistant that sees only the current file, and it is the source of both the power and the risk.

1.5 Models and Effort

Two dials shape how the loop behaves. Both are worth setting deliberately at the start of a session rather than changing in the middle of a task (§3.6 explains why changing them is expensive).

The model is chosen with /model during a session or --model when you start one. Aliases (short names) save you from remembering version numbers:

sonnet
The latest Sonnet, for daily coding.
opus
The latest Opus, for complex reasoning.
haiku
Fast and efficient, for simple tasks.
fable
Claude Fable 5, for the hardest and longest-running tasks.
best
Fable 5 where your organisation has access, otherwise the latest Opus.
opusplan
Opus during plan mode, Sonnet for execution. A genuinely good default — and note it makes every plan-mode toggle a model switch, which invalidates the cache.
sonnet[1m], opus[1m]
A one-million-token context window for long sessions (§3.4).
default
Not a model — clears any override and reverts to your account's runtime default.

A model alias is the usual way to name a model, because an alias keeps working when versions change and a full model ID does not. Model selection is worth treating as a real decision rather than a default. On the same task, Opus costs several times what Sonnet does, and it is also several times better at genuinely hard reasoning. So a wrong choice in either direction is expensive. In practice:

  • Sonnet for most coding;
  • Opus when the problem is about architecture, or the reasoning takes many steps;
  • Haiku for mechanical subagent work (§11.1);
  • opusplan when you want the expensive model only for the part where thinking pays off.

Model selection also interacts with two things covered later. It is part of the prompt-cache key (§3.6), so switching model in the middle of a session means everything is read again at full price. And an organisation can restrict it with availableModels (§15.6); a blocked choice is then replaced with an allowed one rather than refused.

Extended thinking is the related capability, and the two are easy to mix up. Extended thinking is the model reasoning at length before it answers. Effort is the dial that controls how much of that reasoning happens. Subagents inherit the main conversation's extended thinking setting (on if your session has it on, off otherwise), and there is no separate setting for it per subagent.

Effort controls adaptive reasoning: how much the model thinks at each step. The model decides that itself at each step, based on how complex the task is. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max, depending on the model, and the default is high on every model that supports effort (except Opus 4.7, which defaults to xhigh). If you set a level the current model does not support, it falls back to the highest supported level at or below it: xhigh runs as high on Opus 4.6.

Lower effort is faster and cheaper for straightforward work. Higher effort reasons more deeply on hard problems. low, medium, high and xhigh stay set across sessions when you set them interactively. max applies only to the current session, unless you set it through an environment variable.

/effort also offers ultracode, which is not an effort level at all. It sends xhigh to the model and has Claude run dynamic workflows (§11.6), scripts that coordinate many agents, for substantial tasks. It is the setting for "this is a large job, spend what it takes". It also exempts the session from the limit on subagents running at once and from the large-workflow warning.

1.6 Where It Runs

The loop, the tools and everything else in this course are identical everywhere. What changes is where your code runs and how you interact with it. Keeping those two questions separate prevents a lot of confusion.

Execution environment is where the code runs:

Local
Your machine. The default, with full access to your files, tools and environment.
Cloud
Anthropic-managed VMs, or a self-hosted environment your organisation operates. For offloading work and for repositories you do not have locally (§14.7). A self-hosted environment is the same product on infrastructure you control, which is what makes cloud sessions available to organisations whose data policy rules out the managed one.
Remote Control
Your machine, driven from a browser. The web interface, with execution and your files staying local.

Interface is how you interact with it. The options are the terminal in interactive mode, the desktop app, the VS Code and JetBrains extensions, claude.ai/code, Remote Control, Slack, and CI/CD pipelines. The VS Code extension shows changes (diffs) inline and lets you review plans in the editor. The JetBrains extension covers IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm and the rest of that family. The interface decides what you see; the underlying loop is identical. That is why a hook you write for the terminal also fires in the desktop app. Interactive mode is the only one where a permission prompt can actually be answered by a person. That is why §13 treats non-interactive mode as a different problem, not the same one with less screen.

This course is written against the terminal, because that is where every mechanism is visible and every setting is a file you can read. Everything you learn there carries over to the other interfaces.

1.7 Getting Started, Briefly

Install Claude Code, sign in, and start in a real repository. The install is a single native program. You sign in either with a Claude subscription through /login or with an API key. Which one you choose has consequences that show up much later:

  • The Chrome integration needs a subscription sign-in and stays off with an API key (§7.5).
  • Bare mode never reads OAuth credentials (the login from /login). So a scripted --bare run needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an API key helper: an apiKeyHelper command in your settings that creates a key when needed instead of storing one (§13.1).

An API key helper is the right answer anywhere a long-lived secret stored in a file would be a bad idea.

claude

Spend the first session on questions rather than changes. The fastest way to judge the tool is to ask about code you already understand and see whether the answer is right:

What does the auth module do and where does session state live?

If anything about the install itself is wrong (a missing dependency, an old version, a login that did not work), claude doctor diagnoses it. Run it once right after you install Claude Code, not the first time something breaks.

Then try a small change with a check attached. That is the shape of every good prompt in this course:

Add a --json flag to the export command that prints the same data as
machine-readable JSON. Follow the pattern in src/commands/list.ts.
Run the tests when you're done.

Three commands are worth knowing on day one, and each has a section behind it:

/help
Lists what is available in this session — and /help is worth re-running occasionally rather than once, because the list changes as you add skills, plugins and MCP prompts. Typing / alone filters the same list as you type.
/init
Generates a starting CLAUDE.md by analysing the codebase (§4.1).
/context
Shows what is filling the context window right now (§3.1).
/doctor
A setup checkup that diagnoses installation and configuration problems, and can fix them.

And one key: Esc stops Claude immediately. Knowing that before you need it is the difference between watching something go wrong and stopping it.

1.8 The Shape of the Rest

Everything after this section adds a layer to the loop. It helps to see the whole path before walking it.

§2–3
Driving the loop and its one hard constraint. How to steer, and what fills the window.
§4–6
Making Claude know your project, and bounding what it may do. Memory, permissions, configuration.
§7
Closing the loop. The check that lets it verify itself — and the pivot the second half depends on.
§8–12
Extension. Skills, hooks, MCP, subagents, plugins: what Claude knows, what happens deterministically, what it can reach, where the work runs, how you ship all of it to a team.
§13–15
Running it without you. Headless and the SDK, CI and automation, cost and operations.
§16–17
Working a real task. One change from idea to merged pull request, and the same discipline applied to code you did not write and sessions that went wrong.
§18
One repository, cold start to production setup.

That order has a bias worth naming. The sections that make Claude more capable come after the ones that make it bounded and verifiable: permissions before skills, verification before subagents. That is not caution for its own sake. Every extension mechanism increases the distance between you and what happens, and distance is only safe when there is something at the far end that can tell you whether the work is right.

1.9 Not the Only Agent: Primitives Across Agents

Claude Code is one of several coding agents, and a team rarely uses only one. That matters for exactly one practical question: where the project's standing instructions live. It deserves a short section, because the wrong answer gives you two copies of the same file that slowly stop matching.

Every agent of this kind has the same four ideas under different names. Mapping them once removes most of the confusion when a colleague uses another tool:

The idea
In Claude Code
What to ask of any agent
Standing instructions
CLAUDE.md (§4)
Which file does it read at the start of every session, and can it import others?
Reusable procedures
Skills (§8)
Can a procedure load only when it is relevant, or does it always cost context?
Guaranteed behaviour
Hooks and permission rules (§5, §9)
What is enforced by the program, and what is only requested of the model?
Delegated work
Subagents (§11)
Does delegated work get its own context, and what comes back?

The fourth column is the useful one. The names differ but the questions do not. So you learn a new agent by asking those four questions of its documentation, not by working through another course. One distinction travels best of all, the one §5 and §9 draw between what the model is asked to do and what the program guarantees. Whatever the tool, an instruction is a request and an enforced rule is a guarantee.

For standing instructions in particular, §4.3 already gave the answer for a repository that also serves other agents. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md, so the clean setup is a CLAUDE.md that imports the shared file, with the shared content written only once:

@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code
Use plan mode for changes that touch more than one file.

Everything above the Claude-specific heading is read from the shared file. A convention added there reaches every agent that reads it, and no two files can disagree. The course deliberately goes no further than that. The other tools change quickly and their behaviour cannot be checked from here. So what this course teaches is the four questions and the import; anything more would be a claim it could not verify.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1 — Trace the loop. You type: "The /export endpoint returns 500 for users with no orders. Fix it." Write out the tool calls you would expect, in order, and mark which phase each belongs to. Then say what would change if the repository had no tests.

Solution

A plausible trace, with phases:

Grep "export" src/                          gather   find the handler
Read src/api/export.ts                      gather   read it
Grep "getOrders" src/                       gather   find what it calls
Read src/services/orders.ts                 gather   read the dependency
Bash npm test -- export                     verify   see the current state
Edit src/services/orders.ts                 act      handle the empty case
Bash npm test -- export                     verify   confirm the fix

Two things about that trace are worth noticing. The verification step appears before the edit as well as after — running the tests first is a gathering action, establishing what currently fails, and the same command becomes verification once there is a change to check. The phases are not a fixed sequence; they are a description of intent.

And the gather phase is four calls out of seven. That is typical, and it is why §3 spends so long on context: the majority of what enters the window on a bug fix is material Claude read to orient itself, not the fix.

Without tests, the trace loses its ends. The most likely version:

Grep / Read ...                             gather
Edit src/services/orders.ts                 act
                                            (nothing)

The loop terminates at "looks done", because there is nothing that returns a pass or a fail. A careful Claude might curl the endpoint or write a throwaway script, but that is optional behaviour rather than a step the loop requires — and it will not always happen.

So the answer to "what changes" is: you become step seven. Every mistake now waits for you to notice it, which is fine for one fix and does not scale to a session you walk away from. The practical response is not to write a test suite before touching anything, but to give this one task a check: "reproduce it first with a script that calls the endpoint for a user with no orders, then fix it and run the script again." Thirty seconds of prompt, and the loop closes (§7.1).

Exercise 1.2 — Harness or model? For each, say whether the behaviour comes from the model or the harness, and why the distinction matters: (a) Claude decides to read three files before editing; (b) an Edit on .env is refused; (c) Claude re-runs the tests after a fix; (d) the conversation is summarised when the window fills; (e) Claude says it will not help with something.

Solution

(a) Model. Nothing in the harness decides how much to read; that is reasoning about the task. Why it matters: it is influenceable but not controllable. A CLAUDE.md line or a clearer prompt changes it; nothing makes it deterministic. If you need "always read the schema before editing a migration", the reliable version is a hook that injects the schema (§9.7), not an instruction hoping to be followed.

(b) Harness. A permission deny rule is evaluated by Claude Code before the tool executes (§5.1). Why it matters: this one is a guarantee. It does not depend on what the model concluded, what a web page told it, or how a request was phrased. The whole point of §5 is moving requirements from category (a) into category (b) wherever they can be expressed that way.

(c) Either, and telling them apart is the useful skill. If Claude re-runs the tests because it judged that sensible, that is the model. If a Stop hook refuses to let the turn end while the suite is red, that is the harness (§9.8). The two are indistinguishable from the transcript on a good day and very distinguishable on a bad one — which is precisely why §7.3 offers four levels of gating rather than one.

(d) Harness. Compaction is Claude Code managing the request: it clears older tool outputs, summarises the conversation, re-injects CLAUDE.md from disk (§3.3). The model has no say. Why it matters: the rules are knowable and designable-around, which is what §3.3's table is for.

(e) Model. A refusal is the model reasoning about a request. Why it matters: it is not a permission rule, so it is not configurable through settings, and treating it as one leads people to look for a flag that does not exist. If a legitimate task is being refused, the fix is in the prompt — usually more context about what and why.

The general test: ask whether the behaviour would change if the model changed. Yes → model. No → harness. Everything you can guarantee lives on the harness side, and every section of this course that promises reliability is really about moving something across that line.

SECTION 2

Driving a Session

Section 1 described the loop. This section is about the part of it you actually control: what you type, when you interrupt, when you plan, and when you throw the whole conversation away and start again.

That last one matters more than it sounds. Most of the skill in working with Claude Code is not writing clever prompts. It is knowing which of a small set of moves fits the situation:

  • Steer (add a message while Claude keeps working) or interrupt (stop it).
  • Plan first or just ask.
  • Correct the conversation or clear it and start fresh.
  • Branch (try another direction from here) or rewind (go back to an earlier point).

Every one of those moves is cheap, can be undone, and takes one keystroke. People who work well with the tool make them constantly. People who struggle make almost none of them.

2.1 It Is a Conversation

The first thing to unlearn is the idea that you need a good prompt. You need a first prompt. After that, you react to what happens.

Fix the login bug

Claude investigates and tries something. It is not quite right:

That's not quite right. The issue is in the session handling.

Claude adjusts. When the first attempt is wrong, you do not start over — you iterate. That is not a workaround for imperfect prompts. It is how the tool is meant to be used. It is also faster than trying to specify everything up front, because half of what you would have specified turns out not to matter.

The complementary instruction is about how much to specify:

Delegate, don't dictate. Think of handing work to a capable colleague: give context and direction, then trust Claude to work out the details. "The checkout flow is broken for users with expired cards. The relevant code is in src/payments/. Can you investigate and fix it?" — you do not need to name which files to read or which commands to run.

This seems to clash with §2.2's advice to be specific. The way out is worth stating: be specific about the goal and the constraints, and vague about the method. "Investigate and fix" is the method, so leave it alone. "Users with expired cards", "src/payments/" and "write a failing test first" are the goal and the constraints, and that is where precision pays.

2.2 Specificity Where It Counts

Claude can guess what you mean; it cannot read your mind. Four kinds of precision are worth the words they cost:

Scope the task
"add tests for foo.py" → "write a test for foo.py covering the edge case where the user is logged out. Avoid mocks."
Point to sources
"why does ExecutionFactory have such a weird API?" → "look through ExecutionFactory's git history and summarise how its API came to be"
Reference existing patterns
"add a calendar widget" → "look at how existing widgets are implemented on the home page. HotDogWidget.php is a good example. Follow that pattern… build from scratch without libraries other than the ones already used."
Describe the symptom
"fix the login bug" → "users report that login fails after session timeout. Check the auth flow in src/auth/, especially token refresh. Write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it."

The second row is a codebase question rather than a task, and it is the kind people use least. A codebase question asks how does this work, why is it like this, or where does this happen. It is often the cheapest thing you can ask: it costs one exploration and changes nothing. And it is often what you really wanted when you were about to ask for an edit. Pointing Claude at a source that can answer the question (the git history, a specific file, a failing test) is much stronger than asking the question directly. It turns a request for an opinion into a request to go and look.

There is also a prompt library: a collection of copy-paste prompts tagged by task and role. A prompt library entry is less a template to fill in than an example of a shape. It is worth browsing early, for the same reason reading someone else's shell aliases is: not for the prompts themselves, but for the kinds of request you had not thought of.

Vague prompts still have a place. "What would you improve in this file?" brings up things you would not have thought to ask about, and that is a fair use of an agent's breadth. Be vague when you are exploring and can afford to course-correct. Be precise when you know what you want and a wrong guess costs a rewrite.

Getting rich content in

An @-mention
Type @ and pick from the typeahead to reference a file — and the same @-mention syntax reaches subagents (§11.1) and MCP resources (§10.1), so one @-mention gesture covers three different kinds of thing. Claude reads it before responding. Note from §9.2 that an @ reference produces no Read tool call at all — which matters because a Read tool call is what a permission rule and a hook can see — the contents are spliced in while the prompt is built, so no PreToolUse hook fires for it.
Paste an image
Copy-paste or drag and drop. Paste an image of a broken layout, a design mock or an error dialog — pasting an image is often faster and more accurate than describing what you are looking at.
Give URLs
For documentation and API references. Allowlist the domains you use often with /permissions (§5.1).
Pipe data
cat error.log | claude sends contents directly, which also means Claude needs no Bash permission to see them (§13.1).
Let Claude fetch
Tell it to pull the context itself — a Bash command, an MCP tool, a file read. Often cheaper than assembling it yourself.

2.3 Interrupt and Steer

Two keys and one habit make the difference between a session you control and one you watch go wrong.

Press Esc
Stops Claude immediately. The running tool call is cancelled and Claude waits for your next instruction. If you have messages queued, they go next.
Type and press Enter
Sends a correction without stopping the running tool. Claude reads it as soon as the current action completes and adjusts before deciding its next step.

The second key is the one people forget, and most of the time it is the better move. Say Claude is running the test suite, and you notice it is about to edit the wrong file next. You do not need to interrupt the test run. Type the correction, and it reaches Claude at its next decision point. Interrupting throws away work in progress; steering does not.

Course-correct early and often. The cost of a correction grows the longer you wait. A wrong direction caught at the first tool call costs one sentence. The same wrong direction caught eight tool calls later costs those eight tool calls, plus the context they used up. It also adds a risk: the wrong approach is now the most recent thing in the window, and so the most persuasive (§3.5).

You can also queue messages while Claude works, and take back what you queued if you change your mind. With queueing, steering and Esc available, there is never a situation where the right response is to sit and wait for a turn you already know is going wrong.

2.4 Plan Mode

For anything bigger than a one-sentence change, separate the research from the doing. It prevents the one failure no test can catch: a well-built solution to the wrong problem.

There are three ways into plan mode. Shift+Tab cycles into it. /plan in front of a single prompt plans for that question only; use /plan when you want normal behaviour back afterwards. claude --permission-mode plan starts the session in it. In plan mode Claude reads files and runs read-only commands to explore, but does not edit your source, and edits stay blocked until you approve a plan.

claude --permission-mode plan

When the plan is ready, Claude presents it and asks how to proceed:

Yes, and use auto mode
Approve and continue with the classifier reviewing actions (§5.5). Reads "Yes, auto-accept edits" when auto mode is unavailable.
Yes, manually approve edits
Approve and review each edit individually.
No, keep planning
Stay in plan mode and say what to change.

Ctrl+G opens the proposed plan in your editor so you can edit it directly before Claude goes ahead. That is the feature that makes plan mode more than a preview. Rewriting two steps of a plan takes a minute. Rewriting the code those two steps produced takes an afternoon.

Accepting a plan also gives the session a title generated from the plan, unless you already named it (§2.6).

Plan mode has overhead, and the guidance against over-using it is specific: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. Fixing a typo, adding a log line, renaming a variable — just ask. Planning earns its cost when you are uncertain about the approach, when the change spans multiple files, or when you are unfamiliar with the code being modified.

One cost is worth knowing about because you cannot see it. With the opusplan model setting, entering and leaving plan mode is a model switch (Opus plans, Sonnet does the work), and every model switch invalidates the prompt cache (§3.6). Toggling in and out of plan mode again and again on that setting is one of the most expensive habits you can have.

2.5 Checkpoints: The Undo You Did Not Set Up

Claude Code automatically saves the state of your code before each user prompt. These saved points are called checkpoints. It tracks what its own file-editing tools did. So an Edit tool call is captured, but a shell command that rewrote the same file is not; the list below comes back to that limitation. You do nothing to turn this on. It is the reason you can let Claude try something ambitious without first making a defensive commit.

/rewind (or Esc twice on an empty prompt) opens the menu, which lists each prompt you sent. Pick a point, then choose:

Restore code and conversation
Revert both to that point.
Restore conversation
Rewind the messages, keep the current code.
Restore code
Revert the files, keep the conversation.
Summarize from here
Compress everything after this point, freeing context.
Summarize up to here
Compress everything before it, keeping later messages intact.

The useful part is that code and conversation are restored separately. Restoring the conversation without the code is how you keep a good change while throwing away a confused discussion about it. Restoring the code without the conversation is how you undo an edit while keeping everything Claude learned along the way. That is often the better move, because the investigation was the expensive part.

The two summarize options work like a targeted /compact (§3.4). They compress a long debugging stretch from the chosen point onwards, while keeping your original instructions intact. Highlight a Summarize option and type instructions where the row reads add context to guide what the summary keeps.

Three limits to hold:

Bash changes are not tracked
Checkpointing covers Claude's file-editing tools only. A file that a shell command wrote, moved or deleted is not in the snapshot, and /rewind will not bring it back. Git is the backstop.
100 checkpoints per session
Older snapshots are discarded, so a very long session cannot rewind all the way to the start.
30 days
Checkpoints are deleted with the session under the retention sweep; cleanupPeriodDays changes it.

The first one is the one that matters. Suppose Claude ran npm run codegen and a migration script. /rewind would then restore a half-old, half-new tree, because it never saw what those commands changed. Commit before anything that generates or moves files outside the edit tools: it costs ten seconds and gives you a second, complete undo system.

One convenience worth knowing: if you ran /clear earlier in the same process, the rewind menu shows a /resume <session-id> (previous session) entry at the top. So clearing is not quite as final as it looks, as long as you have not exited.

2.6 Sessions: Naming, Resuming, Branching

A session is a saved conversation tied to a project directory. It is stored on your machine, and saved continuously as you work.

claude --continue
Resume a session without naming it — the most recent interactive one in this directory.
claude --resume
Open the session picker. The session picker shows this worktree's sessions by default; Ctrl+W widens it to every worktree of the repository and Ctrl+A to every project on the machine.
claude --resume <name>
Resume a named session directly.
claude --from-pr <number>
Open the picker filtered to sessions linked to that pull request. --from-pr is the one to remember when you come back to a review three days later and cannot recall what the session was called.
/resume
Switch conversations from inside an active session.

To resume a session you have to be able to find it, and you do that from the session picker. That is why the next paragraph matters more than it looks.

Name your sessions. Use claude -n auth-refactor at startup, /rename auth-refactor during the session, or Ctrl+R from the picker. A session name you set replaces the generated title everywhere the session appears, so one session name works both as a handle for resuming and as the label in lists. It is a tiny habit, and it is the one that makes parallel work manageable. Three unnamed sessions in a picker are three rows you have to open to tell apart. Three named ones are three you can resume by name from anywhere in the repository.

Unnamed sessions get two labels, and only one of them works as a handle. A default display name like my-app-3f identifies the session in lists but is not a resume handle: passing it to --resume finds nothing. A generated title, written by a fast model from your first prompt, can be used to resume. Accepting a plan replaces the generated title with one based on the plan.

What resuming restores — and what it does not

Restored
Full conversation history including tool calls and results; the model; the --agent; the permission mode; an active /goal; unexpired scheduled tasks.
Not restored
plan and bypassPermissions modes, ever. --mcp-config, --settings, --plugin-dir, --fallback-model, and --add-dir directories. Background Bash and monitor tasks.

That second row is where resumed sessions go wrong. Configuration passed as a flag must be passed again, while configuration that lives in settings.json is read again at launch and needs nothing. So a session that depended on --mcp-config resumes with no MCP servers. It then gives confident answers based on nothing: the §13.2 failure, arriving by a different route. The fix is the general one: wherever you can, put configuration in settings files rather than flags.

Two permission modes are never restored: plan and bypassPermissions. That is a deliberate safety choice worth remembering. Resuming a session never quietly puts you back in a mode where edits are blocked, or in one where nothing is checked. Fast mode is a launch-time choice in the same way. It is not restored, and turning fast mode on deep into a resumed session costs a full cache rebuild (§3.6), while turning it on at the start costs almost nothing.

Resuming a large old session

On a Pro or Max plan, resuming a session that has been idle for about an hour and holds over 100,000 tokens opens a dialog before your first message. The prompt cache has expired by then, so the next request will process the full history once anyway.

Resume from summary
Runs /compact immediately. Later requests carry the summary rather than the full history — cheaper per request, and whatever the summary omits is gone.
Resume full session as-is
Loads it unchanged. Every detail stays available, at a per-request cost that scales with the conversation's size.
Don't ask me again
Always resume in full, and stop showing the dialog.

An honest way to choose: summary if you are coming back to continue the task, full if you are coming back to answer a question about what happened. The details a summary drops are usually ones you would only need for the second case.

Branching

/branch try-streaming-approach

claude --continue --fork-session

To branch a session is to fork the conversation, not the repository. It copies the conversation so far and switches you into the copy, leaving the original intact and still in the picker. It is the move for "I want to try a different approach and keep the option of coming back". It is genuinely different from /rewind, which throws work away. To branch a session is also not the same as to fork the conversation into a subagent (§11.3). A forked subagent runs alongside you and reports back, while a branch moves where you are working.

What the branch inherits follows from one fact: /branch copies the transcript and switches the running process to write to it. So:

  • "allow for this session" permission grants carry over;
  • background subagents and Bash commands already running keep running, and their output lands in the branch;
  • a Remote Control connection follows you.

--fork-session starts a separate process instead. It does not inherit the grants, and you approve things again there.

Resuming the same session in two terminals without forking interleaves both terminals' messages into one transcript. That is almost never what anyone wants, and it is the reason to reach for /branch or --fork-session rather than opening a second window on the same session.

2.7 The Moves, and When to Make Them

Here are six situations, and the move that fits each. This is the practical core of the section.

Going in the wrong direction, mid-turn
Type the correction and press Enter. It arrives at the next decision point without discarding work in progress.
About to do something you do not want
Esc. Immediate, cancels the running tool call.
Two corrections have failed
/clear and write a better first prompt (§7.6). The window now contains two wrong approaches, and both are evidence for the third attempt.
The change is wrong, the investigation was good
/rewind → restore code only. Keeps everything Claude learned, discards what it wrote.
You want to try a second approach
/branch. Both paths survive, and you can compare rather than guess.
The task genuinely changed
/clear. Carrying a finished problem into a new one costs tokens on every remaining turn and crowds out what you now need.

Notice how many of them are moves that throw something away. The instinct with a long, expensive conversation is to protect it, and the instinct is usually wrong. Context is a budget, not an investment. A session carrying two failed approaches does worse at the third attempt than a fresh one would. The most valuable habit in this section is being quick to clear.

2.8 Directing Versus Hoping

There are two ways to work with an agent. Most of the difference between people who find it transformative and people who find it disappointing is which of the two they are doing.

Hoping: the unstructured session

Hoping looks like this: describe what you want, accept what comes back, run it, and if it is wrong, describe the problem again. This unstructured way of working is sometimes called vibe coding, and it is not silly. On a small, throwaway task where the right result is obvious, it is the fastest way to work, and the guide says below when a vague prompt is exactly right. Its built-in weakness is that the only thing that can tell success from failure is you. In the best-practices guide's words, Claude stops "when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, 'looks done' is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop: every mistake waits for you to notice it."

Directing replaces the hope with three things, stated up front:

An outcome
What done looks like, concretely enough that two people would agree whether it was reached.
Constraints
The files, the pattern to follow, what must not change. §2.2 covered these; they turn a guess into a bounded search.
A check
Something Claude can run that returns pass or fail. §7 is entirely about this, and the guide calls it "the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from".

The guide's before-and-after pairs show the shift better than a description. "implement a function that validates email addresses" becomes "write a validateEmail function. example test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. run the tests after implementing". "Fix the login bug" becomes a symptom, a location and a definition of fixed: "users report that login fails after session timeout. check the auth flow in src/auth/, especially token refresh. write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it". Nothing in either "after" version is clever. Each one states what success looks like, which is the one thing the model cannot guess.

The trade is a cost paid up front in exchange for a cheaper loop. The arithmetic is worth seeing once, with one warning: the inputs below are assumptions for illustration, not measurements, and the exercise is to put in your own. What the model shows is the shape of the trade, not a number to quote:

def expected_minutes(p_success, setup, attempt, review):
    """Expected total time when each attempt succeeds with probability p_success, until one does.
    Every attempt costs `attempt` (model time) plus `review` (your time to judge the result)."""
    expected_attempts = 1 / p_success
    return setup + expected_attempts * (attempt + review)

# Hoping: no setup, a vague prompt succeeds 1 time in 3, and you must read every result.
# Directing: 6 minutes to state the outcome, constraints and check, which lifts success to 3 in 4
# and lets a passing check stand in for most of your reading.
print(f'{"scenario":<44}{"minutes":>9}')
for label, p, setup, review in (('hoping (p=0.33, read every result)', 0.33, 0, 4),
                                ('directing (p=0.75, the check reviews)', 0.75, 6, 1)):
    print(f'{label:<44}{expected_minutes(p, setup, attempt=3, review=review):>9.1f}')

print('\nbreak-even: how low can the success rate of directing fall before hoping wins?')
hoping = expected_minutes(0.33, 0, 3, 4)
for p in (0.75, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.25):
    cost = expected_minutes(p, 6, 3, 1)
    print(f'  directing at p={p:<5}: {cost:>5.1f} min  {"wins" if cost < hoping else "loses"} against {hoping:.1f}')

scenario                                      minutes
hoping (p=0.33, read every result)               21.2
directing (p=0.75, the check reviews)            11.3

break-even: how low can the success rate of directing fall before hoping wins?
  directing at p=0.75 :  11.3 min  wins against 21.2
  directing at p=0.5  :  14.0 min  wins against 21.2
  directing at p=0.4  :  16.0 min  wins against 21.2
  directing at p=0.3  :  19.3 min  wins against 21.2
  directing at p=0.25 :  22.0 min  loses against 21.2

With those inputs, directing wins easily. It keeps winning until its own success rate drops to about a quarter (the break-even is near 26%); below that, the setup cost has bought nothing. That leads to the honest lesson: directing pays when the task is big enough that repeated attempts are expensive and small enough that the check is cheap to write. For a one-line change the setup is the whole cost, and hoping is right. The model also leaves out the largest effect, which is what your attention is worth. Time spent reading results is time not spent on anything else, and a session you can walk away from has a value that does not show up in minutes per task.

Develop your intuition

The guide is careful not to turn this into a rule, and the course should not either. Its closing section is titled "Develop your intuition". It says that sometimes you should let context build up because the history is valuable, sometimes skip planning because the task is exploratory, and sometimes a vague prompt is right "because you want to see how Claude interprets the problem before constraining it". A prompt like "what would you improve in this file?" can bring up things you would not have thought to ask. Directing is a discipline for work where you know what you want; exploring is a genuinely different activity. What the guide asks is that you notice which one you are doing, and that you do not use the exploratory style for work that has a definition of done.

Exercises

Exercise 2.1 — Pick the move. For each, say which single action you would take and why: (a) Claude is halfway through a refactor and you realise it is editing the generated file rather than the source; (b) you asked for a bug fix, Claude has tried two approaches and both are wrong; (c) Claude wrote a good fix but the conversation getting there was a 40-turn mess; (d) you want to see whether a Redis-backed version would be simpler than the Postgres one Claude just built; (e) you finished the auth work and are about to start on the export feature.

Solution

(a) Type the correction and press Enter — do not press Esc. Claude reads it at the next decision point and adjusts before the following edit. Interrupting would cancel whatever tool call is running for no benefit; the wrong edit has not happened yet, and steering catches it. Add the fact rather than just the objection: "src/api/client.ts is generated from openapi.yaml — edit the spec and regenerate instead." One sentence prevents the same mistake recurring later in the session.

(b) /clear and write a better first prompt. After two failed corrections the window holds two wrong approaches, both visible to the model and both weighing on the third attempt. The two failures were not wasted — they told you what your original prompt was missing — so fold that into the new one: the symptom, the file, the constraint, and the check. This is the move people resist most and it is right nearly every time.

(c) /rewind → Summarize up to here, not restore. The code is good, so nothing should be reverted; the problem is purely that forty turns of context are crowding out what comes next. Summarising up to the fix compresses the mess and keeps the recent messages intact. /clear would also work but throws away the fix's immediate context, which you may still want when writing the commit message.

(d) /branch redis-version. Both implementations survive, which lets you compare rather than remember. /rewind would discard the Postgres version — exactly wrong, since the whole question is which is simpler. Note the process detail from §2.6: /branch keeps your session-scoped permission grants because it stays in the same process, while --fork-session starts a separate one and makes you re-approve.

(e) /clear. Unrelated task, so everything in the window is now cost without benefit: it consumes tokens on every remaining message and competes with the files the export work needs. Consider naming the next session first — the auth session stays resumable by name if the export work turns up a question about it.

The pattern: steer when the work is salvageable, rewind when the code is wrong but the understanding is not, branch when both paths have value, and clear when the context has stopped helping. Only one of the five keeps everything, and that is the right ratio.

Exercise 2.2 — The resumed session that lost its tools. A colleague runs claude --mcp-config db.json and works for an hour with a database MCP server connected. The next morning they run claude --continue, ask a question about the schema, and get a confident answer with no tool calls. Explain, and give the fix plus the general rule.

Solution

The --mcp-config flag was not restored. A resumed session restores conversation history, model, agent, permission mode, an active goal and unexpired scheduled tasks. It does not restore configuration passed as a launch flag: --mcp-config, --settings, --plugin-dir, --fallback-model, or directories added with --add-dir. So the session came back with the full conversation — including yesterday's tool calls and their results — and no database server connected.

Why the answer looked fine is the interesting part. The transcript contains yesterday's schema queries and their output, so Claude had plenty of material to answer from without calling anything. The answer is a summary of yesterday's data presented as though it were today's, and it will be wrong exactly when it matters: after a migration. This is §13.2's "confident answer derived from less than you thought it had", produced here by a resume rather than by a validation failure.

The immediate fix is to pass the flag again:

claude --continue --mcp-config db.json

The real fix is to stop using the flag. Standard settings files are re-read at launch, so configuration that lives in them survives every resume without anyone remembering anything. A project-scoped .mcp.json committed to the repository (§10.3) means the server is there for every session, for every teammate, on every resume — and it removes an entire class of "worked yesterday" report.

The general rule: flags are for one run, settings files are for a project. Anything a session depends on to be correct belongs in a file, and anything you would be annoyed to have to remember is exactly that. --mcp-config, --settings and --plugin-dir all have settings-file equivalents; use them.

The habit worth adding alongside it: on resuming a long session, glance at /mcp or /context before trusting the first answer. Both take a second and both show you what actually loaded — the same configuration assertion §13.3 makes a CI gate out of, done by eye.

Exercise 2.3 — Design a working rhythm. Describe how you would work through a two-day feature that touches four packages of a monorepo: when you plan, when you clear, when you branch, when you commit, and how you keep the sessions findable. Then name the thing about this rhythm that is easy to get wrong.

Solution

Start in plan mode, in the right directory. Two days across four packages is squarely in the territory where planning pays: multiple files, uncertain approach, and a wrong direction costs a day rather than an hour. Start Claude in the package where the work begins rather than at the repository root, so the relevant CLAUDE.md files load and less is cheap to reach by accident (§3.7). Explore first, ask for a plan, and open it with Ctrl+G to edit it — the plan is the cheapest artefact in the whole two days to get right.

Name the session from the plan. Accepting a plan generates a title automatically, but naming it yourself is better: claude -n export-pipeline or /rename export-pipeline, so claude --resume export-pipeline works from anywhere in the repository tomorrow.

One session per coherent chunk, cleared between them. Not one session for two days. When the schema work is done and the API work begins, /clear — the schema investigation is finished, and carrying it costs tokens on every remaining turn while competing with the API context. Name each: export-schema, export-api, export-ui. Three findable sessions beat one enormous one, and the transition is also a natural moment to commit.

Commit at every boundary, and before anything that generates files. Commits are the coarse undo and checkpoints are the fine one — and §2.5's limit means checkpointing does not track files written by shell commands, so a codegen step or a migration script leaves /rewind unable to restore a consistent tree. Commit first; it costs ten seconds.

Branch when there is a real fork in the road. "Should the export be streamed or batched?" is a /branch, not a debate: build both far enough to compare, then keep one. Two half-built branches you can read beat one argument you have to imagine.

Worktrees if two chunks proceed in parallel (§11.7), so file edits cannot collide. If the work is sequential, worktrees are overhead.

What is easy to get wrong: clearing too little, and too late. Everything above is easy to follow except the /clear, because a long session feels like accumulated value and clearing it feels like throwing that away. It is not — the value is in the code, the commits and the CLAUDE.md lines you added along the way, all of which survive. What the window holds is a record of how you got there, and past a certain length that record is actively harmful: it fills the budget, it competes with what is relevant now, and it makes compaction fire in the middle of tasks rather than between them (§3.5).

The tell that you have gone too long is when Claude starts forgetting things you established earlier. By then the fix costs a re-explanation, whereas clearing at the boundary would have cost nothing. The rhythm's whole discipline is in the transitions, and the transitions are the part nobody feels like doing.

SECTION 3

The Context Window

Section 1 said the model is stateless (it remembers nothing between requests) and that a conversation is a list of messages sent to it again in full on every turn. Section 2 showed the session as something you steer. This section is about the resource both of those use up. It is the one limit in Claude Code that never goes away: everything Claude knows on any given turn is in one window, and that window fills up. That window is called the context window.

The consequences are practical:

  • A window that is nearly full compacts: Claude Code replaces the older conversation with a summary, and a summary loses things.
  • A window holding a hundred thousand tokens of tool output (a token is roughly a short word or part of one) costs more per turn than one without, on every remaining turn, because all of it is sent again each time.
  • If your instructions are ninety thousand tokens back, they carry less weight than the thing Claude read two minutes ago.

Nearly every feature in the rest of this course exists to manage this. Skills load on demand, because otherwise their full text would sit in the window permanently. Subagents exist to keep large amounts of reading out of your window. MCP tool search delays loading tool descriptions (their schemas) for the same reason. Compaction, /clear, worktrees, forks: all of it is context management in different forms. Understanding the budget is what makes those features look like a system instead of a feature list.

3.1 What Is in the Window Before You Type

A fresh session is not empty. Before you type a single character, several things have already loaded, in a deliberate order:

System prompt
Core instructions for behaviour, tool use and response formatting, plus every tool definition. Always first. You never see it.
Auto memory
Claude's notes to itself from previous sessions — build commands it learned, patterns it noticed. The first 200 lines or 25KB, whichever comes first (§4.6).
Environment info
Working directory, platform, shell, OS version, and whether this is a git repository. Git branch, status and recent commits load as a separate block at the very end of the system prompt.
MCP tool names
Names only, by default. Full schemas stay deferred and arrive on demand through tool search (§10.9).
Skill descriptions
Every skill's name and description, within a budget of 1% of the window (§8.5). Bodies load only when used.
CLAUDE.md
Full content, every level of the hierarchy (§4). This is the one that loads in its entirety and stays.

Run /context at any point and you get this broken down live, by category, with suggestions for saving space. It also shows which CLAUDE.md and auto-memory files loaded. It is the first thing to run when a session feels heavy, and most people never run it at all.

The context cost of each mechanism is worth having in one table. Context cost (how much of the window something takes), not the price per token, is what every later decision trades against. Choosing between these mechanisms is most of the advice in §8 and §10, in short form:

Feature
When it loads
Context cost
CLAUDE.md
Session start
Every request, in full
Skills
Descriptions at start; body when used
Low — descriptions every request, body from first use onward
MCP servers
Tool names at start; schemas on demand
Low until a tool is used
Code intelligence
After edits, and on demand
Low, and it reduces file reads elsewhere
Subagents
When spawned
Isolated — only the summary returns
Hooks
On trigger
Zero, unless the hook returns additionalContext

Two rows carry most of the practical weight. CLAUDE.md is the only thing here that costs its full size on every request forever. That is why §4 insists on keeping it under about 200 lines. And hooks are free, which is a really underrated property. A PostToolUse formatter hook costs one process and zero tokens. The CLAUDE.md line asking for the same thing costs tokens on every request and works less reliably.

3.2 How It Fills

Then you start working, and four things add to the window at very different rates.

File reads are the big one, and their size varies a lot. A 400-line source file is a few thousand tokens. A lockfile or a generated API client is tens of thousands. Claude reading three files to answer a question is cheap. Claude searching a large repository by reading every possible match is not.

Tool output is the unpredictable one. A test suite's failure output, a build log, a git log over a busy month, a dump of a database schema: each is a single tool result that can cost more than an hour of conversation. A tool result stays in the window for the rest of the session, unless compaction clears it. This is exactly the kind of work §11 says to hand to a subagent.

Your conversation grows steadily and slowly. Prose is cheap. It is almost never the reason a window fills.

Loaded skills and path-scoped rules arrive during the session and stay. A skill's body enters as one message and stays for the whole session (§8.6). A rule with paths: frontmatter loads the first time Claude reads a file that matches it.

The imbalance is the lesson: the things that fill your window are rarely the things you typed. People try to manage context by writing shorter prompts, which is like managing a budget by using smaller envelopes. The levers that matter are what gets read and what gets delegated.

3.3 Compaction: What Survives, and What Does Not

When the window gets close to its limit, auto-compaction runs. Claude Code compacts automatically: it first clears older tool outputs, then summarises the conversation if that is not enough. Auto-compaction means a full window does not end your session. But the summary is lossy: it keeps less than the original. Knowing what survives compaction is the difference between a smooth compaction and losing the thread of a task.

Content
After compaction
System prompt and output style
Unchanged — never part of message history
Project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped rules
Re-injected from disk
Auto memory
Re-injected from disk
The plan you approved in plan mode
Re-injected from disk
Rules with paths: frontmatter
Reloaded as Claude reads matching files again
Nested CLAUDE.md in subdirectories
Reloaded as Claude reads files there again
Files Claude read or edited
Up to five re-read, most recently modified first
Invoked skill bodies
Re-injected, 5,000 tokens per skill, 25,000 total, oldest dropped first
Context a hook added earlier
Summarised away with the rest of the conversation
SessionStart hooks matching compact
Run again, and their output added

What survives compaction is not random. The table is most useful read as a design instruction, not just a reference. Anything re-injected from disk is durable; anything that lived only in the conversation is not. Re-injected means read again from its file after the summary. That one distinction explains four pieces of advice given elsewhere in this course that would otherwise look arbitrary:

Put standing rules in CLAUDE.md
It comes back after every compaction. A rule you stated in conversation on turn three does not.
Put the important part of a skill at the top
Truncation to 5,000 tokens keeps the start of the file, so the instructions that must survive belong before the reference material.
Drop paths: from a rule that must persist
A path-scoped rule reloads only when its trigger file is read again. If it must always apply, unscope it or move it to the project-root CLAUDE.md.
Use a SessionStart hook for refreshable facts
Matching the compact source, it runs again after compaction and re-adds the current branch, the ticket, the deploy target (§9.7).

Two details catch people out. First, a re-read file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference without its content, shown as Referenced file rather than Read, though the rules attached to it still reload. Second, a single file or tool output can be so large that the context fills up again straight after each summary. Claude Code then stops auto-compacting after a few attempts and shows a thrashing error instead of looping forever. That error means "something enormous is being re-read". The fix is to stop reading it, not to compact harder.

3.4 Acting Before the Automatic Pass

Automatic compaction has to guess what mattered. You almost always know better, and there are five ways to say so.

/compact focus on the auth bug fix

/compact with instructions keeps what you name instead of what the summariser guesses. Run it at a natural break between tasks rather than letting it fire in the middle of one. That is the most valuable context habit there is, because the summary is written when the task is finished rather than half done.

/rewind can summarise part of the conversation. Select a message and choose Summarize from here or Summarize up to here. It is the right tool when one stretch of the session was expensive and the rest was not.

/autocompact moves the auto-compaction trigger. /autocompact 500k sets how full the window gets before the automatic pass runs. It is useful when you would rather compact early and often than once, late, in the middle of something.

/clear between unrelated tasks is the one people forget. Old conversation crowds out the files you need next, and costs tokens on every message until it is summarised away. If you switch from a bug fix to a new feature in the same window, you pay for the bug fix on every remaining turn of the feature.

Delegate large reads to a subagent (§11.1), so the file contents stay in its window rather than yours.

One item that surprises people when they first read /usage is background token usage: the requests Claude Code makes outside your conversation. Session titles, the summary request behind a compaction, subagent runs and workflow agents are each a real request against your account. Together they explain why a session's reported total can be higher than the visible conversation seems to justify. Background token usage is not waste (a subagent's tokens are tokens you did not spend in your own window), but it is worth recognising rather than mistaking for a billing error.

Sometimes the real problem is that you need a bigger window, not a shorter conversation. Fable 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a one-million-token context window. Sonnet 5 runs at 1M with no special version to pick; the others use a [1m] model variant. Compaction works the same way at the larger limit. It just happens later.

3.5 Why Full Is Worse Than Expensive

The obvious cost of a full window is money and waiting time. Every request carries everything, so a 150,000-token conversation costs 150,000 tokens of input per turn, even when your message was four words.

The less obvious cost is quality, and it is the one that should change how you work. Instructions from early in a long conversation carry less weight than recent content. A convention you stated on turn two has to compete, ninety thousand tokens later, with a file Claude just read that does it differently. Nothing has gone wrong. The early instruction is simply one signal among a great many now.

Two habits follow, and they are the practical core of this section.

Put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md rather than in conversation history — not because CLAUDE.md is better prose, but because it sits in a layer that is re-injected on every compaction and re-read on every request, while a sentence you typed on turn two decays. And clear between tasks rather than carrying a finished problem into a new one. Both are about keeping the ratio of relevant to irrelevant content high, which is a better description of "context management" than any token count.

3.6 Prompt Caching: Why the Same Work Costs Different Amounts

Claude Code uses a cache automatically. You would never need to think about it, except that a handful of ordinary actions make the next turn slow and expensive. Understanding why takes one idea.

Every request sends the whole context again. Most of it is identical to the request before. So the API matches the start of each request, the prefix, against content it recently processed. It reads the matching part from the cache at a much lower price, and fully processes only what changed. The match is exact, and there is no per-file or per-segment caching: a change anywhere in the prefix means everything after it is processed again.

So Claude Code orders each request with the parts that rarely change first:

Layer
Content
Changes when
System prompt
Core instructions, tool definitions, output style
The set of loaded tool definitions changes, or Claude Code is upgraded
Project context
CLAUDE.md, auto memory, unscoped rules
Session start, or after /clear or /compact
Conversation
Your messages, Claude's responses, tool results
Every turn

A change in the conversation layer leaves the two layers above it cached. A change to the system prompt invalidates everything, because all later content now sits behind a different prefix. Two things that are not prompt text at all are also part of the cache key: the model and the effort level. Each has its own cache.

That single rule produces the whole list of what costs you a full-price turn:

Switching models
Every model has its own cache, so a switch is a total cache invalidation: the next request reads the entire history uncached even though the content is identical. opusplan makes every plan-mode toggle a model switch.
Changing effort level
Keyed like the model. A change that resolves to the level already in effect keeps the cache.
Turning on fast mode
Adds a header that is part of the cache key. Costs once per conversation — turning it off and on again later keeps the cache.
Connecting/disconnecting an MCP server
Only when its tools are in the prefix. With tool search on — the default — a server connecting or changing its tool list merely appends.
Denying an entire tool
