A bare-name deny removes the tool from the system prompt, so it is a cache invalidation. A scoped deny like Bash(rm *) is not, because it is checked at call time rather than changing the request.
Compacting
By design: the new history is shorter and shares no prefix with the old one.
Upgrading Claude Code
A new version usually changes the system prompt or tool definitions.

And the opposite list: things that feel as if they should invalidate the cache and do not, because they add to the end rather than change what is already there:

Editing files in your repository
File contents enter context only when read. An edit appends a <system-reminder> that the file changed.
Invoking skills and commands
They inject instructions as user messages at the point of invocation. Nothing earlier changes.
Changing permission mode
Modes do not change the system prompt or tool definitions. (Except opusplan, per above.)
/recap
Appends a summary as command output rather than replacing history — which is the whole difference from /compact, and the reason /recap is free where compaction is not.
/rewind
Truncates back to a prefix that is already cached, so it is cheaper than compaction as a way to abandon a path.

Two of those entries are the most useful facts in this subsection. Editing CLAUDE.md mid-session keeps the cache and also does not apply. The file was read once at the start of the session and is held in memory, and your edit loads at the next /clear, /compact or restart. The same is true of the output style. This is why "I changed CLAUDE.md and Claude ignored it" is a question about how the tool works, not a bug: both facts have the same cause.

And /rewind is cheaper than /compact for leaving a path you regret. Rewinding cuts the conversation back to a prefix the cache was built from. Compacting builds a new one. If you have gone down a road you want to leave entirely, rewind rather than summarise.

Lifetime, and where it lives

Cached prefixes expire when unused, and each cache hit resets the timer. The time a cached entry lives is called its TTL (time to live). The API offers a five-minute TTL, and a one-hour TTL that charges more for cache writes. Claude Code sorts every request into one of two groups:

Bucket
Claude subscription, in plan
Usage credits, API key, cloud
Main conversation
interactive turns, -p, SDK
One hour
Five minutes
Everything else
subagents, workflows, teammates, forks, compaction
Five minutes
(some server-controlled helpers get an hour)
Five minutes

promptCacheTtl and subagentPromptCacheTtl set them explicitly, each taking 5m or 1h. If you sign in with an API key, promptCacheTtl: "1h" is often the most valuable setting in this section for a session you leave and come back to. Note also that going over your plan's usage limit drops the main conversation to the cheaper five-minute TTL. That is a likely explanation for a session that suddenly feels slower with no change on your side.

The cache is shared more narrowly than you would guess: effectively one machine and one directory, because the system prompt includes the working directory, platform, shell, OS version and memory paths. Two worktrees of the same repository cannot use each other's cache. Parallel sessions in the same directory do share it.

The one habit worth taking from all of this: pick your model and effort level at the top of a session, and save /compact for breaks between tasks. Every mid-task change to the top two layers costs one full re-read of everything you have accumulated, and that cost grows with the session — which is why a model switch feels free at turn three and expensive at turn eighty.

Note where the cache physically lives, because it changes what is true.

  • With an API key, a Claude subscription or Claude Platform on AWS, it is on Anthropic's infrastructure.
  • On Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform, it is on your provider's.
  • But behind a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or an LLM gateway it is wherever your requests are forwarded, and whether caching works at all depends on the gateway.

(A gateway is a proxy your company puts between you and the model provider.) A gateway that drops the cache markers can leave a whole conversation billed as uncached input on every turn. Know that before you diagnose a cost spike as people using it too much.

3.7 Large Codebases

Everything above applies to a repository of any size. A monorepo (one repository holding many packages) adds a problem of its own: there is more material than could ever fit, so the question stops being "what do I remove" and becomes "what do I let Claude see at all".

Here are five techniques, roughly in order of how much they help. Notice that several of them narrow what Claude can reach rather than widening it. Extra directories granted with --add-dir are useful; extra directories granted by starting at the repository root usually are not:

Start Claude in the right place
The working directory decides which CLAUDE.md files load and what is cheap to reach. Starting in packages/api rather than the repository root is often the entire fix.
Layer CLAUDE.md by directory
A short root file with what is true everywhere; a per-package file with what is true there. Nested files load as Claude reads files in that directory (§4.3), so you pay for each only when it is relevant.
Reduce what Claude reads
Delegate searches to Explore (§11.1), and make the search targeted. "Find the callers of X" is a subagent task; reading the directory to find out is not.
Add per-directory skills
A package's own conventions live in packages/web/.claude/skills/ and become available when Claude touches that package (§8.2).
Scope worktrees and file access
A worktree per workstream (§11.7), and additional directories granted deliberately rather than by starting at the root.

Layering eventually stops scaling: the same convention ends up repeated in nine package-level files. That is the sign to move it into one skill that every package refers to, instead of copying it again. The rule applies generally: duplication across CLAUDE.md files is a sign the material wanted to be a skill.

3.8 The Failure Patterns, by Name

Sections 3.1 to 3.7 explained how the window works. This last subsection boils it down to practice: five failure patterns from Anthropic's best-practices guide, each with a name, a symptom you can recognise and a fix, plus two underlying effects that explain why they are failures at all. Naming them matters, because a pattern you can name is one you notice while it is happening, and all of these are usually noticed late.

Five patterns, by name: the kitchen sink session, correcting over and over, the over-specified CLAUDE.md, the trust-then-verify gap, unscoped investigation

Pattern
What it looks like
The fix
The kitchen sink session
One task, then something unrelated, then back to the first. The window holds three tasks' worth of material.
/clear between unrelated tasks.
Correcting over and over
Claude gets it wrong, you correct it, it is still wrong, you correct again. The window is full of failed attempts.
After two failed corrections, /clear and write a better first prompt that includes what you learned.
The over-specified CLAUDE.md
A file so long that important rules are lost in it, and half are ignored.
Prune ruthlessly. If Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it, or turn it into a hook.
The trust-then-verify gap
A plausible implementation that does not handle edge cases, accepted because it looks right.
Always provide verification: tests, scripts, screenshots. "If you can't verify it, don't ship it."
The infinite exploration
"Investigate X" with no scope. Claude reads hundreds of files and fills the window.
Scope the investigation narrowly, or use subagents so the reading stays out of your main context.

The guide says two slightly different things about the second pattern, and it is better to say so than to smooth it over. The failure-patterns list says to clear after two failed corrections. The session-management advice says to clear if you have corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue. Read them together as two or three, not as a difference worth arguing about. The point is the cut-off: a failed approach is not harmless history, and a clean session with a better prompt "almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections".

Context rot and topic switching

Two effects sit underneath the table.

The first is the one §3.5 described and this section names: context rot. Claude does not fail all at once when the window fills. Quality declines gradually as the share of relevant material falls, and instructions from early in a long conversation "carry less weight than recent content". A convention stated on turn two has to compete, ninety thousand tokens later, with a file Claude read recently that does the opposite.

The second is topic switching. When unrelated pieces of work are mixed in one session, material from the other task is still in the window. It is still being weighed, and it pulls the current task towards it.

Neither is a bug. Both follow from the window being a single shared workspace. The remedies are the ones already in the table, plus one the guide adds for questions that do not need to stay: /btw, whose answer "never enters conversation history", so a side question does not grow the context.

Both effects cost tokens as well as quality, and the cost is easy to compute, because every turn sends the history again (§3.2). The model below counts how many tokens are processed in total for the same three tasks done two ways, with numbers chosen for illustration:

def tokens_processed(turns):
    """Every turn resends the whole history, so total work is the running sum of history sizes."""
    history, total = 0, 0
    for added in turns:
        history += added
        total += history
    return total

# Three unrelated tasks of 8 turns each; every turn adds about 3,000 tokens (a message, a file read, a reply).
task = [3_000] * 8
kitchen_sink = tokens_processed(task * 3)                       # one session, tasks interleaved
cleared = sum(tokens_processed(task) for _ in range(3))         # /clear between tasks
print(f'one session for three tasks : {kitchen_sink:>9,} tokens processed')
print(f'/clear between the tasks    : {cleared:>9,} tokens processed  ({kitchen_sink / cleared:.1f}x less)')

# Correcting over and over: attempt 1 is 5,000 tokens; each correction adds a failed attempt (4,000) and your note (500).
def with_corrections(n_corrections):
    history, total = 5_000, 5_000
    for _ in range(n_corrections):
        history += 4_500
        total += history
    return total, history

cluttered_total, cluttered_window = with_corrections(3)
partial_total, _ = with_corrections(2)
restart_total = partial_total + 6_000                           # two failed corrections, then /clear and one better prompt (6,000 tokens)
print(f'\nfour tries in one cluttered session : {cluttered_total:>7,} tokens processed, ending with a {cluttered_window:,}-token window')
print(f'two corrections, then clear + retry : {restart_total:>7,} tokens processed, ending with a 6,000-token window')

one session for three tasks :   900,000 tokens processed
/clear between the tasks    :   324,000 tokens processed  (2.8x less)

four tries in one cluttered session :  47,000 tokens processed, ending with a 18,500-token window
two corrections, then clear + retry :  34,500 tokens processed, ending with a 6,000-token window

Two caveats keep this honest. Prompt caching (§3.6) makes resent history much cheaper than new input, so the gap in token cost is smaller than the gap in token count. And the numbers are illustrative inputs, not measurements of a real session. Neither changes the argument, because the argument was never really about money. The quadratic growth (the total grows with the square of the conversation length) stands in for what really matters: the composition of the window. The kitchen-sink session (everything in one conversation) ends with two-thirds of its history irrelevant to the task at hand. The cluttered correcting session ends with a window whose largest occupants are things that did not work.

The routine that follows from all five patterns is short:

  • Name the task when you start it.
  • Clear when it ends.
  • Give it a check before it starts.
  • Keep CLAUDE.md to what Claude cannot work out for itself.
  • When you catch yourself typing the same correction a second time, stop and decide whether the fix is a better prompt, a line in CLAUDE.md, or a hook. §16.8 shows how to make that decision deliberately.

Exercises

Exercise 3.1 — Diagnose the heavy session. A colleague says Claude "gets worse after about an hour" on their monorepo: slower replies, forgetting conventions stated earlier, and re-reading files it already read. Name the four most likely causes, say which single command you would run first, and give the order you would address them.

Solution

Run /context first. It breaks the window down by category with the actual numbers, and it distinguishes between the four causes below in one screen. Everything else is a guess until you have seen it.

One: the window is full and compacting repeatedly. "Forgetting conventions stated earlier" is the signature — a rule stated in conversation is summarised away, while one in CLAUDE.md is re-injected from disk. "Re-reading files it already read" is the same event from the other side: compaction re-reads at most five files, most recently modified first, so the sixth is gone. Fix: move standing rules from conversation into CLAUDE.md, and /clear between unrelated tasks instead of carrying finished work forward.

Two: file reads dominate, which is the usual monorepo cause. /context will show this immediately as a large tool-output or file-read share. Fix: start Claude in the relevant package rather than the repository root, and delegate searches to Explore so the candidates it reads land in its window rather than yours.

Three: the cache keeps being invalidated. "Slower replies" without a corresponding rise in window size points here. The usual culprits are mid-session model or effort switches — and opusplan, which makes every plan-mode toggle a model switch, so a colleague who cycles in and out of plan mode is paying for a full re-read each time. Fix: pick model and effort at the top of the session; if they use opusplan, that trade is now explicit rather than invisible.

Four: an oversized CLAUDE.md or skill listing. Both are permanently resident and both show up as their own rows in /context. A 900-line CLAUDE.md costs its full size on every request forever. Fix: /doctor proposes trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md; move reference material to skills, which cost only their description until used.

The order: cheapest and most reversible first. /clear between tasks (free, immediate), then start in the right directory (free), then move rules into CLAUDE.md and reference material out of it (an afternoon), then fix the model-switching habit (a conversation). Only after all four would I reach for a 1M-token model, because a bigger window makes the same problems arrive later rather than making them go away.

Exercise 3.2 — Predict the cache. For each action mid-session, say whether the next request re-reads the whole conversation, and why: (a) editing src/auth.ts; (b) editing CLAUDE.md; (c) /model opus; (d) adding "deny": ["WebFetch"] in /permissions; (e) adding "deny": ["Bash(rm *)"]; (f) /rewind to turn 12; (g) an MCP server dropping and reconnecting, with tool search on.

Solution

(a) No. File contents enter context only when Claude reads them, and a read is an append. Editing the file afterwards does not retroactively change that earlier message — Claude Code appends a <system-reminder> noting the change, and Claude re-reads if it needs to.

(b) No, and the edit also does not apply. Project-root and user CLAUDE.md are read once at session start and held in memory. The cache survives because nothing in the request changed — which is precisely why your edit has no effect until the next /clear, /compact or restart. Two facts with one cause, and the source of the most common "Claude ignored my CLAUDE.md" report.

(c) Yes, completely. Each model has its own cache, so the next request reads the entire history uncached even though the content is byte-identical. This is the most expensive item on the list and the one that feels the most free.

(d) Yes. A bare-name deny removes the tool from Claude's context entirely, and built-in tool definitions live in the system prompt layer — so everything behind them is now behind a different prefix.

(e) No. A scoped rule does not change which tools Claude sees; it is evaluated when Claude attempts the call. The prefix is untouched. The contrast with (d) is the clearest illustration in this section of why the layer a change lands in matters more than how significant the change feels.

(f) No — and it hits an earlier cache entry. Rewinding truncates back to history the cache was already built from, with the system prompt and project context layers unchanged. Every turn since then read through that prefix, which kept the entry warm. This is why rewinding beats compacting for abandoning a path: one reuses a prefix, the other builds a new one.

(g) No, with tool search on. Deferred tools are not in the cached prefix at all, so a server connecting, disconnecting or changing its tool list only appends. With tool search off it would be a full invalidation — and since a stdio process exiting or an HTTP session expiring can happen with no action from you, that is a real source of mystery slow turns in a gateway setup where tool search is unavailable.

The rule that generates all seven: ask which layer the change lands in. Conversation-layer changes append and cost nothing extra. System-prompt changes — tool definitions, model, effort, the fast-mode header, a Claude Code upgrade — invalidate everything after them.

Exercise 3.3 — Design for compaction. You are setting up a project where sessions routinely run three or four hours. Design the configuration so that the things that matter survive compaction, and name the one thing your design cannot protect.

Solution

Start from the table in §3.3: anything re-injected from disk is durable; anything that lived only in the conversation is not. That is the whole design constraint.

Standing rules go in the project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped. Re-injected on every compaction. Keep it short — under about 200 lines — because it is also the only thing here paying its full cost on every request forever. Path-scoped rules are excellent for per-directory conventions and are explicitly not durable: they reload only when a matching file is read again. If a rule must always apply, drop its paths: frontmatter or move it to the root file.

Volatile facts go in a SessionStart hook matching the compact source. Branch, ticket, deploy target, which migration is pending — all re-run after compaction and re-added, which is the only mechanism here that produces current information rather than a replay. Note the trap from §9.7 in the other direction: additionalContext injected at PostToolUse is replayed verbatim on resume, so a timestamp put there goes stale.

Procedures go in skills, with the important instructions at the top. Skill bodies are re-injected after compaction but truncated to 5,000 tokens each within a 25,000-token total, oldest dropped first, keeping the start of each file. So a long SKILL.md must lead with what must survive, and a session that invoked eight skills will lose the early ones entirely. Re-invoke a skill that still matters after a compaction.

Mandatory steps go in hooks. Free in context, and unaffected by compaction entirely, because they do not live in the window at all. This is the strongest form of "surviving compaction": not being subject to it.

Working habits: /compact with a focus at natural breaks rather than letting it fire mid-task, /clear when the task genuinely changes, and /autocompact set low enough that compaction happens while a task is finished rather than half-done.

What the design cannot protect: the reasoning. Every mechanism above restores inputs — rules, files, procedures, facts. None of them restores the chain of thought that got you to the current state: the three approaches you rejected, why the obvious fix does not work, what the failing test actually turned out to mean. That lives only in the conversation, and the summary compresses it to a few lines chosen by a model that did not do the work.

The practical answer is to write conclusions down as you reach them — into the plan file, a scratch document, or the commit message — so that the durable-input machinery has something to restore. A session that has compacted twice has effectively read a summary of its own history, and if the important conclusion is not in a file, it is not in the session either. That is also the honest argument for /clear over letting a window run for four hours: a fresh session with a written-up state beats a compacted one with a summary of it.

SECTION 4

Memory and Project Instructions

Every session begins with an empty context window. Whatever you explained yesterday is gone: that this repository uses pnpm, that migrations must be reversible, that the integration tests need a running Postgres. The model has no way to know any of it. Explaining things again is the most common cost of working with an agent, and it is entirely avoidable.

Two mechanisms carry knowledge from one session to the next, and they split the work cleanly:

CLAUDE.md
Instructions you write. Coding standards, build commands, architecture, "always do X" rules. Project, user or organisation scope, shared through version control.
Auto memory
Notes Claude writes itself. Your preferences, corrections you have given, project context it could not derive from the code. Per repository, machine-local.

Both load at the start of every conversation. Both also have the same crucial limitation. It is stated here once, because everything in this section depends on it:

Claude treats memory as context, not as enforced configuration. A line in CLAUDE.md is a strong, permanent, well-placed suggestion. It is not a rule the system enforces, and on a long turn with a lot of competing signal it can lose. To make something happen regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook (§9.1) or a permission rule (§5.1). The more specific and concise the instruction, the more consistently it is followed — but "more consistently" is the honest ceiling.

4.1 What Belongs in CLAUDE.md

The test is not "is this true?", since most things are. The test is "would I otherwise re-explain this?" Four signals say yes:

A repeated mistake
Claude makes the same mistake a second time. Once is noise; twice is a missing instruction.
A review comment
Code review catches something Claude should have known about this codebase. The reviewer just wrote your CLAUDE.md line for you.
A repeated correction
You type the same clarification you typed last session. The strongest signal of the four, and the easiest to ignore.
The new-teammate test
A new hire would need the same context to be productive. If the answer is yes, it belongs in a file either way.

What does not belong matters just as much, because CLAUDE.md is the one mechanism in this course that costs its full size on every request, forever (§3.1). Two kinds of content should move elsewhere as soon as you notice them:

A multi-step procedure is a skill (§8.1). Twelve lines about how to cut a release cost tokens on every turn that is not a release. Move them into a skill and their cost drops to a one-line description until they are needed.

Anything that only matters in part of the codebase is a path-scoped rule (§4.4): a rule that loads only for certain files. A frontend convention loaded during backend work is not just wasted context. It is noise competing with the instructions that do apply.

Writing instructions that are followed

Because these files are context rather than configuration, how you write them changes how reliably Claude follows them.

Size
Target under 200 lines per file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence. The second half of that sentence is the one people miss: a 900-line CLAUDE.md is worse than a 150-line one at the same job, not merely more expensive.
Structure
Headers and bullets, not paragraphs. Claude scans structure the way a reader does; organised sections are followed more reliably than dense prose.
Specificity
Write what can be verified. "Use 2-space indentation", not "format code properly". "Run npm test before committing", not "test your changes". "API handlers live in src/api/handlers/", not "keep files organised".
Consistency
Contradictions are resolved arbitrarily. If two rules conflict — across the root file, a nested one and .claude/rules/ — Claude may pick either. Review periodically and delete what is stale.

/init generates a starting file by analysing the codebase: build commands, test instructions, conventions it found. If a CLAUDE.md already exists, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting it. It is a good first draft and a bad final one, because what it can discover is, by definition, what Claude could have discovered anyway. The value you add is the part it could not infer: why the obvious approach does not work here, which of two similar directories is the real one, what broke last time.

4.2 The Four Locations

CLAUDE.md can live in four places. Here they are in the order they load, from the broadest to the most specific:

Scope
Location
For
Managed policy
/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md on Linux/WSL; the equivalents on macOS and Windows
Company standards, security policy, compliance. Everyone in the organisation.
User
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
Your preferences across all projects. Just you.
Project
./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md
Architecture, standards, workflows. The team, via version control.
Local
./CLAUDE.local.md
Your sandbox URLs, preferred test data. Gitignore it.

That table is the memory hierarchy. The one thing to remember about the memory hierarchy is that all discovered files are concatenated rather than overriding each other. Concatenated means joined end to end: every file is read, and none replaces another. This is the opposite of settings precedence (§6.2), where one value wins. Keep the memory hierarchy and settings precedence separate in your head: there is no "winner" among CLAUDE.md files, only an order. Content is ordered from the filesystem root down to your working directory, so instructions closer to where you launched Claude are read last. Within each directory, CLAUDE.local.md is added after CLAUDE.md, which makes your personal notes the last thing read at that level.

When two joined files contradict each other, which one Claude follows is unpredictable, so "later wins" is not a mechanism you should rely on. Do not write a project file that contradicts a user file and expect the project one to take effect. Remove the conflict instead.

4.3 Hierarchy and Loading

Files above your working directory load at launch. Files below it load on demand, when Claude reads a file in that subdirectory. Start Claude in foo/bar/ and you get foo/CLAUDE.md and foo/bar/CLAUDE.md immediately, while foo/bar/baz/CLAUDE.md waits until Claude touches something in baz/.

That lazy loading is what makes a monorepo workable (§3.7): a hundred package-level files cost nothing until their package is involved. It also explains a detail of compaction from §3.3. Nested files live in the message history, not in the project-context layer, so compaction summarises them away, and they reload only when the file that triggered them is read again.

A CLAUDE.md import, written @path/to/import, pulls in another file. It is expanded at launch, together with the CLAUDE.md that refers to it:

See @README for project overview and @package.json for available npm commands.

# Additional Instructions

- git workflow @docs/git-instructions.md

Relative paths are resolved relative to the file containing the import, not the working directory. Imports can be nested four levels deep. Import parsing skips code spans and fenced blocks, so writing `@README` in backticks mentions the path without importing it. That is how you refer to a file in prose without pulling its contents into every request.

An import is not free. Imported files "still load and enter the context window at launch" — the mechanism is organisational, not a cost saving. Splitting a 600-line CLAUDE.md into six imported files makes it easier to maintain and costs exactly the same on every request. If the goal is to reduce cost, the answer is a skill or a path-scoped rule, not an import.

Some imports are external: a CLAUDE.md import in a project-level file whose path leads outside the working directory, for example to a file in your home directory. The first time Claude Code sees one, it shows an approval dialog listing the files. If you decline, the imports stay disabled and the dialog does not come back. That check exists for the same reason as §5.6's: a project file arrives with the repository, and a repository should not be able to quietly pull in files from your home directory. Imports in user-scope files load without the dialog, because you wrote them.

That external-import mechanism has one good use worth knowing. A gitignored CLAUDE.local.md exists only in the worktree where you created it, which is awkward once you work across several worktrees (§11.7). Importing from your home directory shares your personal instructions across all of them:

# Individual Preferences

- @~/.claude/my-project-instructions.md

AGENTS.md

Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md. If your repository already uses AGENTS.md for other coding agents, the clean answer is a CLAUDE.md that imports it. Both tools then read one source, and you can add Claude-specific material below the import:

@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code

Use plan mode for changes under `src/billing/`.

A symlink also works when you need nothing extra:

ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md

On Windows, creating a symlink needs Administrator rights or Developer Mode, so prefer the import there. /init also reads Cursor and Copilot rule files and folds the relevant parts into what it generates. /import brings another agent's whole configuration across in one go: instruction files, MCP servers, commands, subagents and skills.

One small but really useful detail: block-level HTML comments are stripped before the content reaches Claude. <!-- maintainer notes --> costs no context and is invisible to the model. That makes it the right place for a note explaining why a rule is there, which would otherwise be either missing or expensive.

The .claude directory

Almost everything in this course ends up in one place, so it is worth seeing all of it once. The .claude directory holds CLAUDE.md, settings.json and settings.local.json, rules/, skills/, commands/, agents/, hooks/, and worktrees/. The project's half sits in the repository. Your half sits in ~/.claude, along with session transcripts, plugins and auto memory.

The distinction that matters is which parts are configuration you commit and which are application data. A .claude directory in a repository is reviewed, versioned and shared. A .claude directory in your home is local to your machine and partly disposable. Some of it is cleaned up automatically by the retention sweep, some is kept until you delete it, and some is stored as plain, unencrypted text. §15.7 covers which is which, and an organisation with a data policy should read that list rather than guess.

4.4 Rules: Modular, and Conditionally Loaded

.claude/rules/ holds instructions as separate topic files, discovered recursively:

your-project/
├── .claude/
│   ├── CLAUDE.md          # Main project instructions
│   └── rules/
│       ├── code-style.md  # Code style guidelines
│       ├── testing.md     # Testing conventions
│       └── security.md    # Security requirements

A rule without paths frontmatter loads at launch with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md. So splitting a large CLAUDE.md into unscoped rules is the same trade as imports: tidier, not cheaper. The interesting version is a rule with paths:

---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---

# API Development Rules

- All API endpoints must include input validation
- Use the standard error response format
- Include OpenAPI documentation comments

That rule loads only when Claude reads a matching file. In a repository with separate frontend, backend and infrastructure conventions, this is the difference between three sets of rules competing for attention on every turn, and each set arriving only when it is relevant.

Multiple patterns and brace expansion work:

---
paths:
  - "src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"
  - "lib/**/*.ts"
  - "tests/**/*.test.ts"
---

There are two mechanical limits.

  • Brace groups multiply: {a,b}/{c,d}/*.{ts,tsx} expands to eight patterns, and all the patterns in a rule's paths list share a budget of 1,000 expanded patterns. A pattern that would go over the budget is used unexpanded, and its literal braces then match nothing: the rule silently does nothing for it.
  • Glob syntax reads [ as the start of a bracket expression, so photos [2024/** is invalid and matches nothing. Escape it as photos \[2024/**.

In both cases the rule's other patterns keep working. That makes a partly broken rule harder to notice than a fully broken one.

Rules directories support symlinks, which are the cleanest way to share one rule set across projects without a plugin:

ln -s ~/shared-claude-rules .claude/rules/shared
ln -s ~/company-standards/security.md .claude/rules/security.md

And ~/.claude/rules/ holds personal rules that apply to every project on your machine.

Rules versus skills, in one line. A rule loads every session, or whenever a matching file is read — it is context that applies. A skill loads when invoked or when Claude judges it relevant — it is a procedure you run. Instructions that should shape work you did not ask about are rules; instructions that are a task are skills.

4.5 Auto Memory

Auto memory is the half you do not write. As Claude works, it saves notes for itself, tagged by type:

user
Your role, expertise and working preferences. That you want terse answers, that you are new to this codebase, that you prefer to see the plan first.
feedback
Corrections you gave, and approaches you confirmed. The most valuable of the four, because it captures the thing you would otherwise say again.
project
Ongoing work, deadlines and decisions Claude cannot derive from the code or the git history.
reference
Where information lives outside the project — an issue tracker, a dashboard, a runbook.

What it deliberately skips tells you as much as what it saves. It skips anything derivable from the codebase (architecture, file paths, how a bug was fixed), and anything your CLAUDE.md already says. Both exclusions follow from the same principle. A memory is only worth its context cost if it could not be recovered by reading the code, and if it is not already loaded by a mechanism you control.

It also does not save something every session. Claude decides what is worth remembering by asking whether it would help a future conversation, so an uneventful session leaves no trace.

Where it lives, and how much loads

Each project gets ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/. The directory is chosen by the git repository, so all worktrees and subdirectories of one repository share it:

~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/
├── MEMORY.md            # Index, one line per memory, loaded into every session
├── user_role.md         # One memory
├── feedback_testing.md  # One memory
└── ...

The structure uses the same progressive-disclosure idea as skills: load a short index first, and the detail only when needed. Only MEMORY.md loads at session start, up to its first 200 lines or 25KB, whichever comes first. The topic files are read on demand, with ordinary file tools, when Claude needs them. So the standing cost is one index line per memory, and the detail is free until it is relevant.

Claude Code actively enforces that budget. After each write it measures the file:

  • near a limit, it reminds Claude to shorten it: one line per entry, detail into topic files, merge or drop out-of-date entries;
  • over a limit, the write succeeds, but Claude Code returns an error telling Claude to rewrite the index, because everything past the limit is dropped at the next load.

That is worth knowing because otherwise the failure is invisible. A memory index that quietly grew past 200 lines has memories that simply never load.

A few properties matter in practice:

  • Auto memory is machine-local: it is not shared across machines or cloud environments.
  • It is excluded from the retention sweep that deletes old transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays, so memories stay until you or Claude edit them.
  • It is not loaded into subagents, except a fork, which inherits the parent conversation. A subagent can have its own memory directory through the memory frontmatter field (§11.1).
  • When Claude writes a memory file that already has YAML frontmatter, Claude Code adds a modified timestamp, so both you and Claude can tell how current a fact is.

/memory opens both systems for viewing and editing, and it is where the auto-memory switch lives. Turn auto memory off for one project with "autoMemoryEnabled": false, everywhere with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1, or move the directory with autoMemoryDirectory:

{
  "autoMemoryEnabled": false
}
Audit it occasionally, and treat what it records as evidence. A memory reflects what was true when it was written — a preference you have since changed, a deadline that has passed, a decision that was reversed. Reading through /memory takes two minutes and does two things: it removes stale facts, and it shows you which corrections you have been repeating often enough that Claude decided to write them down. That second one is a very direct list of what your CLAUDE.md is missing.

4.6 When Claude Ignores Your CLAUDE.md

Four causes, in the order to check them.

One: you edited it mid-session. The project-root and user CLAUDE.md files are read once at session start and kept in memory. An edit during the session does not invalidate the prompt cache (§3.6), and it also does not apply. Claude keeps working with the version loaded at startup, and yours arrives at the next /clear, /compact or restart. One cause, two symptoms, and by far the most common explanation. (Nested files and path-scoped rules load later, so editing one before it loads does take effect.)

Two: the file did not load at all. Run /context and look under Memory files. A file in a directory that is not on the path from the filesystem root down to your working directory is simply not there. That often surprises people who start Claude in a subdirectory of a monorepo, or whose file is in .claude/CLAUDE.md in one package while they launched in another.

Three: it is too large, or it contradicts itself. Both make Claude follow it less reliably, and both are found by reading the file, not with any tool. /doctor suggests cuts for a checked-in CLAUDE.md and tells you if it has grown past a reasonable size. When one rule competes with another, which one wins is unpredictable, and it will not be the same each time.

Four: the instruction lost to more recent context. This is the §3.5 problem. At ninety thousand tokens, an instruction loaded at startup competes with everything Claude has read since. CLAUDE.md is re-injected after compaction, which helps, but that does not make an instruction weigh more than a file Claude read a minute ago.

And the answer when the instruction genuinely must hold: stop using memory for it. A rule that matters enough to be frustrated about belongs in a permission deny rule (§5.1) or a hook (§9.1). The three mechanisms form a ladder, and knowing which rung you are on is most of using them well:

CLAUDE.md
Usually followed. Cheap, easy to write, applies to judgement as well as mechanics. The right default, and the right answer for anything a human will notice if it is missed.
Permission rule
Always enforced, for anything expressible as a tool and a pattern. Free, and it makes the property true rather than likely.
Hook
Always runs, for anything that needs computing. Costs a process, and it is the only one of the three that can react to what actually happened.

Exercises

Exercise 4.1 — Sort the material. A team is setting up a monorepo with a Python API, a React frontend and Terraform infrastructure. For each item, say where it goes and why: (a) "this repo uses uv, not pip"; (b) "React components go in src/components/, one per file"; (c) "never run terraform apply without a plan file"; (d) "the staging database is reset every night at 02:00 UTC, so a failing integration test in the morning is probably that"; (e) a 30-line procedure for adding a new API endpoint.

Solution

(a) Root CLAUDE.md. One line, true everywhere in the repository, relevant on almost every turn, and getting it wrong produces a broken lockfile every time. This is the shape CLAUDE.md exists for.

(b) A path-scoped rule, paths: ["src/components/**/*.tsx"] — or a nested CLAUDE.md in the frontend package, which loads when Claude reads files there. Either keeps a frontend convention out of context during Terraform work. The rule is the better choice if the frontend has several such conventions, since .claude/rules/ keeps them as separate topic files.

(c) A permission rule, not memory. "deny": ["Bash(terraform apply -auto-approve*)"] plus an ask on Bash(terraform apply *). This is the §4.6 ladder: the instruction could go in CLAUDE.md and would usually be followed, but "usually" is the wrong target for an unplanned infrastructure apply. Put the sentence in CLAUDE.md too, so Claude understands the rule rather than merely hitting it — the explanation belongs where the reader is, the enforcement where it cannot be argued with.

(d) Auto memory would record this on its own — it is exactly the project type: ongoing context that cannot be derived from the code or git history. Writing it into CLAUDE.md is also reasonable if the team all need it, and the deciding question is whether it is a fact about the project (CLAUDE.md, shared) or about your working context (auto memory, machine-local). The nightly reset is a project fact, so CLAUDE.md — one line, under "Environments".

(e) A skill. Thirty lines used a few times a month should not be resident on every request. As a skill it costs a description until someone types /new-endpoint or asks about adding an endpoint. Add paths or a targeted description so it surfaces during API work.

The sorting principle: frequency and enforceability. Always-relevant and short goes to CLAUDE.md; sometimes-relevant goes to a path-scoped rule or a nested file; procedural goes to a skill; and anything whose violation you would want to prevent rather than notice goes to permissions or a hook.

Exercise 4.2 — "It's ignoring my CLAUDE.md." A teammate adds Always use British spelling in user-facing strings. to the project CLAUDE.md, and Claude keeps writing "color". Walk through the diagnosis, and give the fix you would actually recommend.

Solution

First: did they edit it mid-session? Overwhelmingly the most likely cause. Project-root CLAUDE.md is read once at session start and held in memory; a mid-session edit does not apply until /clear, /compact or a restart. The tell is that it "works tomorrow". Ask them to restart before doing anything else.

Second: did it load? /context lists loaded files under Memory files. In a monorepo, starting Claude in packages/web loads that package's CLAUDE.md and the ones above it — a file in packages/api/CLAUDE.md is never seen from there. Confirm the file they edited is one of the loaded ones.

Third: does something contradict it? A user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md saying "use American spelling", a nested package file, an imported style guide. Files are concatenated rather than overriding, and a contradiction is resolved arbitrarily — which produces exactly this symptom: it works sometimes. Grep the loaded set for the competing rule.

Fourth: is it losing to recent context? If the session is long and Claude has just read two thousand lines of existing code full of color, a one-line instruction from startup is one signal among many. §3.5's problem, and the reason it looks intermittent.

The fix I would actually recommend is none of the above, and it is the point of the exercise. Spelling in user-facing strings is mechanically checkable, so it should not be a memory instruction at all. Add a lint rule — most projects already have a linter that can carry a word list — and a PostToolUse hook (§9.1) that runs it after every edit. The property then becomes true rather than likely, on turn one and turn ninety, in a fresh session and a resumed one.

Keep the CLAUDE.md line as well, because it is cheap and it makes Claude write it correctly the first time instead of writing it wrongly and being corrected by the hook. That combination — the instruction where the reader is, the enforcement where it cannot be argued with — is the general pattern, and §4.6's ladder is a way of asking which rung a given rule deserves. "Frustrating enough to complain about" is a reliable signal that the answer is not CLAUDE.md.

Exercise 4.3 — Design the memory setup. You are joining a team of six on a two-year-old repository with no CLAUDE.md. Design what you would put in place over the first month, in the order you would do it, and say what you would deliberately not write down.

Solution

Week one: run /init, then delete most of what it produced. It gives you build commands, test instructions and discovered conventions — a useful skeleton and, by definition, only things Claude could have discovered anyway. Keep the commands, because having them stops Claude guessing, and cut the rest. Aim to end week one at forty lines, not two hundred.

Weeks one to four: write down every correction you type twice. This is the actual method, and it is the reason to do this over a month rather than in an afternoon. A CLAUDE.md written up front is a list of what someone imagined would be needed; one accumulated from repeated corrections is a list of what actually was. Watch /memory as well — auto memory's feedback entries are a direct log of the corrections you have been repeating, which is the same list arriving from the other direction.

Week two or three: split by area. Once the file has material for three different parts of the repository, move each into a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/. Six people working on different areas otherwise each pay for the other five's conventions on every request, and — worse than the cost — those conventions compete with the ones that apply.

Week three or four: promote the enforceable ones. Anything that has been violated despite being written down is a candidate for a permission rule or a hook. Formatting, protected paths, "never push to main" — all better as enforcement than as text. Expect two or three, not twenty.

Throughout: commit it and review it in pull requests. A CLAUDE.md is code. It goes stale exactly like documentation, and the mechanism that keeps documentation honest — someone reading the diff — is the one that works here too.

What I would deliberately not write down.

Anything derivable from the code. Directory layout, what modules exist, how a function works. Claude can read; a stale description of the layout is worse than no description, because it will be believed over the file that contradicts it.

Anything that changes faster than the file. The current sprint, who owns what, which branch is deploying. That is auto memory's project type or a SessionStart hook (§9.7) — something that regenerates — not a line someone must remember to update.

Aspirations. "We use TDD" when the team does not is an instruction that produces confused output, because Claude will write tests first while the surrounding code shows it was never done. Write what is true, and if you want it to become true, make it enforceable instead.

And the thing that is hardest to leave out: explanations. A CLAUDE.md that argues for its rules is a CLAUDE.md that is three times as long and followed less well. Put the rule in the file and the reasoning in an HTML comment — stripped before it reaches Claude, visible to the next maintainer, and costing nothing. That single trick keeps a file honest for longer than any other habit in this section.

SECTION 5

Permissions, Trust and Sandboxing

The three sections before this one gave Claude a task, a session and a memory. This one decides what it may actually do. It is the point where the course stops being about getting more done and starts being about consequences.

Everything else in this section follows from one sentence. It is worth reading twice.

Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model. Instructions in your prompt or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do. They do not change what Claude Code allows. The two live on opposite sides of a line, and confusing them is the root of nearly every mistake in this area.

That line is what makes the whole arrangement work. Ask a model nicely not to touch production, and it will usually not touch production. Put a deny rule (a setting that forbids a command) on the deployment command, and it cannot. That holds no matter what it concluded, what a web page told it, or what a convincing comment in an issue tracker suggested. §4 was about what Claude knows; this section is about what it can reach.

There are three layers of control. They are genuinely separate, not three names for the same idea.

Permission rules
Which tools, on which arguments. Allow, ask and deny patterns evaluated by Claude Code on every tool call. Precise, and they cover every tool.
Permission modes
The default answer when no rule matches. Six of them, from asking about everything to asking about nothing. Switched mid-session with Shift+Tab.
Sandboxing
OS-level enforcement on what a shell command can reach. Filesystem and network, applied to Bash and its child processes — including the ones no permission rule can see.

The third exists because the first two have a hole. A Read deny rule on ~/.ssh/** stops Claude's own file tools, and the shell commands Claude Code recognises, such as cat and head. It does not stop a Python script that opens the file itself. To Claude Code that is just one subprocess (a program started by another program) doing ordinary work. Sandboxing closes that hole at the operating-system level. That is why the two layers are described as complementary: each covers what the other cannot.

5.1 Rules: Allow, Ask, Deny

A permission rule is written Tool or Tool(specifier), and it goes in one of three lists.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run *)", "Bash(git commit *)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git push *)"],
    "deny":  ["Read(./.env)", "Edit(**/migrations/**)"]
  }
}

The part in parentheses is the permission specifier. A permission specifier turns a rule about a tool into a rule about one use of that tool: Bash versus Bash(npm run *), Read versus Read(./.env). Each tool has its own specifier syntax, covered in §5.2 and §5.4.

Permission precedence is one order — deny, then ask, then allow — and the first match wins. How specific a rule is plays no part. This surprises people more than anything else here, because it is the reverse of how firewall rules and .gitignore behave, where the more specific or later rule can override.

That permission precedence leads to a rule worth stating on its own: a deny rule cannot carry exceptions. Bash(aws *) in deny blocks aws s3 ls even if Bash(aws s3 ls) is in allow, because the deny list is checked first and matches. The same holds between ask and allow: a matching ask rule asks you even when a narrower allow rule would have let the call through silently. If you want "everything except", write narrow allow rules instead of a broad deny with holes in it.

Deny rules behave differently depending on their shape, and the difference is more than cosmetic:

A bare tool name
"deny": ["Bash"] removes the tool from Claude's context entirely. Claude never sees it, never tries to use it, and never wastes a turn discovering it is unavailable.
A scoped rule
"deny": ["Bash(rm *)"] leaves the tool available and blocks matching calls when Claude attempts them. Claude finds out by being refused.

The first form is better when you mean it. A session with no Bash tool at all is cleaner and cheaper than one that keeps proposing shell commands and being refused. (EndConversation is the one exception: a deny rule cannot remove it while any other tool remains.)

/permissions opens the interactive view: every rule, and the settings file it came from. It works while Claude is running, and a rule added in the middle of a turn applies from Claude's next tool call.

5.2 Bash Rules, and Why They Are Hard

Bash rules match against the whole text of the command, with * standing for any text, spaces included. That sounds simple, but it is the most subtle matching in the product, because a shell command is a small program, not just a string.

You write
Matches
Does not match
Bash(npm run build)
npm run build
npm run build --watch
Bash(npm run *)
npm run build, npm run
npm install
Bash(git log * main)
git log --oneline main
git log main
Bash(ls *)
ls -la, ls
lsof
Bash(ls*)
ls -la, lsof

Three rules explain every row of that wildcard pattern table; each wildcard pattern behaves as it does because of them.

  • A * stands in for whatever text is in its place. So in Bash(git * main) it stands for the subcommand, and the rule matches git push origin main just as well as git merge main.
  • A trailing * with a space before it also matches the bare command. That is why Bash(ls *) covers plain ls. It holds only when the trailing * is the rule's only wildcard.
  • The space before a trailing * is part of the rule. That is the whole difference between Bash(ls *) and Bash(ls*), and the reason the second one accidentally allows lsof.
Put the * after the subcommand. Claude Code matches everything before the first * literally, so those words are what actually constrain the rule. Bash(git log *) allows only git log. Bash(git * main) allows every git subcommand including push — and including git -c core.fsmonitor=<script> diff main, which runs a program you named in a config option. Claude Code warns at startup about an allow rule with a wildcard before the subcommand, and the warning is worth acting on.

Four behaviours make Bash rules stronger than a simple text match. Each exists because the simple version could be exploited.

Compound commands are split. Claude Code recognises &&, ||, ;, |, |&, & and newlines, and every subcommand must match a rule independently. So Bash(safe-cmd *) does not permit safe-cmd && rm -rf /. When you approve a compound command with "don't ask again", Claude Code saves one rule per subcommand rather than one rule for the whole string, up to five.

Wrappers are stripped. A wrapper is a command that runs another command. timeout, time, nice, nohup, stdbuf, the builtins command and builtin, zsh's noglob, and bare xargs are removed before matching, so Bash(npm test *) covers timeout 30 npm test. A leading assignment of a known-safe environment variable is also stripped, so the rule covers NODE_ENV=test npm test. But an allow rule will not match past an assignment of any other variable, while a deny rule matches past any assignment at all. That imbalance is deliberate: stripping is generous where it restricts, and stingy where it permits.

The wrapper list is fixed, and environment runners are not on it. npx, docker exec, direnv exec, devbox run and mise exec all run their arguments as a command, so Bash(devbox run *) matches devbox run rm -rf .. To approve work inside a runner, write the runner and the inner command: Bash(devbox run npm test), one rule per inner command. In the same way, exec wrappers like watch, setsid and flock, and find with -exec or -delete, can never be auto-approved by a prefix rule, and always ask in Manual mode.

Redirections are checked as file writes. ls > out.txt gets a write check on out.txt against your Edit rules, the protected paths and the working directories. Bash(git commit *) allows the command, not the file its output is redirected to. /dev/null is exempt; a target starting with ~ or containing a glob needs approval.

There is one shape you should simply stop trying to write:

Bash patterns that constrain arguments are fragile. Bash(curl http://github.com/ *) looks like it restricts curl to GitHub. It does not match curl -X GET http://github.com/… (option first), curl https://… (different protocol), curl -L http://short.example/xyz (redirects there), or URL=http://github.com && curl $URL (a variable). The reliable version is to deny curl and wget outright and use the WebFetch tool with WebFetch(domain:github.com) — and to know that if Bash is allowed at all, some other binary can still reach the network.

Claude Code also has a built-in read-only set of commands that run without asking in every mode: ls, cat, echo, pwd, head, tail, grep, find, wc, which, diff, stat, du, cd and read-only forms of git. You cannot configure it, though an ask or deny rule can take a command out of it. A few cases ask anyway, and each one teaches something about what "read-only" means:

  • an unquoted glob on a command with flags that can write (the glob could expand to -delete);
  • docker with a flag pointing at another daemon;
  • file with --magic-file (which opens paths named in the flag);
  • a Windows UNC path (which can send your credentials to the host it names);
  • any command Claude Code cannot fully parse.

5.3 Matching by Parameter, and by Tool Name

Two extensions to the syntax cover cases the specifier form cannot.

Deny and ask rules can match a top-level input parameter, written Tool(param:value):

{
  "permissions": {
    "ask": ["Agent(model:opus)", "Bash(run_in_background:true)"]
  }
}

These rules are narrow on purpose. The parameter must be a direct field of the tool's input, not a nested one. Each rule names one parameter, so checking two means writing two rules. * works as a wildcard in the value. A parameter the model leaves out is never matched, so Agent(model:*) does not match a call that leaves model unset. The value is compared against the literal input Claude sends, before any normalisation: Agent(model:opus) matches the alias, not the full model ID.

Allow rules deliberately cannot do this, because knowing one parameter's value does not prove a call is safe overall. And no rule can match a tool's primary content field: command, file_path, path, notebook_path, url. Bash(command:rm *) could be bypassed trivially with a compound command, so Claude Code ignores it and warns at startup.

Tool-name globs work in deny and ask rules: "*" matches every tool, "mcp__*" every MCP tool. A deny with a bare-name glob removes the matched tools from context, just like a bare tool name. Allow rules accept a glob only after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix. mcp__github__get_* is fine, but mcp__* in an allow list is skipped with a warning and approves nothing, because an allow glob with no fixed prefix is the same as "allow everything".

A deny or ask rule that names no known tool produces a warning at startup, which catches the most common kind of typo. Note too that the label shown in the transcript is not always the tool's real (canonical) name. The tool shown as Stop Task is really TaskStop, and rules match only the canonical name.

5.4 File Paths: Read, Edit, and Nothing Else

File permissions are checked against Edit(path) and Read(path) rules only. A path rule written for Write, NotebookEdit, Glob or MultiEdit is accepted, never consulted, and warned about at startup. Write Edit(docs/**) where you would have written Write(docs/**), and Read(docs/**) where you would have written Glob(docs/**). Edit covers every built-in tool that edits files. A Read deny rule also blocks Edit and Write on the same path, but not NotebookEdit, so a path that no tool may change needs an Edit deny rule too.

Patterns use gitignore syntax, and the prefix decides where the path starts from. This is where most of the confusion lives:

Pattern
Means
Example
//path
Absolute, from filesystem root
Read(//Users/alice/secrets/**)
~/path
From your home directory
Read(~/Documents/*.pdf)
/path
Relative to the settings source
Edit(/src/**) in project settings → <project>/src/**
path or ./path
Relative to the current directory
Read(*.env)
/Users/alice/file is not an absolute path. A single leading slash anchors at the settings source, not at the filesystem root. In user settings, Read(/secrets/**) blocks ~/.claude/secrets/** — not a secrets directory in your project, which is almost certainly what was meant. Absolute paths take two slashes: //Users/alice/file. For a rule in user settings that should apply inside every project, use // or ~/.

How deep a pattern matches has one asymmetry, and it is the right one. A relative directory pattern with a single segment behaves differently by rule type: Edit(src/**) as an allow rule matches only <cwd>/src, while the same pattern as a deny or ask rule matches a src directory at any depth. So a deny rule automatically covers a nested copy under vendor/, and an allow rule does not accidentally grant access to it. Every other pattern shape matches at the same depth in every rule type. Bare filenames follow gitignore rules and match at any depth: Read(.env) and Read(**/.env) are the same rule.

Symlinks are checked as a pair (the link and the file it points to), with the same asymmetry: an allow rule applies only when both match; a deny rule applies when either matches. With Read(./project/**) allowed and Read(~/.ssh/**) denied, a symlink at ./project/key pointing to ~/.ssh/id_rsa is blocked, because the target fails the allow and matches the deny. Both halves of that are what you want.

And the limit, stated plainly: Read and Edit rules cover Claude's built-in file tools and the file commands Claude Code recognises in Bash, such as cat, head, tail and sed. They do not cover a Python or Node script that opens a file itself. For enforcement that binds every process, you need §5.7.

5.5 Modes: The Answer When No Rule Matches

Rules cover the cases you thought of in advance. The permission mode decides everything else, and it is the dial you actually touch during a session: Shift+Tab cycles through the modes.

default — Manual
Reads only. Everything else asks. Labelled Manual in the interface; manual is accepted as an alias, but hooks and the SDK see "default". For sensitive work and unfamiliar code.
acceptEdits
Reads, file edits, and common filesystem commands — mkdir, touch, mv, cp — inside the working directory. For iterating on code you are reading as it changes.
plan
Reads and exploration; no source edits. Claude researches and proposes; edits stay blocked until you approve the plan. §2.6.
auto
Everything, with a classifier reviewing each action. A second model checks whether the action fits your request before it runs. The built-in starting mode on Pro, Max and Team plans.
dontAsk
Only pre-approved tools; everything else is denied rather than prompted. For CI and scripts with an exact allowlist.
bypassPermissions
No prompts at all. Containers and VMs only.

A mode sets a baseline, and rules sit on top of it. Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions. Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions, because nothing is being asked.

The classifier

auto is worth understanding, not just switching on, because it is a genuinely different mechanism. A separate model (a classifier) reviews each action before it runs. It blocks anything that goes beyond your request, targets infrastructure it does not recognise, or looks driven by hostile content Claude read. That last part is the interesting one: it is a defence against the attack in §5.9, applied at the moment of acting rather than the moment of reading.

What it trusts is narrow and worth knowing: your working directory, and the git remotes that were configured when the session started. A remote added or changed during the session with git remote add is not trusted. Everything else counts as external until you configure trusted infrastructure explicitly.

What it blocks by default reads like a list of afternoons someone has already lost:

  • curl | bash, and sending sensitive data to outside endpoints;
  • production deploys and migrations, and mass deletion on cloud storage;
  • granting IAM or repository permissions;
  • force push, and terraform destroy and its equivalents;
  • git reset --hard / git clean -fd / git stash drop and the rest of the family that throws away uncommitted work;
  • git commit --amend on a commit it did not create, or that has already been pushed;
  • permanently destroying files that existed before the session.

It also blocks committing or pushing a change that would send secrets outside the repository or widen what a deploy exposes. That applies on any branch, whether or not the repository is public, and whether or not the push itself starts the pipeline.

Auto mode reduces prompts; it does not guarantee safety. Use it where you trust the general direction, not as a replacement for review on sensitive operations. It is a second model's judgement, which is much better than nothing and is not the same kind of thing as a deny rule.

The five things no mode auto-approves

This list is the real safety floor of the product, and it holds even in bypassPermissions:

Tools matched by an explicit ask rule
An ask rule you wrote always prompts.
Connector tools your org set to ask
Organisation policy outranks session mode.
Tools needing user interaction
AskUserQuestion, and MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction (§10.5).
rm/rmdir on a critical path
No allow rule and no PreToolUse hook returning "allow" can approve a critical path removal — rm -rf /, rm -rf ~ and their relatives, including inside command substitution. A circuit breaker against model error rather than against you.
Cross-session messaging safeguards
Cross-session messaging lets your sessions talk to each other, and a message arriving that way is labelled as coming from another Claude session rather than from you — so it never counts as your approval (§11.5).

Protected paths

Separately, writes to a small set of paths are never auto-approved outside bypassPermissions: .git, .config/git, .vscode, .idea, .husky, .cargo, .devcontainer, .yarn, .mvn, and .claude (except .claude/worktrees). The same goes for a list of files that includes .gitconfig, every shell rc file, .envrc, .npmrc, .yarnrc, .pre-commit-config.yaml, gradle-wrapper.properties, .mcp.json and .claude.json.

The pattern behind the list is the point: these are the files that decide what runs next. A write to .envrc, .zshrc or a pre-commit hook is not an edit to your project. It is an edit to the machinery that runs your project, and an agent that can quietly change it can widen its own access at the next command. That is why permissions.allow rules do not pre-approve protected-path writes at all: the safety check runs before allow rules are looked at, so Edit(.claude/**) in your settings changes nothing. In modes that ask, the prompt offers an "allow Claude to edit its own settings" option for the session, and that is the intended route.

5.6 Trust: What Runs Before You Say Yes

A repository can carry its own configuration: hooks, settings, .mcp.json, skills, subagents. Cloning it means getting that configuration too. Workspace trust is the gate that controls it.

permissions.allow rules and additionalDirectories in a project's .claude/settings.json grant capability, so they apply only after you accept the trust dialog for that folder. The dialog lists what the folder would grant. deny and ask rules are not affected, because they only restrict: a repository is always allowed to make itself more locked down.

Trust is tied to where you started. Inside a git repository it is tied to the repository root (covering the whole repository, but not a nested one such as a submodule). Outside a repository it is tied to the starting directory. And it is held for the session only, never written to disk, when you start in your home directory.

The rule that matters most is the one about non-interactive runs. The trust dialog appears in interactive sessions only. A claude -p run or an SDK session never shows it, and trusting a parent folder does not count instead. Here is what each session type actually uses from an untrusted repository:

Repository content
Parent trusted only
-p / SDK, never trusted
Hooks in settings, env, apiKeyHelper, a project skill's hooks and allowed-tools
Used
Used
permissions.allow, additionalDirectories
Not until you accept
Not used; warning to stderr
Frontmatter hooks in a project subagent, extraKnownMarketplaces
Not used, no dialog offered
Not used
Inline mcpServers in subagent frontmatter
Not used, no dialog offered
Not used
Servers in .mcp.json
You are asked before connecting
Connected without asking

The first and last rows are the ones to remember. Hooks run, and .mcp.json servers connect, in a -p session in a folder you have never trusted. That is not a bug, since a non-interactive run has nobody to ask. But it means that scripting claude -p across repositories you did not write is a decision, not a convenience. There are four defences, from the bluntest down:

claude -p "summarise this diff" --setting-sources user
claude -p "summarise this diff" --bare
claude -p "summarise this diff" --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'

--setting-sources user reads neither the project's settings files nor its .mcp.json. --bare skips hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins and .mcp.json servers, though the project's env block still applies. --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' turns hooks off for that one run. It has to be passed on the command line rather than set in your user settings, because the repository's project settings take precedence over yours and could set it back to false. A disabledMcpjsonServers entry rejects a named server in every session type.

Settings precedence for permissions has one absolute rule: if a tool is denied at any level, no other level can allow it. A managed deny (set by your organisation) survives --allowedTools. A user-level deny blocks a project-level allow. Managed settings outrank everything, including command-line arguments. Deny flows downward and cannot be undone from below, which is the only sensible direction for it to flow.

5.7 Sandboxing: The Layer That Binds Every Process

Everything so far is Claude Code deciding whether to run a command. Sandboxing is the operating system deciding what the command can reach once it is running. That is a different kind of guarantee, because it also holds for any process that the command itself starts.

It is built in and runs on macOS, Linux and WSL2 (native Windows is not supported). macOS needs nothing installed, because it uses the built-in Seatbelt framework. Linux and WSL2 need two packages:

sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat

bubblewrap enforces the filesystem isolation, and socat passes network traffic through the sandbox proxy. /sandbox opens a panel showing what is missing, which mode is set, and the final configuration. If a required package is missing, the Dependencies tab is the only one shown.

Two layers, independently configurable:

Filesystem isolation
By default, sandboxed commands can write only to the working directory and the session temp directory. Reads and writes are configured with allowWrite, denyWrite, allowRead and denyRead.
Credential masking
sandbox.credentials unsets or masks named environment variables for sandboxed commands. Credential masking matters because a sandboxed command inherits the parent environment by default, tokens included — so filesystem and network isolation can both be correct while the secret travels in the process environment. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB is the blunter version, stripping provider credentials from every subprocess.
Network isolation
An egress allowlist of domains, enforced by a proxy. The first time a command needs a new domain, Claude Code prompts — or sends it to the classifier in auto mode.
{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "filesystem": {
      "denyRead": ["~/"],
      "allowRead": ["."]
    },
    "network": {
      "allowedDomains": ["github.com", "*.npmjs.org"]
    }
  }
}

That configuration blocks reading anywhere in your home directory while keeping the project readable, and limits outgoing network traffic to two domains. It belongs in the project's .claude/settings.json, because . resolves to the project root only in project settings. In ~/.claude/settings.json it would resolve to ~/.claude and block the project too.

Note that sandbox path prefixes are not the permission-rule prefixes from §5.4. Here /tmp/build is an ordinary absolute path, ~/ starts from your home directory, and a bare or ./ path is relative to the settings file's location. One leading slash means what it usually means. Keep the two syntaxes straight, because a rule written in the wrong one silently points somewhere you did not intend.

When read rules overlap, they are resolved by specificity — the narrower path wins. That lets you express both directions. denyRead: ["~/"] with allowRead: ["~/projects"] opens one hole in a blocked area. allowRead: ["~/"] with denyRead: ["~/**/.env"] keeps every .env blocked inside a broadly readable area. The second shape is the one you want for secrets, and the wildcard deny holds inside the wider allow just as an exact path does. Lists from different settings scopes are merged, not replaced.

Two modes control approval, and they are independent of the filesystem and network rules. Auto-allow runs commands that can be sandboxed without asking, on the idea that the sandbox boundary is the check. Regular permissions keeps the normal prompts even for sandboxed commands. In auto-allow, deny rules still apply, ask rules about content like Bash(git push *) still ask, and removals of critical paths still go through the normal flow.

By default, a sandbox that cannot start is a warning, not a failure — Claude Code runs commands unsandboxed and tells you. For a deployment where sandboxing is the security gate rather than a convenience, set sandbox.failIfUnavailable to true and make it a hard error.

The limits are documented openly, and three matter.

  • The proxy does not terminate TLS by default. It decides using the hostname the client provides, without looking inside the encrypted connection. So a broad allowlist entry like github.com can become a route for stealing data (exfiltration) through a trick called domain fronting. A threat model that needs more requires a custom proxy that does terminate TLS.
  • allowUnixSockets can hand over the machine. Allowing /var/run/docker.sock effectively grants access to the host.
  • And broad filesystem writes escalate. Write access to a directory on $PATH, to system configuration, or to .bashrc becomes code execution somewhere else later. The protected-paths list in §5.5 is the same insight applied one layer up.

What it covers, exactly: the sandbox isolates Bash subprocesses. Read, Edit and Write go through the permission system directly. Computer use runs on your real desktop. Subagents share the parent session's sandbox configuration. And sandboxed commands inherit the parent environment including credentials, unless you use sandbox.credentials to unset or mask specific variables, or CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB to remove provider credentials from every subprocess.

5.8 Choosing an Isolation Boundary

The Bash sandbox is one point on a range of options, and for truly unattended work it is not the right one. Here are the five options, from cheapest to strongest:

Nothing
Manual mode, you approve each action. The oversight is the boundary. Correct for sensitive work on a machine with credentials.
Bash sandbox
OS-level limits on shell commands. Cheap, local, no container. The default recommendation for everyday local work with fewer prompts.
Dev container
The whole session in a devcontainer with a curated toolchain. Reproducible for a team, and the filesystem boundary is the container's — which is why a devcontainer is often the least effort per unit of isolation for a project that already has one.
Sandbox runtime / VM
A dedicated isolated environment. The sandbox runtime is what --dangerously-skip-permissions requires: a place where "no prompts at all" is survivable, because the boundary moved outward rather than away.
Cloud session
Someone else's machine entirely (§14.7). Nothing of yours is reachable, which is the strongest and least convenient boundary.

The pairing that matters: bypassPermissions without one of the last three is not a configuration, it is an accident waiting for a bad afternoon. Run it in a container or virtual machine, as a non-root user on Linux and macOS, and understand that inside that boundary Claude can do anything the container can. That is the whole point: you moved the wall further out rather than removing it.

A CI run needs a different combination. dontAsk with an explicit --allowedTools list gives you an exact allowlist, and denies everything else instead of hanging on a prompt nobody will answer:

claude -p "run the test suite and summarise failures" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Bash(npm test)" "Read"

5.9 Prompt Injection, and Why Any of This Matters

Permissions get a whole section, not a paragraph, because Claude reads text from places you do not control. A web page, a dependency's README, a comment on an issue, the output of a command, a file in a repository you cloned. All of it arrives in the same context window as your instructions, and from the model's point of view all of it is just more text.

An attacker who can put text in front of the model can try to give it instructions. That is called prompt injection. The defence is not to make the model harder to persuade. It is to make persuasion not enough.

Instructions do not hold
"Never send data to external hosts" in CLAUDE.md is text. So is the injected instruction. They compete on equal terms, and you are relying on the model to win an argument.
Deny rules hold
A deny rule is evaluated by Claude Code before the tool runs, and no amount of persuasion changes it. The model cannot argue with the code that gates the call.
The sandbox holds
An egress allowlist stops the exfiltration attempt at the operating system, regardless of which binary made it or why.
The classifier helps
Auto mode explicitly checks whether an action looks driven by hostile content. A second model's judgement — better than nothing, weaker than a rule.

Claude Code's own defences run alongside yours:

  • subagent reports are scanned before the main conversation reads them (§11.1), because a subagent may have read a web page you never saw;
  • the auto-mode classifier reviews messages passed between agents;
  • a permission prompt is, in the end, a human in the loop at exactly the point where it counts.

The practical stance that follows is short.

  • Deny the paths whose contents would be worth stealing, such as .env, key material and credential stores, so neither the file tools nor the recognised shell commands can read them.
  • Turn the sandbox on and keep the domain allowlist small, so a command that does read something cannot send it anywhere.
