  • Put ask on the operations you would want to see (pushes, deploys, anything that spends money), even in a permissive mode, because an ask rule outranks every mode.
  • And treat any session that has read untrusted content as one whose conclusions need checking. That is a habit rather than a setting, and it is the one that applies everywhere.

Exercises

Exercise 5.1 — Read the rules. Given this configuration, say what happens for each command and why.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(git *)", "Bash(npm run *)", "Read(src/**)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git push *)"],
    "deny":  ["Read(.env)", "Bash(rm *)"]
  }
}

(a) git push origin main (b) npm run build && rm -rf dist (c) reading packages/api/src/db.ts (d) reading config/.env (e) FOO=bar rm -rf tmp/ (f) timeout 60 npm run test

Solution

(a) Prompts. Bash(git push *) is in ask, and ask is evaluated before allow, so the broader Bash(git *) allow rule does not silence it. This is the intended way to carve one operation out of a broad allow — you cannot do it with a deny rule carrying an exception, because deny has no exceptions.

(b) Blocked. Compound commands are split on && and every subcommand must match independently. npm run build matches the allow rule; rm -rf dist matches Bash(rm *) in deny. The deny wins and the whole command is refused. Note the useful property: the allowed half does not get to run first.

(c) Prompts — and this is the trap. Read(src/**) is an allow rule with a single-segment relative pattern, so it matches only <cwd>/src and its contents. packages/api/src/ is a different directory at a different depth, so no rule matches and the normal mode behaviour applies. To allow src at any depth you must write Read(**/src/**). (The same pattern as a deny rule would have matched at any depth — that asymmetry is deliberate and it is working correctly here.)

(d) Denied. Read(.env) is a bare filename, and bare filenames follow gitignore semantics: it is equivalent to Read(**/.env) and matches at any depth under the current directory. So the nested config/.env is covered without writing a second rule.

(e) Denied. A leading environment-variable assignment is stripped before matching for deny and ask rules regardless of which variable it is, so Bash(rm *) matches. Had this been an allow rule, it would not have matched past FOO=, because allow rules only see past assignments of known-safe variables. Generous where it restricts, stingy where it permits.

(f) Allowed silently. timeout is on the fixed wrapper list and is stripped before matching, so Bash(npm run *) covers it. nice, nohup, time, stdbuf, command, builtin and bare xargs behave the same way — but npx, docker exec and devbox run do not, which is why an allow rule mentioning one of those covers whatever follows it.

Exercise 5.2 — The rule that did nothing. A colleague wants Claude never to read secrets. They add this to ~/.claude/settings.json, and Claude reads secrets/api-keys.json in their project the same afternoon. Explain, and give a configuration that actually works.

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Read(/secrets/**)", "Write(/secrets/**)"]
  }
}
Solution

Two independent bugs, either of which alone would defeat the rule.

One: /secrets/** in user settings anchors at ~/.claude. A single leading slash means "relative to the settings source", not "absolute". In ~/.claude/settings.json the rule resolves to ~/.claude/secrets/** — a directory that almost certainly does not exist — so it matches nothing in any project. This is the highest-frequency mistake in the whole permission system, and it fails completely silently because a rule matching nothing is indistinguishable from a rule that has not fired yet.

Two: Write(...) is never consulted. File permissions are checked against Edit(path) and Read(path) rules only. A path rule on Write, NotebookEdit, Glob or MultiEdit is accepted and ignored, with a startup warning that is easy to scroll past.

A configuration that works:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Read(secrets/**)",
      "Read(**/.env)",
      "Read(~/.ssh/**)",
      "Read(~/.aws/**)",
      "Edit(secrets/**)"
    ]
  }
}

Read(secrets/**) as a deny rule matches a secrets directory at any depth under the current directory — the depth asymmetry from §5.4 works in your favour here. ~/ prefixes reach the home directory from any project. Edit replaces the ineffective Write.

The third bug, which no rule fixes. Read and Edit deny rules cover Claude's file tools and the shell commands Claude Code recognises — cat, head, sed. They do not cover python -c "print(open('secrets/api-keys.json').read())", or a test script that loads its own fixtures, or any binary that opens the file itself. If the requirement is genuinely "Claude must not be able to read this", the rule is a first layer and the sandbox is the enforcement:

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "filesystem": { "denyRead": ["./secrets", "~/.ssh", "~/.aws"] }
  }
}

That is enforced at the OS level for every process in the sandbox, including children. The general lesson: a permission rule expresses intent to Claude Code, and a sandbox rule expresses it to the kernel. For anything whose disclosure would actually matter, write both — and remember §5.9's second half: reading is only half the attack, and an egress allowlist is what stops the other half.

Exercise 5.3 — Design the CI configuration. You want Claude to triage failing builds in CI: read the repository and the build log, run the test suite, and post a summary comment on the pull request. The repository accepts community pull requests. Design the permission configuration, and name the two things you are relying on that are not permission rules.

Solution

Mode: dontAsk. In CI nobody can answer a prompt. Manual mode would hang; bypassPermissions would run anything. dontAsk denies whatever is not pre-approved, which is the correct failure direction for an unattended run: a task that needed an unlisted tool fails visibly rather than doing something unreviewed.

An exact allowlist, and nothing broader than the job:

claude -p "$PROMPT" --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --allowedTools "Read" "Grep" "Glob" "Bash(npm ci)" "Bash(npm test)" \
  --setting-sources user \
  --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'

Note what is absent. No Bash(git *) — a triage job has no reason to commit or push. No Edit at all — it reads and reports, and a job that cannot write cannot leave a surprise in the tree. No Bash(npm run *), because a community pull request can add a script to package.json, and that rule would run it.

That last point is the heart of the exercise. The repository accepts community pull requests, which means the checked-out code is untrusted input, and §5.6's table says exactly what that costs: in a -p run the folder is treated as trusted, so hooks in the branch's .claude/settings.json run, and its .mcp.json servers connect, without anyone approving them. --setting-sources user and --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' are therefore not belt-and-braces; they are the actual defence, and the second must be on the command line because project settings outrank your user settings and can set it back to false.

Sandboxing on, with a tight egress list:

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "network": { "allowedDomains": ["registry.npmjs.org", "*.npmjs.org"] }
  }
}

npm ci is running a package install from an untrusted branch's lockfile, and install scripts execute arbitrary code. The sandbox is what stops that code reaching anything but the registry.

The two non-permission things you are relying on.

One: the token. Posting the comment needs credentials, and no permission rule constrains what a credential can do once a process has it. A token scoped to "write comments on this pull request" is a stronger control than every rule above, because it binds the service, not the client. If the token can also merge, the configuration is decorative.

Two: the isolation of the runner itself. A CI runner is a container that is destroyed afterwards, and that is the boundary doing the heaviest lifting — it is why running untrusted code here is acceptable at all. The permission rules make the job precise; the ephemeral container makes it survivable.

The judgement worth keeping: ask what happens if this session is fully persuaded by something in the branch it checked out. Under this configuration it can read the repository, run two known commands inside a sandbox with two allowed domains, and reach a token that can only comment. That is a bounded and unexciting answer, which is the goal. §9.10 makes the same argument for hooks, and §14.2 for what a workflow's own credentials should be able to do.

SECTION 6

Configuration and the Settings Layers

Sections 4 and 5 both wrote settings without explaining where they live. That was deliberate, because the mechanisms were the point. But it leaves a gap, because the file you put a setting in decides who gets it, whether it survives a resume, and who can override it. Those are three different questions, and people often get all three wrong at once.

This section covers the layers (the several settings files, from personal to company-wide), the precedence rules (which file wins when two disagree) that are not obvious, and the handful of interface settings worth changing on day one. It is the least exciting section in the course and the one that saves the most time, because "I set that and it did nothing" is the most common thing that goes wrong.

6.1 Five Files, Five Audiences

Claude Code reads settings from four files, plus managed settings that an organisation can push to every machine.

Scope
File
Who it affects
Managed
managed-settings.json, MDM, or the claude.ai console
Everyone the organisation deploys it to. Nothing you set overrides it, apart from a few security-sensitive exceptions.
User
~/.claude/settings.json
You, in every project on this machine.
Shared project
.claude/settings.json
Everyone who starts Claude Code in that folder — once you commit it.
Project local
.claude/settings.local.json
You, in this one project. Kept out of git automatically when Claude Code creates it.

Claude Code keeps a fifth file, ~/.claude.json, for itself. It holds your sign-in session, MCP server configurations, per-project state such as trust decisions, and the global config keys that /config writes. You do not edit it by hand.

Installing Claude Code creates none of these. A settings file exists because someone made it, or because Claude Code wrote one for you. It writes ~/.claude/settings.json the first time you change a /config option that is stored there, and .claude/settings.local.json the first time you answer a permission prompt with "don't ask again".

That second case is worth understanding, because it is how most people's first settings file appears. A standing permission approval is saved as an allow rule in the local file. In a git repository, Claude Code reads and writes that file at the repository root, so an approval given in a subdirectory or a worktree applies to the whole repository. The shared .claude/settings.json does not move: it is read only from the folder you start in. That is a good reason to start Claude at the repository root.

The first time it writes that file, Claude Code also adds **/.claude/settings.local.json to your global git excludes (a gitignore that applies to every repository), so the file stays out of your commits everywhere. If you created the file by hand, add it to .gitignore yourself.

6.2 Precedence, and the Parts That Surprise People

When a key appears in more than one place, the highest level that sets it wins:

1
Managed settings
Your organisation. Nothing overrides it — not --settings, not a flag.
2
Command line
claude --settings. One session, written to no file.
3
Project local
.claude/settings.local.json. You, this project.
4
Shared project
.claude/settings.json. Everyone in the project.
5
User
~/.claude/settings.json. You, every project.
Shared project settings sit above your user settings. That is the ordering that catches everyone, because it is the opposite of how CLAUDE.md and skills work (§4.2, §8.2). A preference in ~/.claude/settings.json is silently overridden by a committed team file that sets the same key — and the way to get your value back is .claude/settings.local.json, which sits above the shared file. Not a change to your user settings, which will not help.

Three refinements matter more than the stack itself.

Lists merge instead of overriding. If permissions.allow is set in three files, the result is all three lists combined, not just the highest file's copy. That is what lets a team file grant the shared rules while your local file adds your own without deleting theirs. Three keys that list models are exceptions. They are taken whole from the highest file that sets them, because their order or completeness carries meaning: fallbackModel (an ordered chain), modelPicker (one ordered list plus a replace flag) and availableModels when a managed source defines it.

Environment variables are not a level. Some behaviours have both a shell variable and a settings key. Which one wins is decided per pair, not by position in the stack. ANTHROPIC_MODEL exported in your shell applies over the model key from any file, while ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL applies only when no file sets model. There is no general rule; the environment-variable reference is the authority for each pair. An env block inside a settings file, though, is an ordinary key and follows the stack.

A few security keys keep their strict value regardless of level. For these, Claude Code honours a restrictive value from a lower level over a permissive managed one. So a project that sets disableClaudeAiConnectors to true keeps it on. The exception always points towards safety, which is the only sensible way for such an exception to work.

6.3 Changing a Setting, Three Ways

/config opens a short menu of personal options (theme, editor mode, verbose output), not every key. It saves most of them to ~/.claude/settings.json, a few (such as Show tips) to .claude/settings.local.json, and the global config options to ~/.claude.json. /config verbose=true sets one option without the menu.

Editing a file covers everything else. Settings files are strict JSON: a // comment or a trailing comma is a syntax error, and Claude Code reports the file as a Settings Error the next time it starts.

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run lint)",
      "Bash(npm run test *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)"
    ]
  }
}

Include the $schema line in every file you write by hand. It gives you autocompletion and validation in any editor that understands JSON Schema, which catches a mistyped key before Claude Code does.

--settings changes a key for one session. It takes a file path or inline JSON. It sits above every file except managed settings, writes nothing to disk, and is the right tool for a one-off. The --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' from §5.6 is the classic example.

When edits take effect

Claude Code watches your settings files and applies most edits to the running session, including permissions, hooks and credential helpers such as apiKeyHelper. For each change it detects, it runs the ConfigChange hook (§9.2). That is a really nice property, and it makes adjusting permission rules painless.

Three keys are read once, at session start, and an edit does not reach a session that is already running:

model
Use /model mid-session. Remember each model has its own prompt cache (§3.6).
effortLevel
Use /effort.
outputStyle
Part of the system prompt, so it applies after /clear or a restart.

Managed settings that arrive through MDM (the device-management system your company uses) or the claude.ai console reach a running session on a schedule, not when they are saved. So "the admin changed it and nothing happened" usually means "restart".

6.4 Finding Out What Actually Loaded

There are three commands, and knowing which one answers which question is all there is to debugging configuration.

/status
Which settings sources loaded. A Setting sources line naming each file, and — when managed settings apply — how they reached your machine. It does not show which file supplied each key.
claude doctor
Which entries were rejected. The details of every error and every value Claude Code dropped. This is the one you want after a -p run, which shows no dialog and silently skips broken values.
/context
What is in the window, including which CLAUDE.md and memory files loaded (§3.1).

A broken file leads to one of four outcomes, and telling them apart is useful:

Settings Error
Invalid JSON or a schema-rejected value in a user, project or local file. An interactive session offers to fix it with Claude's help, exit, or continue without it.
Settings Warning
Individual entries failed — a malformed permission rule, an unknown hook event name. Those values are skipped and the rest of the file stays in effect.
Managed settings
The rest of the file keeps being enforced; some keys fall back to a stricter value until fixed.
Configuration error
~/.claude.json cannot be parsed. Claude Code backs it up to ~/.claude/backups/ and offers to reset. Five recent backups are kept.

The Settings Warning case is the quiet one. A hook event you misspelled is skipped, the rest of the file works, and everything looks fine. That is exactly the §9.11 failure, arriving through the configuration layer. Run claude doctor after writing any settings file by hand, once, and you will find the typo immediately instead of a month later.

6.5 The Interface

A handful of settings change the experience enough to be worth setting on day one.

The status line replaces the default bottom line with the output of your own command. Your command receives JSON on stdin with the model, the session name, working directory, git branch, effort level and a current_usage object. So the session name you set with /rename (§2.6) can be something you see, not something you have to remember. The current_usage object is how you watch the cache hit rate live (§3.6). A status line showing cache read and write tokens turns an invisible property into a number you glance at, and a falling cache hit rate shows up within seconds instead of at the end of a session.

Keybindings can be customised in ~/.claude/keybindings.json, including chord bindings (two keys pressed one after the other). It is worth doing if a default clashes with a terminal or tmux shortcut you already use.

Terminal configuration covers the setup that makes multi-line input, notifications and key handling work properly. It is the kind of thing that is a five-minute annoyance every day until you fix it once.

Vim mode is available for the input line, with normal and insert modes, navigation, text objects and visual mode. Ctrl+R searches backwards through your command history.

Fullscreen rendering changes how the interface draws, and it also changes behaviour: in fullscreen, dialog commands such as /theme and /help open immediately instead of waiting behind a running turn.

Screen reader support is a full mode, not an afterthought. --ax-screen-reader renders plain text with no decorative borders or animations, and it changes real behaviour elsewhere too. For example, the footer hint for a finished background subagent is not announced in screen reader mode (§11.2).

Voice dictation is available for input. Voice dictation is worth trying for the long, descriptive prompts §2.2 recommends: dictating makes a three-sentence prompt about as cheap to produce as a three-word one.

Shell mode with ! runs a command directly instead of asking Claude to run it. It is the fastest way to check something yourself in the middle of a session without leaving the interface.

The two worth doing first: a status line that shows context usage and cache hit rate, because it makes §3's abstractions concrete and visible; and Ctrl+O for verbose mode, so you can see what a hook or a background task actually did rather than inferring it.

6.6 What Belongs Where

The decision is almost always the same three questions, in order.

Does the team need it?
Yes → .claude/settings.json, committed. Permission rules that define the project's boundaries, hooks that enforce its conventions, the plugins it depends on, the environment variables it needs. This is the file that makes a repository work the same way for everyone.
Is it just you, everywhere?
Yes → ~/.claude/settings.json. Theme, editor mode, your default model, your own permission rules. Remember it is the lowest level, so a team file can override it.
Is it just you, here?
Yes → .claude/settings.local.json. Personal overrides of a team setting, and anything you are testing before sharing.

Three things belong in the committed file more often than they end up there. Each is worth arguing for in code review:

Permission rules, because they are the project's boundary, and every teammate should have the same one (§5.1). Hooks, because a formatter that runs for one developer and not the others produces exactly the review noise it was meant to prevent (§9.3). And env, because an environment variable the project needs belongs to the project, not to whoever set it up first.

Two things should stay out. Anything carrying a credential: use ${VAR} expansion or a helper instead (§10.3). And anything about how you personally like to work, because a committed outputStyle or theme becomes a small annoyance for everyone else.

The general rule behind all of this: put a setting at the widest scope where it is still true. A rule that is true of the project goes in the project file. One that is true of you goes in yours. One that is true only today goes on the command line.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 — Where does the value come from? Your ~/.claude/settings.json sets "model": "claude-opus-4-8". The project's committed .claude/settings.json sets "model": "claude-sonnet-5". You launch with ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 exported in your shell. Which model runs, and how would you get Opus back for your sessions in this project only?

Solution

Haiku runs. ANTHROPIC_MODEL exported in the shell applies over the model key from any file — this is one of the pairs where the environment variable wins outright rather than sitting somewhere in the file stack. Note the contrast that makes this worth knowing: ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL applies only when no file sets model, so the two variables behave completely differently against the same key. There is no general rule; the environment-variable reference decides each pair.

Without the variable, Sonnet would run — because shared project settings sit above user settings. That is the ordering that surprises people, and it is worth restating: your personal preference loses to a committed team file, and editing your user settings again will not change that.

To get Opus back for this project only: put it in .claude/settings.local.json, which sits above the shared project file.

{
  "model": "claude-opus-4-8"
}

And unset ANTHROPIC_MODEL, or the variable keeps winning over the file you just wrote.

Two practical notes. model is one of the three keys read once at session start, so this takes effect on the next session — mid-session, use /model, and expect the cache invalidation that comes with a switch (§3.6). And if the model still is not what you set, /status names the loaded sources and the startup header names the file that set a project- or managed-supplied model, which resolves the question in one glance.

The general lesson: three mechanisms can set the same key — files by precedence, environment variables per pair, and flags per key — and only the first is a stack. When a value is not what you expect, check for a variable before re-reading the precedence list.

Exercise 6.2 — Design the team's settings file. You are the first person on a six-person team to set up Claude Code on a Python/Postgres service. Write the committed .claude/settings.json you would open a pull request with, and justify each key. Then say what you deliberately left out.

Solution 
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(uv run *)",
      "Bash(pytest *)",
      "Bash(ruff *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Bash(git log *)",
      "Bash(git status *)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(git push *)",
      "Bash(alembic upgrade *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Edit(**/migrations/versions/**)"
    ]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "if": "Edit(*.py)",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/format.sh",
            "args": []
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  "env": {
    "DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://localhost:5432/service_dev"
  }
}

The allow list is the project's daily commands — the ones every developer approves in their first hour anyway, so committing them saves six people six identical decisions and, more importantly, makes them consistent. Note Bash(uv run *) rather than Bash(*): the * goes after the subcommand (§5.2), and a wildcard before it would allow far more than intended.

The ask list is the two operations with consequences. git push and a migration are both reversible-with-effort rather than free, and an ask rule outranks every permission mode (§5.5) — so this holds even for a teammate running in auto mode. That property is the reason to put it in the committed file rather than trusting everyone's local setup.

The deny list has one rule that is not obvious. .env is standard. Edit(**/migrations/versions/**) blocks editing applied migrations, which is the class of change that produces a schema drift nobody notices for a week. Note Edit, not Write — a path rule on Write is accepted and never consulted (§5.4).

The hook makes formatting a property rather than a habit (§9.1), with if narrowing it to Python files so it does not spawn on every edit.

env carries the local database URL because it is a fact about the project, and a teammate who has to discover it is a teammate whose first session fails confusingly.

What I left out, and why.

Anything with a credential. No API keys, no production URLs, no tokens. The dev database URL is fine because it is local and useless elsewhere; anything else uses ${VAR} expansion or a helper.

model and effortLevel. Committing a model choice overrides every teammate's user setting — shared project sits above user — and imposes a cost profile on six people who may reasonably differ. Let them choose.

outputStyle, theme, vimMode, spinnerTipsEnabled. Personal taste, and a committed value is a small daily irritation for five people.

defaultMode. Tempting, and I would leave it out on a first pass. It is a real change to how everyone's sessions behave, and it deserves a conversation rather than arriving in a settings pull request.

The reviewable rule I would state in the PR description: this file should contain only things that are true of the project — its commands, its boundaries, its conventions, its environment. Anything true of a person belongs in their own file. That test resolves nearly every future argument about what goes in here.

SECTION 7

Verification: Making Claude Prove Its Work

One practice in this course changes more than any other, and it is not a feature. It is this:

Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available — and you become the verification loop. Every mistake waits for you to notice it.

Give Claude something that produces a pass or a fail, such as a test command, and the loop closes on its own. Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and tries again until the check passes. Nothing else in this course changes how a session feels as much, and nothing else takes as much work off your attention. It is the difference between a session you have to watch and one you can walk away from.

That is why this section sits where it does. Sections 1–6 got Claude configured. From here on, the course is about extending that setup: to skills, hooks, subagents and CI (continuous integration, the automated checks that run on every change). None of that scaling is safe without verification, because every mechanism after this one puts more distance between you and the work. A run nobody watches, with no check, is just a faster way to produce something that looks right.

7.1 What Counts as a Check

The bar is lower than people assume. A check is anything that returns a signal Claude can read in the conversation. It does not have to be a formal test suite or a CI pipeline. It just has to give a signal.

A test suite
The strongest signal, when one exists. Names the failure, points at the line, and distinguishes "broken differently" from "still broken".
A build gate
Weaker but universal. A build gate — the compiler or type checker exiting non-zero — catches an entire class of error and needs no test authoring at all, which makes it the check to reach for in a repository with no tests. A type check is also the fastest of the three, so it is the one that can afford to run after every edit.
A linter
Narrow and cheap. Style, unused symbols, common bug patterns — and a linter runs in a second, which matters when it runs after every edit rather than once at the end.
A diff against a fixture
The underrated one. A script that runs the thing and compares output to a known-good file works where no test framework exists, and takes ten minutes to write.
A screenshot
For anything visual. Claude opens the page, captures it, compares it against the design, lists the differences, fixes them (§7.5).

The prompt-level version costs nothing and works today. Compare these pairs. In each one, the difference is that the second prompt carries a check:

Verification criteria
"implement a function that validates email addresses" → "write a validateEmail function. example test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. run the tests after implementing"
Visual verification
"make the dashboard look better" → "[screenshot] implement this design. take a screenshot of the result and compare it to the original. list differences and fix them"
Root cause, not symptom
"the build is failing" → "the build fails with this error: [error]. fix it and verify the build succeeds. address the root cause, don't suppress the error"

The third pair carries an extra instruction worth noticing. "Address the root cause, don't suppress the error" is there because a check creates an incentive, and sometimes the cheapest way to make a check pass is to switch it off. An agent told only "make the build pass" may quite reasonably add a type assertion, widen a catch block, or skip a test. Each of those satisfies the letter of the check. So state the constraint, and combine it with the habit from §7.7: read the evidence.

7.2 The Verification Loop

The loop has four steps, and it is worth naming them, because most of the rest of this section is about making one of the steps automatic.

Work
Claude makes a change.
Check
Claude runs the thing that produces a signal.
Read
Claude reads the result — the failure message, the diff, the exit code.
Iterate
Claude changes the code and goes back to step two, until the check passes.

The step that does the real work is the third one. That is why a check with specific output beats a check that only says yes or no. A test suite that says expected 200, got 401 at auth.test.ts:44 gives the next attempt somewhere to go. A script that exits 1 with no output gives it nothing but permission to guess. When you build a check for Claude, spend your effort on what it prints when it fails, not on what it prints when it passes.

The loop also explains why the first thing to do in an unfamiliar repository is find out how to run the tests, and then to write that command into CLAUDE.md (§4.1). If a project's test command is a three-step ritual nobody wrote down, every session starts by working it out again, and sometimes Claude will give up and declare the work done instead.

7.3 Four Ways to Gate the Stop

Once the check exists, decide how strictly it should hold Claude back. There are four levels. Each one trades more setup effort for less of your attention.

In one prompt
"Run the tests and iterate until they pass." Zero setup, works on any task today, and applies only to that task. Start here.
Across a session — /goal
A separate evaluator re-checks a condition after every turn and Claude keeps working until it resolves. Session-scoped, typed rather than configured.
Deterministic — a Stop hook
Your check as a script, blocking the turn from ending until it passes (§9.8). Lives in settings, applies to every session in its scope.
Adversarial review
A verification subagent or a workflow that refutes its own findings (§11). An adversarial review has a fresh model try to disprove the result, so the agent doing the work is not the one grading it.

/goal is the one most people have not met, and it fills a real gap:

/goal all tests in test/auth pass and the lint step is clean

Setting a goal starts a turn immediately, with the condition as the instruction. After each turn, a small fast model checks whether the condition holds. If not, Claude starts another turn instead of handing control back to you. The goal ends when the condition is met, when the model judges it impossible, or when a turn fails with an error you have to fix. A ◎ /goal active indicator shows how long it has been running, and Ctrl+O shows the reason behind each verdict.

Two constraints shape how you write the condition, and both follow from one fact: the evaluator judges your condition against what Claude has surfaced in the conversation. The evaluator does not run commands or read files itself. So the condition must be something Claude's own output can prove. "All tests in test/auth pass" works, because Claude runs the tests and the result appears in the transcript. "There are no remaining race conditions" does not, because nothing Claude prints can prove it.

The second constraint is about permissions: a goal does not change your permission mode. In Manual mode, Claude still asks before every tool call your settings do not already allow. So a /goal meant to run unattended needs auto mode or the right allow rules (§5.1). Otherwise it will sit waiting for you at the first test run.

Approach
Next turn starts when
Stops when
/goal
The previous turn finishes
A model confirms the condition, or judges it impossible, or a turn fails on an error you must fix
/loop
A time interval elapses
You stop it, or Claude decides the work is done
Stop hook
The previous turn finishes
Your own script or prompt decides

/goal and a Stop hook both fire after every turn. The differences are scope and determinism (whether the same input always gives the same verdict). /goal is typed by you, lasts for one session, and is judged by a model. A Stop hook lives in a settings file, applies to every session in its scope, and can run a script. A script is what you want when the condition is mechanical and you would rather have no model judgement in the loop at all.

Note also that auto mode and /goal are complementary rather than alternatives. Auto mode removes the prompts for each tool call inside a turn. /goal removes the stop at the end of each turn. Together they are what an unattended run actually needs; either one alone leaves a gap where the session waits for you.

7.4 Explore, Plan, Code, Verify

The instruction to explore first begins a four-phase routine that is worth adopting in full, and verification is its last phase. The reason to adopt all of it is that the failure it prevents, a well-built solution to the wrong problem, is invisible to every check you could write.

Explore first
Plan mode: read and understand, change nothing. "Read src/auth and understand how we handle sessions and login. Also look at how we manage environment variables for secrets."
Plan
Ask for a plan while still read-only. "I want to add Google OAuth. What files need to change? What's the session flow? Create a plan." Ctrl+G opens it in your editor to edit directly.
Implement
Approve the plan and let Claude code against it — with the check named in the same breath: "implement the OAuth flow from your plan. Write tests for the callback handler, run the test suite and fix any failures."
Commit
"Commit with a descriptive message and open a PR." The commit is the last verification step, because the diff is the artefact a human will actually read.

The value of separating the first two phases from the third is that a plan is cheap to reject and an implementation is not. Reading a plan takes a minute. Reading a 600-line diff only to discover it solved the wrong problem takes twenty, and leads to an awkward conversation about whether to keep any of it.

Plan mode does have real overhead, and the advice against overusing it is specific: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. Fixing a typo, adding a log line, renaming a variable: just ask. Planning is worth its cost when you are unsure about the approach, when the change spans several files, or when you do not know the code being changed.

7.5 Verifying What You Cannot Test

Some changes have no natural check: a layout, an animation, the formatting of a CLI's output, an error message a person will read. Three mechanisms cover them.

Chrome integration connects Claude to your browser. It opens new tabs, uses your existing logins, and carries out actions in a visible window in real time. It stops to ask you when it reaches a login page or a CAPTCHA. That makes a real verification loop possible for web work: build the UI from a mock-up, open it, take a screenshot, compare, fix, repeat. It also reads console errors and DOM state directly (the DOM is the browser's live structure of the page), which covers the whole category of bug that only appears in a browser. Note the requirements: a Chromium-based browser, the Claude in Chrome extension, and a direct Anthropic plan with /login sign-in. An API key or a long-lived token keeps Chrome integration off, because the extension cannot authenticate with those credentials.

For mobile work the same idea has its own surface. The desktop app opens your app in an iOS simulator pane when Claude builds or runs it, with a separate iOS simulator for each session. That gives you a screenshot loop on a mobile platform, where there is no browser to point at. Watching a run from your phone is a different thing again; §14.6 covers the mobile app.

Computer use goes further. With computer use, Claude opens applications, clicks, types and sees your screen. It runs on your actual desktop, not in an isolated environment (§5.7), and each application needs your permission first. It is the right tool for a native app or a workflow that only has a graphical interface. It is the wrong tool for anything you would not want happening on the machine you are sitting at.

/run and /verify (§8.8) are the built-in skills for this. /run launches and drives your app. /verify builds and runs it to confirm a change does what it should, deliberately without falling back to tests or type checks, and that is the point. A change can pass every test and still not work, and /verify exists to catch exactly that gap. Both work out how to launch the app from your project type and from what is in the README, package.json or Makefile. That guess gets worse for anything that needs a database, an env file or a multi-step build. /run-skill-generator records the real recipe once, and every agent in the repository follows it after that.

7.6 Where the Loop Breaks

Here are five failure modes, each with a specific fix. Learn to recognise them by their symptom, because the fix is rarely "try harder".

The kitchen-sink session
One task, then something unrelated, then back. Context is full of irrelevant material. Fix: /clear between unrelated tasks (§3.4).
Correcting over and over
Wrong, corrected, still wrong, corrected again. The window is now polluted with failed approaches, each of which is evidence for the next attempt. Fix: after two failed corrections, /clear and write a better initial prompt incorporating what you learned.
The over-specified CLAUDE.md
Too long, so half of it is lost in the noise. Fix: prune ruthlessly. If Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it — or convert it to a hook (§4.6).
The trust-then-verify gap
A plausible implementation that does not handle the edge cases. Fix: always provide verification. If you cannot verify it, do not ship it.
Infinite exploration
"Investigate this" with no scope; hundreds of files read. Fix: scope the investigation, or delegate it to a subagent so it fills someone else's window (§11.1).

The second one deserves emphasis, because instinct pushes the other way. After two failed corrections, the temptation is to correct a third time, and the third correction usually goes worse than the first. The window now holds two wrong approaches, both visible to the model, and the conversation has drifted from the problem to the misunderstanding. Starting over with a better prompt is faster nearly every time. And the two failures were not wasted: they showed you what the prompt was missing.

7.7 Evidence, Not Assertion

The habit that makes all of this reviewable: have Claude show evidence rather than assert success.

"Fixed and tested" is a claim. The test output, the command it ran and what that command returned, the screenshot of the result: those are evidence. Reviewing evidence is faster than running the verification again yourself. It is also the only thing that works for a session you were not watching, which is the whole basis of §11's parallel work and §14's automation.

The failure this catches is specific and common. An agent that ran the tests, saw two failures, fixed one, and reported "tests are passing" is not lying. It is summarising, and summaries lose exactly the detail you needed. The output would have shown the second failure. Asking for the output costs one sentence in the prompt.

Two habits follow from it.

Ask for the command as well as the result. "The tests pass" is much less useful than "npm test -- test/auth → 14 passed, 0 failed", because the second tells you which tests ran. An agent that ran only the auth tests and reported success has told you nothing about the rest of the codebase, and the summary hides that difference.

Treat a passing check as evidence about the check, not only about the code. If a test suite still passes after a change that should have broken it, the suite has a hole. That is a really valuable finding, and you only get it if you read the output: the same argument as before, arriving from the other direction.

The sentence worth keeping from this whole section: a check Claude can run is worth more than any amount of instruction about being careful. Instructions shape intent; a check produces a fact. Everything after this section — hooks, subagents, CI, unattended runs — is a way of putting more distance between you and the work, and the check is the only thing that makes that distance safe.

Exercises

Exercise 7.1 — Build a check where there isn't one. You inherit a Python CLI with no tests, no type hints, and a README showing four example invocations with their expected output. Claude needs to refactor its argument parsing. Design a verification loop, and say how long you would spend building it.

Solution

The README is already a test suite; it just is not executable yet. Four invocations with expected output is a fixture set, and turning it into a check is a twenty-line script:

#!/bin/bash
# check.sh — run each documented example and diff against expectations
set -u
fail=0
for case in tests/cases/*.txt; do
  cmd=$(head -1 "$case")
  expected=$(tail -n +2 "$case")
  actual=$(eval "$cmd" 2>&1)
  if [[ "$actual" != "$expected" ]]; then
    echo "FAIL: $cmd"
    diff <(echo "$expected") <(echo "$actual") | head -20
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit "$fail"

This is also where a test-driven loop earns its reputation with an agent, for a reason that has nothing to do with design purity: a failing test written first is a check that exists before the code does, so the loop can close on the very first iteration. "Write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it" is the most reliable single instruction in this course, and it is test-driven development arrived at from the direction of verification rather than of methodology.

Time budget: about thirty minutes, and that is the answer to the second half of the question. A refactor of argument parsing on an untested CLI without a check is a change nobody can review with confidence, and thirty minutes buys the entire rest of the work. If the refactor is a two-hour job, the check pays for itself the first time it catches something.

Two design decisions matter more than the code. The script prints the diff on failure, not just "FAIL" — §7.2's point that the third step of the loop is the one doing the work, and a check with no output gives the next iteration nothing to go on. And it captures stderr as well as stdout with 2>&1, because an argument parser's most interesting behaviour is what it says about bad input.

Then hand Claude the loop, not just the task: "Refactor the argument parsing in cli.py to use argparse subcommands. Run ./check.sh after each change and fix any failures. Do not modify the files in tests/cases/ — they are the specification."

That last sentence is §7.1's incentive problem stated in advance. The cheapest way to make a fixture-diff check pass is to edit the fixtures, and an agent asked only to make the check pass may reasonably do so. Once the fixtures are named as the specification, the only route left is fixing the code.

A second-order benefit worth naming: you now have a regression suite the project did not have. The verification you built for one refactor is permanent, which is often the strongest argument for spending the thirty minutes at all.

Exercise 7.2 — /goal, hook, or prompt? For each, choose one of the four gating levels from §7.3 and justify it: (a) migrating 60 call sites to a new API until everything compiles; (b) making sure nobody's turn ever ends with a failing type-check, on any session in this repository; (c) a one-off "fix this flaky test"; (d) confirming a security-sensitive refactor did not introduce a vulnerability.

Solution

(a) /goal. Sixty call sites is many turns of mechanical work with a verifiable end state — exactly what /goal is for. /goal every call site of the old client compiles and the test suite is green starts a turn immediately and keeps starting them until the evaluator agrees. Two things to get right: run it in auto mode or with allow rules for the build command, since a goal does not change your permission mode and will otherwise stop at the first prompt; and write the condition as something Claude's own output can demonstrate, because the evaluator reads the transcript rather than running anything itself. "Everything compiles" works because the build output lands in the conversation.

(b) A Stop hook. "On any session in this repository" is the deciding phrase: /goal is session-scoped and typed each time, while a hook lives in .claude/settings.json, is committed, and applies to every teammate's sessions automatically. It is also deterministic — a script, not a model's judgement — which is what you want for a mechanical condition. Remember the stop_hook_active guard and the eight-block cap (§9.8), and expect it to need a background_tasks check so it does not fire while a generation step is still running.

(c) In the prompt. A one-off needs no configuration: "This test fails about one run in twenty. Run it fifty times, classify the failures, then fix the root cause and prove it by running it fifty more times." Note that the prompt itself contains the check and its threshold — the loop is fully specified in one message, which is what makes prompt-level gating work at all.

(d) A second opinion, plus a prompt-level check. Security is the case where the agent doing the work is the worst possible grader, because a vulnerability it did not consider while writing is a vulnerability it will not consider while reviewing. A fresh subagent with a read-only tool list and an adversarial brief — "try to find a way to bypass the authorisation check in this diff" — is a genuinely different model attempt rather than a re-read. /security-review is the bundled version. Keep the ordinary tests as well: they catch the regressions the security review is not looking for.

The dividing lines: scope (one task → prompt; one session → /goal; every session → hook) and who judges (mechanical → script; requires judgement → model; adversarial → a different model with a different brief).

Exercise 7.3 — The check that was gamed. A Stop hook runs npm test and blocks until it passes. After a week, a teammate notices the suite is green but three tests now start with it.skip, and a fourth asserts expect(result).toBeDefined() where it used to assert a value. Nobody did this deliberately. Explain what happened, and redesign the gate.

Solution

What happened: the gate specified the wrong thing, and got exactly what it asked for. The hook says "the test command must exit 0", and skipping a test and weakening an assertion are both legitimate ways to make a test command exit 0. There is no bad intent here in either the agent or the teammates — it is a straightforward optimisation against a stated objective, and the objective was under-specified.

This is §7.1's incentive problem at scale. The Stop hook applies to every session in the repository and blocks the turn from ending, which makes it a strong pressure — and the stronger the gate, the more valuable it becomes to satisfy it cheaply. A weak check that is merely suggested rarely gets gamed; a hard gate on a weak check reliably does.

Redesign, in three parts.

One: gate on more than the exit code. The hook should fail if the test count drops or the skip count rises:

#!/bin/bash
input=$(cat)
[[ "$(jq -r '.stop_hook_active' <<<"$input")" == "true" ]] && exit 0
result=$(npm test --silent --json 2>&1) || {
  jq -nc --arg r "$result" '{decision: "block", reason: ("Tests failing:\n" + $r)}'
  exit 0
}
skipped=$(jq -r '.numPendingTests' <<<"$result")
baseline=$(cat .claude/test-baseline 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
if (( skipped > baseline )); then
  jq -nc --arg s "$skipped" --arg b "$baseline" \
    '{decision: "block", reason: ("Skipped tests rose from " + $b + " to " + $s + ". Unskip them or explain why in the commit message.")}'
fi

Two: put the weakened-assertion problem where it belongs. No exit code can catch toBeDefined() replacing a value assertion — that is a semantic change, and the mechanism for semantic changes is human review of the diff. Add tests to the paths a reviewer must look at, and if you want it caught earlier, an agent hook (§9.9) can read the diff and object to assertions that got weaker. Note the honest limit: that is a model judging, so it is a filter, not a gate.

Three, and most important: state the constraint in CLAUDE.md. "Never skip a test or weaken an assertion to make the suite pass. If a test is wrong, fix the test and say so; if the code is wrong, fix the code." That does not enforce anything — §4.6's ladder is explicit about it — but it changes the default behaviour, and the checks above catch what it misses. The instruction where the reader is, the enforcement where it cannot be argued with, which is the same pairing §4 and §9 both arrive at.

The general lesson, and the one worth carrying past this exercise: a check is a proxy for the property you care about, and a hard gate applies pressure to the proxy rather than the property. So the design question is not "does this check pass?" but "what is the cheapest way to make this check pass, and would I be happy with it?" Ask that of every gate before you install it, and prefer a check whose cheapest satisfying answer is the one you actually wanted.

SECTION 8

Slash Commands and Skills

CLAUDE.md holds the facts that are always true. Section 4 was explicit: a fact belongs there only if it is worth its cost on every request, because CLAUDE.md is loaded into every conversation. Most of what a team wants to write down fails that test. A twelve-step release procedure is worth writing down. It is not worth carrying in the window for the eleven months of the year you are not releasing.

A skill is where that material goes. It is a SKILL.md file with instructions, and its body loads only when it is used. The list of skill names and descriptions always costs a little context. The content itself costs nothing until the moment it is relevant. That one property is why skills exist, and it is the whole basis for choosing between a skill and CLAUDE.md.

The sign that you want one is similar to §10's sign that you want MCP: when you notice yourself pasting the same instructions, checklist or procedure into chat, that material is a skill. The same goes for a part of CLAUDE.md that has quietly grown from a fact into a procedure.

Custom commands (your own /name shortcuts) have been merged into skills, and the merge is worth understanding properly. .claude/commands/deploy.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy and behave the same way. Existing command files keep working. Skills add three things a command file does not have: a directory for supporting files, frontmatter that controls who may invoke them, and the ability for Claude to load them on its own when relevant. (Frontmatter is a short block of settings at the top of the file.) Write new material as skills; leave working command files alone.

8.1 Two Kinds of Skill Content

Everything here is reached through a slash command: something you type starting with /. Your skills, the bundled skills, the built-in commands and MCP prompts all appear in the same slash command menu, and a custom command file in .claude/commands/ adds one too. To whoever types it, a custom command and a skill with the same name are the same thing.

Before any syntax, here is a distinction that decides everything else about how you write a skill.

Reference content
Knowledge Claude applies to the work in front of it. Conventions, patterns, a style guide, domain vocabulary. It runs inline, alongside your conversation, because it is meant to shape what happens next rather than to be a task.
Task content
Step-by-step instructions for a specific action. A deployment, a release, a code-generation recipe. You usually want to invoke these yourself with /name rather than have Claude decide when to run them.
---
name: api-conventions
description: API design patterns for this codebase
---

When writing API endpoints:
- Use RESTful naming conventions
- Return consistent error formats
- Include request validation

---
name: deploy
description: Deploy the application to production
context: fork
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Deploy the application:
1. Run the test suite
2. Build the application
3. Push to the deployment target

The second one carries two fields the first does not, and both follow from it being a task. disable-model-invocation: true means Claude will never decide by itself that now is a good moment to deploy. context: fork runs the skill in its own subagent context, covered in §8.7.

Keep the body concise, for a reason that surprises people. Once a skill loads, its content stays in context for the rest of the session — so every line is a recurring token cost from that point on, not a one-time one. State what to do rather than narrating why. The conciseness test is the same one §4 applies to CLAUDE.md, and it applies from the moment of first use rather than from session start.

8.2 Where Skills Live, and Who Wins

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/summarize-changes

The directory name becomes the command you type. Skills can live in four locations, and the precedence between them is the opposite of what most configuration systems do:

Location
Path
Applies to
Enterprise
Managed settings directory
Everyone in the organisation
Personal
~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
All your projects
Project
.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
This project only
Plugin
<plugin>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
Where the plugin is enabled

Enterprise overrides personal, and personal overrides project. The last part is the surprise. With a deploy skill in both ~/.claude/skills/ and the project's .claude/skills/, /deploy runs your personal one. Everywhere else in Claude Code (settings, CLAUDE.md, subagents) the more specific scope wins. Here the more personal one wins instead, on the reasoning that your own procedure should not be quietly replaced by one that arrived with a repository. That is a reasonable choice, and a real trap for anyone who assumes the usual direction.

Plugin skills live in a plugin-name:skill-name namespace, so they cannot clash with anything. A local skill overrides a bundled one with the same name, but not the bundled skill's aliases. So a project code-review skill replaces /code-review, while /review still runs the bundled one. That mismatch has fooled people into thinking their skill did not load.

Claude Code finds skills by looking upwards and inwards. Project skills load from .claude/skills/ in your starting directory and every parent up to the repository root, so starting Claude in a subdirectory still finds the root's skills. Skills in directories below your starting point are not loaded at startup. They become available the first time Claude reads or edits a file in that subdirectory, and stay for the session. Until then they do not appear in autocomplete and cannot be invoked. In a monorepo that is exactly right: packages/frontend/.claude/skills/ appears when you start working on the frontend.

When a nested skill has the same name as a root one, both stay available. The nested one appears under a name that includes its directory, such as /apps/web:deploy. Typing the plain /deploy loads the root skill plus a list of those longer-named variants, with an instruction to also invoke whichever one matches the files being worked on. Nothing is lost by typing the short name.

Skill directories are watched, so adding or editing a SKILL.md takes effect within the session. Creating a top-level skills directory that did not exist at startup needs a restart, because the watcher only covers directories that were already there.

8.3 Frontmatter That Earns Its Place

Skill frontmatter has many fields, and all of them are optional; only description is recommended. The fields below are the ones that change behaviour rather than just labelling the skill. Learn the two invocation-control fields first: nothing else in the skill frontmatter changes as much about how a skill is used.

description
What it does and when to use it. This is the routing rule Claude reads. Omitted, it falls back to the first paragraph of the body.
when_to_use
Extra trigger phrases, appended to description in the listing.
disable-model-invocation
true means only you can invoke it. Also stops it being preloaded into subagents and stops a scheduled task firing it.
user-invocable
false means only Claude can. Hidden from the / menu — for background knowledge nobody should trigger by hand.
allowed-tools
Tools usable without a permission prompt during the turn that invokes the skill. §8.6.
disallowed-tools
Tools removed from the pool while the skill is active. For an autonomous skill that must never call AskUserQuestion.
context: fork
Run in a forked subagent context. §8.7.
agent
Which subagent type context: fork uses.
paths
Glob patterns limiting automatic activation. Claude loads it on its own only when working with matching files.
model, effort
Override the model or effort level while the skill is active, for the current turn only.
arguments
Named positional arguments, for $name substitution in the body.
hooks
Hooks registered on invocation and kept for the rest of the session (§9.9).

A command file in .claude/commands/ supports the same command frontmatter as a skill, with two exceptions: name and paths are ignored there, and the command is invoked by its file name. That is the practical difference between the two formats. Command frontmatter is a subset, so anything that uses paths or supporting files has to be a skill.

name does not name the command in a personal or project skill; the directory does. There, name is only the label shown in lists. In a plugin skill it does set the last part of the command, with the plugin prefix in front. A file at .claude/skills/deploy-staging/SKILL.md is /deploy-staging no matter what name says.

String substitution covers arguments and paths:

$ARGUMENTS
Everything passed on invocation. If the placeholder is absent, arguments are appended as ARGUMENTS: <value>.
$0, $1, $ARGUMENTS[N]
One argument by zero-based index.
$name
A named argument declared in arguments, mapped by position.
${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}
The directory holding this SKILL.md. The reliable way to reference a bundled script whatever the working directory.
${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}
The project root — the same value hooks and stdio MCP servers receive.
${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}, ${CLAUDE_EFFORT}
The session ID and the active effort level.

8.4 Dynamic Context: Data, Not Instructions to Fetch Data

What makes a skill different in kind from a saved prompt is that a skill can run commands before Claude sees it. The command's output replaces the placeholder in the skill text.

---
description: Summarizes uncommitted changes and flags anything risky. Use when the user asks what changed, wants a commit message, or asks to review their diff.
---

## Current changes

!`git diff HEAD`

## Instructions

Summarize the changes above in two or three bullet points, then list any risks
you notice such as missing error handling, hardcoded values, or tests that need
updating. If the diff is empty, say there are no uncommitted changes.

Compare that with a skill that says "run git diff HEAD and summarise it". That second version costs a tool call, a permission check and a round trip, and Claude might decide to look at something else first. The first version arrives with the diff already inlined: Claude's very first token is written with the data already there.

For several commands there is a block form: open a fence whose language is a bare ! and put one command per line. In the SKILL.md source it looks like a normal fenced block opened with ! and closed with, holding lines such as node --version, npm --version and git status --short. Each one runs in order, and the whole fence is replaced by their combined output.

Both forms run before Claude sees a single character of the skill. That is the difference between a skill that tells Claude to gather data and one that arrives carrying it — and it is why a skill can be worth writing for a task you only do once a week.

The mechanics have edges worth knowing.

  • Substitution runs once over the original file. Command output is inserted as plain text and is not scanned again, so a command cannot print a placeholder for a later pass to expand.
  • The inline form is recognised only when ! starts a line or follows a space; KEY=!cmd`` is left as literal text.
  • Commands run in the session shell's current working directory, which changes when Claude runs cd. Anything that must always point to the same place should use ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} or ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}.
  • With the default bash shell, stderr (error output) is merged into stdout and appears in the inserted text.
  • Each command runs under the Bash tool's two-minute timeout.

"disableSkillShellExecution": true switches the whole mechanism off for user, project, plugin and additional-directory skills, replacing each command with a placeholder. It exists for managed settings. It is the right lever for an organisation that does not want skills supplied by a repository running shell commands as they load.

8.5 The Description Is the Product

For a skill Claude may invoke on its own, the description is not documentation. It is the whole mechanism Claude uses to decide when to use the skill, and it is where nearly all skill failures happen.

Claude Code loads a listing of every skill's name and description, so Claude knows what exists. The listing has a character budget of 1% of the model's context window, and each entry's combined description and when_to_use text is capped at 1,536 characters. When the listing goes over budget, Claude Code drops descriptions starting with the skills you invoke least. The names always survive; the descriptions do not.

That causes a failure worth recognising, because it looks as if the skill is broken. A skill that used to trigger stops triggering after you add a dozen more, and nothing about it changed. Its description was dropped to fit the budget, so Claude now sees a name with no text to match your request against. /doctor estimates the listing's cost and names the biggest contributors. The Skills row in /context reports the size after the budget is applied, so it matches what the model actually received.

Put the use case first
The cap truncates the end. "Use when the user asks what changed or wants a commit message" belongs in the first clause, not after two sentences of description.
Use the words people say
Match the request, not the implementation. "Summarizes uncommitted changes" routes; "Wraps the git plumbing for diff extraction" does not.
Raise the budget deliberately
skillListingBudgetFraction (e.g. 0.02) or SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET. Or set low-priority skills to "name-only" in skillOverrides to free room for the rest.
Or stop matching entirely
disable-model-invocation: true takes a skill out of the routing problem. If you always type /deploy, its description costs budget for nothing.

Two settings control skill visibility without editing anyone's file. skillOverrides in settings can set a skill to "off" to hide it entirely, "user-invocable-only" to keep it out of Claude's choices while you can still type it, or "name-only" to list it without a description. Skill visibility matters most for skills you did not write, such as a plugin's or a teammate's, where editing the frontmatter is not an option and the description is using up budget you want back.

Skill evaluation is the other half of getting a description right, and it is worth doing once for any skill the whole team relies on. The skill-creator tooling runs a skill against sample requests and reports whether it triggered when it should have. A skill eval turns "the description feels clear" into a number, the same move §7 makes for code.

Two more failures have simple causes. A skill that never triggers may have broken YAML. Claude Code then loads the body with empty metadata, so /name still works but Claude has no description to match against. It is a maddeningly specific symptom, and --debug explains it in one line. A skill that triggers too often needs a narrower description, a paths restriction, or disable-model-invocation.

And one that is not a failure at all. If a skill seems to stop influencing behaviour after the first response, the content is almost always still there, and the model is simply choosing other approaches. §8.6 covers what the content does over time. The fix is a stronger description and stronger instructions or, where something must happen every time, a hook (§9.1).

8.6 Lifecycle: What Persists and What Does Not

Two things happen when a skill is invoked, and they last for different lifetimes. Getting this wrong produces both of the classic skill bugs.

The content persists
The rendered SKILL.md enters the conversation as one message and stays for the rest of the session. Claude Code does not re-read the file on later turns.
The permissions do not
An allowed-tools grant clears when you send your next message. Invoking the skill again re-applies it for that turn.

The first half means write standing instructions, not one-time steps. A skill that says "first, do X" reads oddly on turn forty, when X happened half an hour ago. Guidance meant to apply throughout the task should be written as though it applies throughout the task, because it will stay in the window either way.

Invoking a skill again is cheap when nothing changed. If the rendered content is identical to the copy already in context, Claude Code adds a short "already loaded" note instead of a second copy. If the content differs (different arguments, or a ! command producing new output), the full content is added again. So a dynamic-context skill invoked five times puts five copies of its rendered output in the window. That is usually what you want, but know it before you invoke one in a loop.

Compaction handles skills specially, and the numbers matter in a long session. When the conversation is summarised, Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill after the summary, keeping the first 5,000 tokens of each. All of them together must fit a combined 25,000-token budget, filled starting from the most recently invoked skill and going backwards. In a session where you invoked many skills, the older ones are dropped entirely at compaction. If a skill mattered and the session has compacted, invoke it again.

The permission half is allowed-tools. It grants permission; it does not restrict anything:

---
name: commit
description: Stage and commit the current changes
disable-model-invocation: true
allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) Bash(git status *)
---

Those three commands run without asking during the turn that invoked the skill. It does not restrict anything: every other tool can still be called and is still governed by your normal permission settings. For a grant that lasts the whole session, use permission rules (§5.1) instead.

The pattern that makes allowed-tools really useful combines it with ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}, which is substituted in both the body and the Bash rules of allowed-tools:

---
name: render-chart
description: Render a chart from a CSV file
allowed-tools: Bash(${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/render.sh *)
---

Run `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/render.sh <csv-file>` to render the chart.

Both occurrences expand to the same path. So the rule matches exactly the command the body tells Claude to run: a bundled script that runs without a prompt and grants nothing else.

Workspace trust does not gate allowed-tools. Claude Code applies a project skill's grant whenever the skill is invoked, including in a -p run in a folder you have never trusted. A skill checked into a repository can therefore grant itself broad tool access. Review the allowed-tools of any repository's skills before running Claude Code in it — this is the same class of exposure as §9.10's hooks, arriving through a different file.

8.7 Supporting Files and Forked Skills

Two mechanisms extend a skill past a single file.

A skill is a directory, so it can hold more than SKILL.md:

my-skill/
├── SKILL.md        (required — overview and navigation)
├── reference.md    (detailed API docs — loaded when needed)
├── examples.md     (usage examples — loaded when needed)
└── scripts/
    └── helper.py   (executed, not loaded)

The rule is to keep SKILL.md under about 500 lines and to reference the others so Claude knows what each contains and when to read it:

## Additional resources

- For complete API details, see [reference.md](reference.md)
- For usage examples, see [examples.md](examples.md)

This is progressive disclosure one level deeper than §8's opening argument, and progressive disclosure is the whole design. The listing costs a description. The skill costs its body. The body costs the reference file only when the task needs it. A 6,000-line API specification can sit in a skill directory and cost nothing until the day it is relevant.

context: fork runs the skill in its own subagent context. The skill content becomes the prompt that drives the subagent, and the subagent does not see your conversation history:

---
name: deep-research
description: Research a topic thoroughly
context: fork
agent: Explore
---

Research $ARGUMENTS thoroughly:
1. Find relevant files using Glob and Grep
2. Read and analyze the code
3. Summarize findings with specific file references

The fork runs in the background by default: you keep working, and its result arrives when it finishes. background: false makes the invoking turn wait for it. Claude Code waits anyway in -p mode and in the SDK, when background tasks are disabled, when an earlier invocation of the same skill is still running, and when a scheduled task fires the skill.

Two consequences of running in the background are easy to get caught by. First, a backgrounded fork runs with the narrower background tool set from §11.2. The skill's subagent is a regular agent type, so the fork exemption does not apply, and a skill whose steps need a tool outside that set must set background: false. Second, a backgrounded fork's edits fall outside your session's checkpoints, so /rewind will not undo them; git will.

context: fork only makes sense for a skill with an explicit task. A reference skill that says "use these API conventions" hands the subagent a set of guidelines and no work to do, and it returns with nothing. Reference content runs inline; task content forks.

Skills and subagents combine in both directions, and the table is worth keeping in mind. A skill with context: fork takes its system prompt from the agent type and its task from SKILL.md. A subagent with a skills field takes its system prompt from its own body and its task from Claude's delegation message, and it preloads the skills as reference material. Pick the first when what you wrote down is the task, and the second when what you wrote down is the worker.

8.8 Bundled Skills and Built-In Commands

Not every / command is something you wrote. Claude Code ships built-in commands, whose behaviour is coded into the CLI, and bundled skills, which are prompts handed to Claude exactly like your own: /doctor, /code-review, /batch, /debug, /loop, /claude-api. Claude invokes some of these by itself. Others, including /verify, run only when you ask, so a long check never spends your tokens without being asked.

Three bundled skills form a loop worth knowing about, because they fill the gap §7 is about:

/run
Launch and drive your app to see a change working.
/verify
Build and run the app to confirm a change does what it should — deliberately without falling back to tests or type checks.
/run-skill-generator
Teach the other two how to build and launch this project, recording the recipe as a per-project skill.

/run and /verify work with no setup: they work out how to launch the app from your project type and from what is in the README, package.json or Makefile. That guess gets worse for anything that needs a database, an env file, a graphical session or a multi-step build. /run-skill-generator gets the app running from a clean environment, records what worked, and commits it to .claude/skills/run-<name>/. From then on every agent in the repository follows the recipe instead of working it out again. Run it once per project, and again when the build changes.

An MCP prompt is the third source of / commands, next to your skills and the bundled ones. A connected MCP server can offer prompts. They appear as /mcp__servername__promptname, take arguments separated by spaces, and insert their result straight into the conversation (§10.1). So an MCP prompt is a command someone else maintains. That is useful, and worth knowing when a / command you did not write appears in the menu.

disableBundledSkills turns all of them off except /doctor. Chaining works too: /skill-a /skill-b do XYZ loads both and passes the trailing text to each, up to six.

8.9 Skill, CLAUDE.md, Subagent, or Hook?

All four put instructions in front of the model, and the differences are sharp once stated.

CLAUDE.md
Always loaded, always true, small. Facts about the project that shape every turn: the package manager, the test command, the one rule that is always violated. §4.
Skill
Loaded when relevant, arbitrarily long. Procedures, reference material, checklists. The body costs nothing until used, so length is affordable in a way it never is in CLAUDE.md.
Subagent
A worker with its own window and its own tool restrictions. Reach for it when the isolation is the point rather than the instructions. §11.
Hook
Runs whether the model wanted it to or not. The only one of the four that is a guarantee rather than a strong suggestion. §9.

Projects really do move material between them, and it helps to recognise the path. A fact goes into CLAUDE.md. Over months it gathers steps and becomes a procedure, and CLAUDE.md is now paying for twelve lines on every request that matter one day in thirty, so move it to a skill. Then you notice the procedure gets skipped when the session is long and the stakes are high. So the step that must not be skipped becomes a hook, while the rest of the procedure stays a skill. Each move is triggered by something you observed, not by taste, and using all three together is what a mature configuration looks like.

Exercises

Exercise 8.1 — Place the material. For each, say whether it belongs in CLAUDE.md, a skill (and if so, which frontmatter fields), a subagent, or a hook: (a) "this repo uses pnpm, never npm"; (b) a 40-line procedure for cutting a release, run about once a month; (c) a 2,000-line internal API reference that Claude needs only when touching the billing module; (d) "run the formatter after editing"; (e) a checklist for reviewing a database migration, which you want applied whenever a migration file changes.

Solution

(a) CLAUDE.md. One line, always true, and relevant on almost every turn — this is the shape CLAUDE.md is for. Note it also passes §4's cost test: the wrong package manager produces a lockfile conflict every time, so the line pays for itself.

(b) A skill, with disable-model-invocation: true. Forty lines used monthly is exactly the material that should not sit in CLAUDE.md. The frontmatter matters: you never want Claude to decide on its own that now is a good moment to cut a release, and disabling model invocation also frees the description from the listing budget, since you will always type /release. Consider context: fork if the procedure is long and self-contained.

(c) A skill with supporting files. SKILL.md is short — what the API is, which file holds what, when to read each — and the 2,000 lines live in reference.md beside it. Add paths: packages/billing/** so Claude loads it automatically only when working in that module. The cost profile is the whole point: the description costs a few dozen characters always, the SKILL.md costs a page when billing work starts, and the reference costs nothing until a question needs it.

(d) A hook. PostToolUse on Edit|Write. It must happen every time, the model will occasionally forget on a long turn, and the miss is invisible until review — §9.1's exact criteria. Written as a skill or a CLAUDE.md line it would be followed most of the time, and "most" is the wrong target for a mechanical step.

(e) A skill with paths, plus a hook if it must be enforced — and the split is the interesting part. The checklist is judgement (is this migration reversible, will it lock the table) and belongs in a skill with paths: **/migrations/** so it loads when a migration is in play.
