Unrelated to both: these control approval of servers defined in a project's .mcp.json.

Claude Code checks exactly one list per server, so neither overrides the other, and an entry in the wrong list is ignored without any warning. Adding a regular server to enabledMcpServers does nothing at all. That looks exactly like a bug, and it is not one.

Finally, the direction nobody expects: Claude Code can itself be an MCP server, offering its own tools to another MCP client over stdio. It is a small feature with a large implication. "Client" and "server" here are roles, not properties of the software, and a Claude Code session can sit inside someone else's agent as one of its tools.

10.9 Tool Search: Why Ten Servers Are Affordable

§10.1 said tool definitions cost context on every request. Left alone, that puts a hard limit on how many servers you can connect, and it is a low limit, because tool definitions arrive with full JSON Schemas.

MCP tool search removes the ceiling by deferring the definitions. Only the tool names and the server's own instructions load at session start. The full definition arrives when Claude searches for a tool and picks it. Adding servers then costs almost nothing until their tools are used, and the practical limit becomes your context budget instead of a limit per server.

It is on by default. The cases where it is off are worth knowing, because they explain a session that suddenly feels heavy:

  • it is disabled when ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at a host that is not Anthropic's own, because most proxies do not pass on tool_reference blocks;
  • it is refused on the server side on Microsoft Foundry deployments hosted on Azure, and no setting overrides that, because the refusal comes from the Microsoft Foundry deployment itself;
  • it needs a model that supports tool_reference blocks: Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5, Opus 4.5 and later.
(unset)
All MCP tools deferred, with the fallbacks above.
true
Deferred even through a proxy — and requests fail on a proxy that cannot handle tool_reference blocks.
auto
Threshold mode: load tools upfront while their definitions total under 10% of the context window; defer all of them once they reach it.
auto:N
Threshold mode with your own percentage, 0–100.
false
Everything upfront, no deferral.
ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto:5 claude

auto is the setting worth understanding, because it captures the real trade-off. A search step costs a round trip. A definition loaded up front costs tokens on every request. Below a certain volume, loading up front is simply better: the definitions are cheap and Claude never has to look anything up. Threshold mode loads up front while that is cheap and defers once it is not, switching at a number you can set.

The escape hatch in the other direction is per-server:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "core-tools": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
      "alwaysLoad": true
    }
  }
}

alwaysLoad exempts a server from deferral entirely, for the few tools Claude needs on every turn. It has a startup cost: alwaysLoad: true makes startup wait for that server's tools, up to the 5-second connect timeout, because they must exist when the first prompt is built. Use it on one server, not on five.

If you write MCP servers, MCP tool search changes what your server instructions field is for. With definitions deferred, those instructions (capped at 2KB, like tool descriptions) are much of what Claude sees when deciding whether to search your server at all. Write them the way you would write a skill description (§8.5): what kind of task the tools handle, when to look for them, and what the server can do. Put the most important part first, because cutting happens at the end.

10.10 Choosing What to Connect

Three questions, in order, decide whether a server belongs in your configuration.

Am I pasting from it?
If you are not, do not connect it. A server you might use one day costs context and widens the trust surface today. This is the whole heuristic and it is a good one.
Can a CLI do it?
Often, and better. gh, aws, kubectl and psql already exist, already authenticate, and cost nothing in tool definitions because Bash is one tool. An MCP server earns its place when the CLI is missing, awkward to script, or returns unstructured output.
What can it reach?
State the blast radius in one sentence before connecting. "Read-only on our issue tracker" is a sentence. "Full access to production" is also a sentence, and a reason to scope the token down first (§10.5).

The second row deserves emphasis, because it is the least obvious. A GitHub MCP server and the gh CLI overlap heavily, and the CLI wins on context. Every gh command goes through the single Bash tool definition you were already paying for, while the MCP server brings twenty schemas. The server wins when you want structured results Claude can use without parsing text, when signing in through the CLI would be a chore for every teammate, or when there is no CLI at all. Both are legitimate. The point is that "there is an MCP server for it" is not an argument on its own.

Where a server really is useful, the setup that works is narrow and limited. A read-only database server pointed at a replica (a copy of the database). An issue tracker with read access plus an explicit create_issue you approve each time. A monitoring server that can query alerts but not silence them. §5's permission rules apply to MCP tools like any other: mcp__sentry__.* in allow, a specific dangerous tool in ask. A narrow token combined with a narrow permission rule is what makes a connected server something you can stop thinking about.

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Server or CLI? For each, decide whether to connect an MCP server or use an existing command-line tool, and justify it: (a) reading and commenting on GitHub pull requests; (b) querying a production PostgreSQL replica for support investigations; (c) fetching the current on-call rota from an internal service with a REST API and no CLI; (d) reading Figma designs to implement a component.

Solution

(a) The gh CLI. It exists, it is already authenticated on most developer machines, and it costs one Bash tool definition rather than twenty schemas. Claude writes gh pr view 412 --json files,body as naturally as it writes any command, and the --json flag gives structured output where it matters. Connect the GitHub MCP server instead if your team wants a single permission surface for GitHub actions — mcp__github__.* in an allow rule is easier to reason about than a set of Bash(gh *) patterns — but that is a permissions argument, not a capability one.

(b) An MCP server, and this is the clearest case for one. psql would work, but the server buys two things a CLI cannot: results returned as structured data rather than a formatted table Claude must parse, and — more importantly — a connection scoped once, in configuration, rather than in every command. Point it at the replica with a read-only role. The trap to avoid: MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS will not save you from a careless SELECT *; the discipline of asking for LIMIT belongs in CLAUDE.md.

(c) An MCP server, or a small script. With no CLI, the alternatives are a server or curl plus a token in an environment variable. If the rota is the only thing you need from that service, a two-line Bash recipe in CLAUDE.md is less machinery than a server. If it is the first of several things you will want, write the server — and note that a stdio server here is fine and probably simpler than hosting an HTTP one.

(d) An MCP server. There is no CLI, the data is not text you can pipe, and images and structured design metadata are exactly what the resource and tool mechanisms are for. This is the case where MCP is doing something no other route can.

The general rule: MCP wins on structured data and scoped connections; a CLI wins on context cost and already existing. When both work, count the tool definitions before deciding.

Exercise 10.2 — The committed configuration. Your team commits this .mcp.json. Identify every problem, and say what each one does when a colleague clones the repository.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "metrics": {
      "url": "https://mcp.metrics.internal/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer sk-live-9f2a41c8" }
    },
    "workspace": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/tools/workspace-server.js"]
    },
    "db": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "${DB_MCP_URL}",
      "alwaysLoad": true
    }
  }
}
Solution

Four problems, one per entry and one across them.

metrics has a url and no type. Claude Code reads a typeless entry as a stdio server, so this one is skipped entirely with MCP server "metrics" has a "url" but no "type". The colleague sees no metrics tools and, unless they read that line, no obvious reason why. Add "type": "http".

metrics also has a live bearer token committed to the repository. This is the serious one: it is now in the git history of everyone who has ever cloned, it survives deleting the line, and it must be rotated rather than removed. Replace it with "Bearer ${METRICS_TOKEN}" and document the variable — or use headersHelper to mint a short-lived token, which removes the class of problem rather than relocating it.

workspace is a reserved name. workspace, claude-in-chrome, computer-use, Claude Preview and Claude Browser name built-in servers. Claude Code skips the entry at load time and shows a rename warning. Rename it — project-tools, say. Note that ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} in the args also needs a default here: the variable is set in the server's environment, not Claude Code's, so a project-scoped entry should write ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.} to expand reliably.

db combines an unset variable with alwaysLoad. If DB_MCP_URL is not set on the colleague's machine, the config still loads: Claude Code warns in claude mcp list and uses the literal ${DB_MCP_URL} as the URL, which then fails to connect in a way that looks like a network problem. And because alwaysLoad: true makes startup wait for this server's tools up to the 5-second connect timeout, every session on that machine now starts five seconds slower for a server that will never connect. Give it a default, and drop alwaysLoad unless Claude genuinely needs database tools on every turn.

And the thing that is not a problem but will look like one: the colleague is prompted to approve all three servers before they are used, and if they clone into a folder they have never trusted, approvals committed in .claude/settings.json are ignored and the servers sit at ⏸ Pending approval. That is the trust model working — a repository cannot grant itself connections — and the fix is to run claude in the directory once and accept the dialog, not to work around it.

The reviewable rule this produces: a committed .mcp.json should contain no secrets, no reserved names, an explicit type on every remote entry, and a default on every variable. Those four checks take ten seconds and catch everything above.

Exercise 10.3 — The context budget. A colleague connects six MCP servers and reports that sessions now start with 38% of the context window already consumed and that Claude feels slower to respond. Diagnose it, and give three concrete changes in the order you would make them.

Solution

The diagnosis: tool search is off. With it on, only tool names and server instructions load at session start, and six servers cost very little. Thirty-eight per cent before a first message means the full definitions — names, descriptions and JSON Schemas for perhaps 150 tools — are loading upfront. Confirm with /context, which breaks the window down by source (§3.3).

Why it would be off is the actual question, and there are four documented causes worth checking in this order: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointing at a proxy or gateway, which disables tool search because most proxies do not forward tool_reference blocks; ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false set explicitly, perhaps inherited from a team settings file; CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS, which keeps it off and cannot be overridden by setting ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH; or a model older than the 4.5 generation, which does not support tool_reference blocks at all. A gateway (§15.7) is the most likely culprit in a company setting, and it is also the one where the fix needs someone else.

Three changes, in order.

One: fix or work around tool search. If it is a proxy, ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true forces deferral — but be honest that requests then fail if the proxy genuinely cannot handle tool_reference blocks, so test it before recommending it to the team. If it is an old model, the answer is the model. This change alone probably recovers most of the 38%.

Two: disconnect what is not being used. Six servers is a lot, and the §10.10 test — am I pasting from it? — will usually retire two of them. This is worth doing regardless of whether change one succeeds, because it also narrows the trust surface, and it costs nothing.

Three: move the survivors to the right scope. A server in user scope loads in every project, including the ones that will never call it. Anything project-specific belongs in that project's .mcp.json. If tool search cannot be turned on, consider ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto:10 as the compromise — upfront while cheap, deferred once it is not — and alwaysLoad on the single server needed every turn.

On the slowness: it is a symptom, not a separate problem. A window that starts 38% full has less room, compacts sooner (§3.4), and every request carries the whole tool block. Fixing the context usage fixes the feel. The general lesson is that MCP's cost is paid on every request while its benefit is paid on the turns you actually use it — which is exactly the asymmetry tool search exists to correct, and why a session that has lost it degrades so noticeably.

SECTION 11

Subagents, Teams and Parallel Work

Section 3 established the limit this section exists to work around: one context window, filling up, and getting worse as it fills. Every technique here is a way of getting a second window, or a tenth. The work that produces a lot of text (reading many files, long searches) can then happen somewhere other than the conversation you are trying to keep clean.

That framing matters. Running work in parallel in Claude Code is usually presented as a speed feature. It is mostly a context feature. A subagent that reads forty files and returns eight lines has not made anything faster; the reading still took as long as it took. What it did was keep thirty-nine files' worth of tokens out of the window you will still be using in an hour. Speed comes later, from running several of these at once, and it is the smaller of the two benefits.

Claude Code offers six mechanisms for this. They really are different, not six names for handing work off. It is worth telling them apart before using any of them.

Subagent
A worker with its own window, spawned inside your session. Fresh context, its own system prompt and tool restrictions, returns one summary. The default answer, and the one to reach for first.
Fork
A subagent that inherits the whole conversation instead of starting fresh. For a side task that would take too long to explain to a stranger.
Background session
A whole separate Claude Code session, hosted for you, monitored from agent view. For work measured in tens of minutes that you want to walk away from.
Agent team
Peer sessions that message each other and share a task list. A lead coordinates; teammates talk directly. Experimental, expensive, and the right answer for genuinely collaborative work.
Dynamic workflow
A script that orchestrates dozens to hundreds of agents. The plan moves out of a context window and into code that you can read and rerun.
Worktree
Not an agent at all — an isolated checkout. Orthogonal to the five above: it separates files, while they separate attention. Combine as needed.

11.1 The Subagent, and What It Costs

A subagent is a specialised assistant that runs in its own context window, with its own system prompt (its standing instructions), its own list of allowed tools, and its own permissions. Claude hands a task to one when the task matches the subagent's description. The subagent works alone and returns a summary.

The economics are worth stating plainly, because the excitement around subagents hides a real trade-off. Say a search would have cost 30,000 tokens in your window. Delegating it costs you only the summary in your window, perhaps 400 tokens. But the subagent's own full run is not free, and it is billed like any other request. You do not save money by delegating; you save context. What you buy is a window that still makes sense forty turns later. Given how sharply quality drops in a window that is 85% full (§3.5), that is usually worth paying for.

The second cost is time, and it works the opposite way from what people expect. A subagent that is not a fork starts fresh. It has not read the files you have read, does not know what you concluded three turns ago, and cannot see your conversation. Claude writes it a delegation prompt summarising the task, and it must find out everything else again by itself. For a five-file investigation that is fine. For "fix the bug we have been discussing", it is a slow way to lose context, and the main conversation is simply better.

The test that decides it. Would you be happy to receive only a summary of this work? If yes, delegate. If you will want to see the intermediate steps, argue with a conclusion, or redirect halfway through, keep it in the main conversation — because a subagent's tool calls are gone and only its final report survives.

The built-in subagents

Four matter, and knowing them prevents you from rebuilding one.

Explore
Fast, read-only search. Write and Edit are denied. It inherits the main conversation's model, capped at Opus on the Claude API — so it is never more expensive than the model you already chose. Claude passes it a thoroughness level: quick, medium, or very thorough.
Plan
Research during plan mode. Also read-only. It exists so that exploration output stays in a separate window while the main conversation remains read-only (§2.6).
general-purpose
Exploration plus action. Every tool available to subagents. For multi-step work that has to change something as well as find it.
claude
The catch-all, with every tool available to subagents, and the default agent for a dispatched background session (§11.4).

Explore and Plan skip your CLAUDE.md files and the parent session's git status. Every other built-in subagent and every custom one loads both. This is a deliberate trade for speed, with a consequence you must remember: a project rule such as "ignore the vendor/ directory" does not reach Explore. The main conversation reads its results with full CLAUDE.md context, so most rules do not need to reach it. When one does, repeat it in the prompt. There is no frontmatter field to change which agents skip these files.

If you define your own user or project subagent named Explore, it replaces the built-in one, and its own model field applies. That is how you pin exploration to Haiku, if you want it cheaper than your session's model.

Writing one

A subagent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter, kept in .claude/agents/ for the project or ~/.claude/agents/ for you alone:

---
name: migration-auditor
description: Checks a database migration for reversibility and lock risk. Use proactively whenever a file under migrations/ is created or changed.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
---

You audit database migrations for two properties and report on nothing else.

**Reversibility.** Every migration must have a `down` that restores the prior
schema. Report a missing or incomplete `down` as a blocking finding.

**Lock risk.** On PostgreSQL, flag any `ALTER TABLE` that rewrites a table,
any index creation without `CONCURRENTLY`, and any `NOT NULL` added to a
populated column without a prior check constraint.

Report findings as a list of `file:line — property — what to do instead`.
Say "no findings" and stop if there are none. Do not review anything else
about the migration, and do not edit files.

Two things in that file do most of the work, and neither of them is the prompt body.

The description is what drives automatic delegation. Automatic delegation means Claude reads the descriptions of every available subagent and picks one when a task matches. So the description is not documentation; it is the rule that routes work to the subagent. It should say when to use it, not what it is. "Checks migrations" routes badly. "Use proactively whenever a file under migrations/ is created or changed" routes well. The phrase "use proactively" is the documented way to encourage automatic delegation without being asked.

The tools list is enforcement, not advice. This subagent cannot write files at all. So a whole class of problem cannot happen: the reviewer "helpfully" fixing things, leaving changes in the diff you never reviewed. That guarantee is worth more than the prompt.

The frontmatter has more fields than anyone needs at once, but a handful earn their place:

tools
Allowlist. Omit to inherit everything available to subagents. Accepts MCP patterns: mcp__github or mcp__github__* for a whole server.
disallowedTools
Denylist, applied first; tools then resolves against what remains. A tool in both is removed.
model
sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model ID, or inherit. Defaults to inherit.
permissionMode
The subagent's own mode (§5.5) — plan for a reviewer that must not act, for instance.
maxTurns
A hard stop on agentic turns. The cheapest bound you can put on an unfamiliar agent.
skills
Skills preloaded into its context at startup — full content, not just the description (§8.7).
memory
user, project or local: persistent memory of its own across sessions.
isolation
worktree runs it in a temporary git worktree, branched from your default branch. §11.7.
effort
Overrides the session effort level while this subagent is active.
hooks
Hooks scoped to this subagent, removed when it finishes (§9.9).

name and description are the only required fields, and a file missing either is skipped silently. With no name, Claude Code treats the file as documentation kept next to your agents. With a name but no description, a name containing :, or YAML that does not parse, it writes the reason to the debug log and moves on. A subagent that "does not exist" is almost always one of those four cases. Run with --debug to see which, or run claude plugin validate .claude/agents to check the directory before a session.

Claude Code looks for subagents in priority order: managed settings, then --agents on the command line, then .claude/agents/, then ~/.claude/agents/, then a plugin's agents/ directory. Project agents are found by walking up from the working directory, so every .claude/agents/ between there and the repository root is scanned. Where the same name appears twice along that path, the definition closest to the working directory wins. Within a single directory tree, two files with the same name give unpredictable results: one loads, depending on the order the filesystem returns them.

Invoking one on purpose

Three escalating levels of control:

Use the migration-auditor subagent on the new migration          (Claude decides)
@"migration-auditor (agent)" check db/migrate/0043_add_index.sql (guaranteed)

claude --agent migration-auditor

The @-mention guarantees which subagent runs, but not what prompt it receives: your full message still goes to Claude, which writes the delegation prompt. The third form is different in kind. --agent makes the main thread itself take on that subagent's system prompt, tools and model, replacing the default Claude Code system prompt entirely. CLAUDE.md still loads through the normal message flow. Set "agent": "migration-auditor" in .claude/settings.json to make it the project default; the flag wins if both are present.

11.2 Foreground, Background, and the Tool Filter Nobody Expects

Subagents run either in the foreground, blocking your conversation until they finish, or in the background, at the same time as you keep working. Background is the default in interactive sessions, because fork mode is on by default there, and fork mode runs everything in the background.

This leads to one of the least obvious behaviours in Claude Code: a background subagent gets a smaller built-in tool set than the same definition running in the foreground. Two filters apply.

  • The first removes a short list of tools from every subagent, wherever it runs: AskUserQuestion, EnterPlanMode, ScheduleWakeup, TaskOutput, WaitForMcpServers, Workflow, EndConversation, and ExitPlanMode unless the subagent's permissionMode is plan.
  • The second applies only in the background, and it is an allowlist: a background subagent keeps every MCP tool, but only these built-in tools:
Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, PowerShell, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite, Skill, ToolSearch, EnterWorktree, ExitWorktree, Monitor, TaskStop, SendMessage, Artifact.

Everything else is removed, whether it was inherited or listed explicitly, and with no error. The exception is when the removal leaves the tools list with nothing in it at all: then the launch fails with an error naming the entries. The same definition can therefore resolve to different tools depending on where it runs. A subagent that works when you test it in the foreground but behaves strangely in the background has almost certainly lost a tool to this filter.

Permission prompts from a background subagent appear in your main session, labelled so you know who is asking. If you approve with a choice that lasts beyond the single call, such as "allow for the rest of the session", it applies to the whole session, including your main conversation. That is the right default, and it is worth knowing before you approve something broad on a subagent's behalf.

Two limits bound the whole system.

  • Twenty concurrent subagents by default. Starting a twenty-first fails with Concurrent subagent limit reached, and the error tells Claude not to retry. Change the limit with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS.
  • Separately, subagents can nest three layers deep below the main conversation by default: a subagent can start its own subagents, three levels down. At the limit, Claude Code withholds the Agent tool, so the deepest subagent does its own work and returns one summary. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH changes the depth, and 1 turns nesting off:
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH": "2"
  }
}

Nesting is really useful for one setup: a reviewer that sends a verifier to check each finding, so the in-between checking never reaches your window and only the reviewer's summary comes back. To stop one particular subagent from nesting while allowing it elsewhere, leave Agent out of its tools or add it to disallowedTools.

11.3 Forks: Delegation Without the Re-Explanation

A subagent's isolation is its value, and also its main cost: the worker knows nothing. To fork the conversation removes exactly that cost. A fork inherits the entire conversation so far, along with the same system prompt, tools and model, and gives you a worker that already knows the situation.

/subtask draft unit tests for the parser changes so far

The fork appears in a panel below your prompt and runs in the background while you keep working. When it finishes, its result arrives as a message in your conversation. Its own tool calls stay out of your window, so that half of the isolation is kept. The arrangement is "shares the past, does not clutter the present".

Fork
Non-fork subagent
Context
Full conversation history
Fresh, plus the delegation prompt
Prompt and tools
Same as the main session
From its definition file, filtered for background runs
Model
Same as the main session
From its model field
Permissions
Prompts surface in your terminal
Prompts surface in your main session
Prompt cache
Shared with the main session
Separate cache

That last row is the one with money attached. A fork's system prompt and tool definitions are identical to the parent's, byte for byte, so its first request reads the parent's prompt cache instead of writing a new one (§3.7). Starting a fresh subagent means paying to cache a new prefix. For a side task that needs the same context, forking is clearly cheaper as well as better informed.

Forks also skip both tool filters from §11.2 and get exactly the main conversation's set of tools. The one thing they cannot do is start further forks. At the nesting depth limit, the Agent tool stays in a fork's list but returns an error instead of disappearing.

Use a fork when any other subagent would need too much background to be useful, or when you want to try several approaches in parallel from the same starting point. Three forks from one conversation, each trying a different fix, is a really good use of the mechanism, and hard to set up any other way.

Fork mode is on by default in interactive sessions and off in -p and the Agent SDK. Setting CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT to 1 or 0 overrides that in either direction. While fork mode is on, Claude Code removes the Agent tool's run_in_background parameter entirely, so Claude cannot ask to run in the foreground.

11.4 Background Sessions and Agent View

A subagent lives inside your session. Sometimes what you want is a different session: a full Claude Code instance working on a separate task for twenty minutes, which you check on rather than wait for. That is a background session, and claude agents opens agent view, the dashboard for them.

claude agents

claude --bg "migrate the remaining callers of the deprecated logger API"

Agent view lists every background session and its state, with a summary for each row and its pull-request status. It lets you peek at a session's recent output, reply without fully joining it, or attach to take it over interactively. It is also where you dispatch a session, meaning start one: from the view, from inside a session, or from your shell as above. When you dispatch a session you choose its model, permission mode and effort, and by default it runs as the claude catch-all agent.

Before using it, understand how file edits are isolated. Background sessions work on your repository, and two of them editing the same files would collide, exactly as two people would. Claude Code's answer is worktrees (§11.7). That is why .claude/worktrees/ filling up is a documented, expected effect and not a bug. Sessions are hosted by a supervisor process, and their state lives on your machine; claude agents can also list sessions as JSON for scripts.

The picture that keeps these straight: a subagent is a worker in your session, a background session is a colleague with their own desk. You do not watch a colleague's every keystroke. You check what they have produced, and you can interrupt them.

11.5 Agent Teams

Everything so far has one coordinator: you, or Claude acting for you. Results flow up to a single point. Agent teams change that shape. A lead session starts teammates that are full Claude Code instances. Teammates message each other directly, take work from a shared task list, and challenge each other's findings without going through the lead.

Agent teams are experimental and off by default. They are enabled with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, and they have known limitations around session resumption, task coordination and shutdown. Turning them on also changes ordinary delegation: while teams are enabled, any subagent Claude names launches as a teammate, so a team can form when you did not ask for one. 
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "1"
  }
}

The design has four parts.

  • The team lead is your session.
  • Teammates are separate Claude Code instances. Each has its own context window, loads the project context (CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, skills) as a normal session would, and receives the lead's spawn prompt (the instructions it starts with).
  • The task list is shared, and Claude Code manages dependencies automatically: finishing a task unblocks the tasks that were waiting on it, with nothing for you to do.
  • The mailbox is a JSON file per agent under ~/.claude/teams/{team}/inboxes/. A message counts as sent only when it has been written to the recipient's mailbox successfully.

The lead's conversation history does not carry over to a teammate. This is the most common cause of a disappointing team run, and the fix lies entirely in the spawn prompt:

Spawn a security reviewer teammate with the prompt: "Review the authentication
module at src/auth/ for security vulnerabilities. Focus on token handling,
session management, and input validation. The app uses JWT tokens stored in
httpOnly cookies. Report any issues with severity ratings."

Compare that with "spawn a security reviewer", and the difference in the output is obvious. A teammate is a colleague on their first day, not a continuation of your conversation.

When a team is the right shape

Research and review
Several teammates investigate different aspects, then share and challenge each other's findings. The strongest case, because disagreement between peers is the product.
Competing hypotheses
Three theories about one bug, tested in parallel. Cheaper than testing them sequentially and much cheaper than committing to the wrong one.
Cross-layer work
Frontend, backend and tests, each owned by a different teammate. Works because the file sets are disjoint.
Not: sequential work
Anything with real dependencies between steps. The coordination overhead exceeds the parallelism, and a single session is faster.
Not: same-file edits
Two teammates editing one file overwrite each other. Split the work by file ownership or do not split it.

Start with three to five teammates. Token cost grows in step with the number of teammates, since each one is a separate Claude instance with its own window. The cost of coordinating grows faster than that, and the benefit of each extra teammate shrinks. If you have fifteen independent tasks, start with three teammates, not fifteen. Five or six tasks per teammate keeps everyone busy and leaves the lead room to reassign work when someone is stuck. Three focused teammates regularly beat five scattered ones.

You can reuse a subagent definition as a teammate role. Name the type in your spawn instruction, and the teammate follows the definition's tools allowlist and model, with the body added to its system prompt as extra instructions rather than replacing it. Two fields do not apply this way: skills and mcpServers are ignored, because a teammate loads those from project and user settings like any session.

Teammates start with the lead's permission settings, and their permission prompts appear in the lead session for you to answer. You cannot set a different mode per teammate when starting them, only change it afterwards. And there is a security property worth stating explicitly, because people tend to assume it is missing: a message from one agent to another is labelled as coming from another Claude session, not from you. A teammate cannot approve a permission prompt for you. A teammate that was refused an action cannot pass it to a colleague to get it done. In auto mode the classifier goes further and reviews every message between agents before delivery, treating a passed-on claim of approval as untrusted input.

Two practical notes. teammateMode in ~/.claude/settings.json chooses how teams are displayed: "in-process" (the default, with everyone in your terminal and arrow keys to move between them) or split panes using tmux or iTerm2. And an in-process teammate's requests fall outside your main conversation's cache TTL group (§3.6), so the cache TTL that applies to a teammate is five minutes, not an hour. Set subagentPromptCacheTtl to 1h if the extra cost of cache writes is worth it.

11.6 Dynamic Workflows: Moving the Plan into Code

Subagents, skills and teams all leave Claude holding the plan and deciding, turn by turn, what to run next. That works up to about a dozen delegated tasks and then falls apart, because organising the work is itself using up the window it is trying to protect.

A dynamic workflow moves the plan into a JavaScript script that a runtime runs in the background. Claude writes the script from your description. Intermediate results live in script variables instead of in a context window, and only the final answer comes back.

Subagents
Agent teams
Workflows
Who decides next
Claude, turn by turn
The lead, turn by turn
The script
Intermediate results
Claude's window
A shared task list
Script variables
What is repeatable
The worker definition
The team definition
The orchestration itself
Scale
A few per turn
A handful of peers
Dozens to hundreds per run
Interruption
Restarts the turn
Teammates keep running
Resumable in the session

The clearest way to see one is the bundled /deep-research workflow:

/deep-research What changed in the Node.js permission model between v20 and v22?

It spreads searches across several angles, cross-checks the sources it finds, and returns one report with citations. /workflows opens the progress view: each phase with its number of agents, total tokens and time so far, and you can drill down to what each agent found.

The second thing a workflow gives you, beyond scale, is a repeatable quality pattern. Because the script holds the structure, it can have independent agents critically review each other's findings before anything is reported, or draft a plan from several angles and weigh them against each other. That kind of setup is fiddly to arrange through conversation and easy to write down once in a script.

Know the constraints before you hand a large task to one:

No mid-run user input
Only agent permission prompts can pause a run. For sign-off between stages, run each stage as its own workflow.
No filesystem or shell access
From the script itself. Agents read, write and run commands; the script coordinates agents.
No module loading
A script containing import() fails before the run starts. Work needing a library goes inside an agent's task.
16 concurrent agents
Fewer when Claude Code has fewer CPUs, including in a CPU-limited container.
1,000 agents per run
The bound on a runaway loop.

Resuming has a rule that should change how you design a workflow. If you stop a run, finished agents usually return cached results. But replay follows the order agents started, and caching stops at the first agent that did not finish. Say four agents A, B, C and D start in that order, and you stop while B is running. On resume, A comes from the cache. B runs again because it never finished. And C and D run again too, even though they had finished, because they started after B. So a workflow that spreads its work over many small agents keeps far more progress than one built from a few long ones.

Cost control is explicit. The default size guideline is medium, where Claude aims for fewer than 15 agents. small (under 5), large (under 50) and unrestricted are available through /config or the workflowSizeGuideline setting. Claude Code flags a run that plans more than 25 agents, or is projected to use more than 1.5 million tokens, with a Large workflow warning. The warning is only advice and pauses nothing. To estimate the spend, run the workflow on one directory before running it on the whole repository.

11.7 Worktrees: Isolating Files Rather Than Attention

Everything above separates context. None of it separates files: two background sessions in the same checkout overwrite each other's work, exactly as two people would. A git worktree is a separate working directory with its own files and its own branch, sharing the repository's history and remote.

claude --worktree feature-auth

By default this creates .claude/worktrees/feature-auth/ at the repository root, on a new branch worktree-feature-auth, and starts Claude there. Run it again with another name in another terminal for a second isolated session. Leave out the name and Claude makes one up. Add .claude/worktrees/ to .gitignore, so worktree contents do not show up as untracked files in your main checkout.

A worktree is a fresh checkout, so its environment is not set up: dependencies are not installed, and gitignored files such as .env are not there. A .worktreeinclude file lists gitignored files to copy into every new worktree automatically. That is usually the difference between worktrees being pleasant and being a chore.

Isolation is enforced, not merely conventional. While a session is in a worktree, Claude Code applies four checks:

File edits
An Edit, Write or NotebookEdit targeting a path in the main checkout is blocked.
Working directory
A Bash, PowerShell or Monitor command whose working directory resolves to the main checkout — or that cannot be verified to stay outside it — is blocked.
Git redirects
A command redirecting git into the main checkout is blocked, whether through git -C, --git-dir, GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, or a cd before running git.
Command shape
A command whose containment cannot be traced without running it is refused, even when it runs no git at all — brace expansion, heredocs with unquoted delimiters. This check cannot be turned off.

Together, those four checks are what git isolation means here. It is not a convention that the session should stay in its worktree; it is a set of refusals that make leaving it fail. The fourth check surprises people, and the surprise is git isolation working as designed. A worktree guarantee that a clever enough shell command could defeat would not be a guarantee. So Claude Code refuses what it cannot verify and tells Claude how to rewrite the command, usually by splitting a compound command into simple separate ones.

Worktrees combine with everything else in this section. A subagent with isolation: worktree gets its own copy of the repository. By default that copy branches from your default branch, not from the parent session's HEAD, and it is cleaned up automatically if the subagent made no changes. Background sessions use worktrees to keep their edits apart. And when the main session itself is isolated, the same checks apply to every subagent it starts, including ones that did not ask for isolation.

What happens on exit depends on what the worktree contains.

  • A clean, unnamed session's worktree and branch are removed automatically.
  • For a named session, you are asked first.
  • A worktree with changes, untracked files or new commits always asks, because removing it deletes the branch and the work with it.

A -p run has no exit prompt and therefore never cleans up. The worktree and its lock stay until a later session's sweep for stale locks. To remove one by hand, use git worktree remove (after git worktree unlock if git refuses).

One trap that connects back to §9: hook paths do not follow the worktree. ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} stays fixed to where the session started, so ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/check-style.sh runs the script from the main checkout. The worktree's path arrives in the cwd field of the hook's input JSON. A hook that assumes those two are the same silently checks the wrong tree.

11.8 Choosing, and the Failure Modes of Each

A decision procedure, in the order the questions actually arise.

Do I need the intermediate steps?
Yes → main conversation. Everything in this section trades visibility for context, and if you will want to argue with a conclusion halfway through, you have traded away the thing you needed.
Does the worker need what we already discussed?
Yes → fork. Cheaper than a fresh subagent because it shares the prompt cache, and it needs no re-explanation.
Is it a repeatable role?
Yes → a defined subagent. Write it once with a routing description and a restrictive tools list, commit it, and stop re-describing it every session.
Do the workers need to talk to each other?
Yes → agent team. This is the only question that justifies a team, and if the answer is "not really", subagents are cheaper and simpler.
Is it more than a dozen units of work?
Yes → dynamic workflow. Past that scale the orchestration itself starts consuming the window, and moving it into a script is the only thing that scales.
Will they edit the same files?
Yes → worktrees, regardless of which of the above you chose. It is an orthogonal decision, and the only one about files.

The typical failure of each mechanism is worth naming too, because each is easy to recover from once you recognise it.

A subagent returns a useless summary. This is almost always because the delegation prompt did not say what to report. Subagents do not know what you will do with the answer. "Report only the failing tests with their error messages" produces a usable result, where "run the tests" produces a paragraph.

A team produces four confident reports that do not engage with each other. The spawn prompts were too thin, or the teammates were never told to review each other's findings. Teams are for disagreement. If nothing disagrees, you paid for four windows to get one opinion.

A workflow burns a large budget on the wrong shape. Run it on a small slice first. The /workflows view shows each agent's token usage while the run is going, and stopping usually keeps the work already finished.

Parallel sessions produce a merge conflict with themselves. Use worktrees, or give each session its own set of files. There is no third answer.

Exercises

Exercise 11.1 — Pick the mechanism. For each, choose from: main conversation, fork, defined subagent, background session, agent team, dynamic workflow — and say why. (a) Find every call site of a deprecated function across a 4,000-file monorepo and report which are safe to auto-migrate. (b) Understand why one flaky test fails about 5% of the time. (c) Review a 900-line pull request from four angles: security, performance, API compatibility, tests. (d) While you keep working, draft a migration plan for the schema change you have been discussing for twenty turns. (e) Add a --json flag to the CLI.

Solution

(a) Dynamic workflow. Thousands of files and a per-file judgement is exactly the scale where Claude-as-orchestrator stops working — the coordination alone would fill a window. The script holds the file list and the per-file results in variables, and only the classification comes back. Note the resumption rule from §11.6 argues for many small agents here rather than a few large ones, so that stopping the run mid-sweep does not discard completed work.

(b) Main conversation. A 5% flake is an iterative investigation: run it, look, hypothesise, instrument, run again. Every one of those steps is a thing you will want to see and redirect. Delegating it produces a summary of a search you would have steered differently. If it turns into "run it 200 times and classify the failures", that part is a subagent — high-volume output, one summary.

(c) Agent team, and it is the textbook case. Four genuinely independent angles, no shared file edits, and the value is in the reviewers disagreeing — a security reviewer objecting to something the performance reviewer proposed is the product. Four subagents would give four reports with no engagement between them. Reuse subagent definitions for the four roles so this is repeatable.

(d) Fork. Twenty turns of context is precisely what a fresh subagent lacks and cannot cheaply reacquire, and the fork also reads the parent's prompt cache rather than paying to build its own. /subtask draft the migration plan for the schema change and keep working.

(e) Main conversation. A small, targeted change with fast iteration and no volume problem. Reaching for parallelism here costs a delegation prompt, a fresh context and a summary round-trip in exchange for nothing.

The pattern: volume goes to subagents, scale goes to workflows, disagreement goes to teams, continuity goes to forks, and iteration stays where you can see it.

Exercise 11.2 — The subagent that lost its tools. You write a dependency-auditor subagent with tools: Read, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, AskUserQuestion so it can ask you which of two upgrade paths to take. It works when you test it. A week later, in a normal session, it silently stops asking and just picks one. Explain what changed, and redesign the subagent so it cannot fail this way.

Solution

What changed: it is now running in the background. AskUserQuestion is removed from every subagent by the first filter in §11.2, wherever it runs — so strictly it never worked as designed even in your test; what changed is more likely that a foreground run let it hand the question back to Claude in its report, and a background run does not.

Either way the diagnosis is the same and generalises: the tool list in a subagent definition is a request, not a guarantee. Two filters shrink it. The first removes a fixed set from all subagents — AskUserQuestion, EnterPlanMode, ScheduleWakeup, TaskOutput, WaitForMcpServers, Workflow, EndConversation, and ExitPlanMode unless permissionMode: plan. The second, applied only in the background, keeps just the allowlist of nineteen built-ins. Neither removal reports an error unless the list resolves to nothing.

The redesign is to stop trying to ask. A subagent is the wrong place for a decision that needs you, because its whole contract is "go away, come back with a summary". The fix is to move the question to the boundary:

---
name: dependency-auditor
description: Audits dependency upgrade paths and reports the options with evidence. Use before any major-version bump.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, WebSearch
model: sonnet
---

For each dependency you are asked about, produce the available upgrade paths
and report, for each: the target version, the breaking changes that affect
this codebase specifically (cite file and line), the migration effort, and
the security posture of staying put.

Do not choose. End your report with a section titled "Decision required"
listing each choice as a question with the evidence for each option, so the
main conversation can put it to the user.

The subagent gathers; the main conversation — which does have AskUserQuestion — asks. That is a better design independent of the tool filter, because the person answering can see the whole conversation rather than one worker's slice of it.

The wider lesson: design subagents around one-way delegation. Anything that needs a round trip with a human belongs in the main conversation, and any subagent that seems to need one is telling you the boundary is in the wrong place. If you genuinely need interaction inside delegated work, the mechanism is an agent team — where teammates are real sessions you can open and message — not a subagent.

Exercise 11.3 — Design the parallel run. Your team must migrate 120 React components from a deprecated styling library. Each component is independent, most take one small mechanical change, and about 15% need judgement. You want it done in an afternoon and you want to review it. Design the run: which mechanism, how the work is divided, how files are kept from colliding, and what you review.

Solution

Mechanism: a dynamic workflow, with a triage phase first. 120 units is past what a conversation can orchestrate and well inside a workflow's 1,000-agent bound. But the important design decision is that this is two passes, not one.

Phase one is classification, not migration. Fan out read-only agents over the 120 components and have each answer one question: is this a mechanical conversion or does it need judgement? That produces two lists and costs almost nothing, and it means the expensive phase runs on a known population instead of discovering the 15% halfway through.

Phase two runs only the mechanical set — roughly 100 components — one agent per component, each making a small change with a fixed recipe. Small agents rather than "one agent per twenty components" is deliberate: §11.6's replay rule means stopping the run re-runs every agent that started after the first unfinished one, so many small agents preserve far more progress than a few large ones. Set the size guideline to large, and run it on ten components first to see the token cost per unit before committing to a hundred.

The 15% do not go in the workflow at all. They go on a list you work through in the main conversation, or hand to two or three background sessions. Judgement calls are exactly the work whose intermediate steps you want to see, and forcing them into an automated fan-out produces the plausible-looking wrong answer that survives review because it looks like its 100 correct neighbours.

File collisions: none, by construction. One agent per component means disjoint file sets, which is the cleanest possible answer and the reason this task suits parallelism at all. Worktrees are unnecessary within the workflow. They are worth it for the background sessions handling the 15%, since those may touch shared files such as a theme module — give each its own worktree and merge deliberately.

What you review: not 120 diffs. Review the recipe — read the first three completed migrations closely, and if the pattern is right, the remaining 97 are the same transformation applied by the same prompt. Then review all of the 15% individually, and run the full test suite plus a visual check on a sample. The review effort is deliberately unbalanced, and that is correct: uniform work needs its rule checked once, while heterogeneous work needs each case checked.

The judgement worth keeping. The instinct with 120 units of work is to parallelise all 120. The better move is to split by kind first, because mechanical work and judgement work want opposite handling — one wants maximum parallelism and minimum supervision, the other wants the reverse. A run that treats them identically either supervises the easy 85% too closely or the hard 15% too loosely, and in practice it does both.

SECTION 12

Plugins

Sections 8 through 11 each produced a file that lives in .claude/: a skill, a hook, an MCP configuration, a subagent. Every one of them works, and every one of them is stuck where it was written. A skill in ~/.claude/skills/ is yours alone. One in a project's .claude/skills/ belongs to that repository. Neither one travels to other people or other projects.

A plugin is the unit that travels. It is a self-contained directory that can hold any combination of these:

  • skills, agents and hooks;
  • MCP servers and LSP servers (language servers, which give editors features like go-to-definition);
  • background monitors and executables;
  • default settings.

It is installed with one command, has a version number, and updates when you raise that number. It is how a working setup stops being something you did once and becomes something a team has.

Approach
Skill names
Best for
Standalone — the .claude/ directory
/hello
Personal workflows, project-specific customisation, quick experiments
Plugin — a directory with a manifest
/plugin-name:hello
Sharing with teammates, distributing to a community, versioned releases, reuse across projects

The recommended path sounds obvious and is rarely followed: start standalone in .claude/ for quick iteration, and convert to a plugin when you are ready to share. A plugin brings more machinery: a manifest (a file describing the plugin), a namespace (the plugin-name: prefix on its names) and a marketplace (a catalogue it is installed from). Paying that cost before anyone else wants the thing is how a good skill ends up unfinished.

12.1 The Anatomy

A plugin is a directory. The manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json (a small file describing the plugin) gives it a name and identity:

{
  "name": "my-first-plugin",
  "description": "A greeting plugin to learn the basics",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": {
    "name": "Your Name"
  }
}
name
Unique identifier and skill namespace. Skills are prefixed with it: /my-first-plugin:hello.
description
Shown in the plugin manager when browsing or installing.
version
Optional. When set, users only receive updates when you bump it — which is the mechanism that makes a plugin a release rather than a live feed.
author
Optional, for attribution.

Everything else lives at the plugin root, the top level of the plugin's directory, and this is where the one mistake everybody makes happens:

Only plugin.json goes inside .claude-plugin/. skills/, agents/, hooks/, commands/ and the rest belong at the plugin root, one level up. Putting them inside the manifest directory produces a plugin that installs cleanly and contains nothing. And the plugin root is the individual plugin's own directory — never ~/.claude/, so a .mcp.json at ~/.claude/.mcp.json is read by nothing.
skills/
Skills as <name>/SKILL.md directories (§8).
commands/
Skills as flat markdown files. Use skills/ for anything new.
agents/
Subagent definitions (§11.1).
hooks/hooks.json
Event handlers (§9.3).
.mcp.json
MCP server configurations (§10.8).
.lsp.json
An LSP server per language, which is what gives Claude the LSP tool.
monitors/monitors.json
A background monitor watches something and reports into the session; a background monitor is one of the components a project-scope skills-directory plugin is not allowed to load (§12.4).
bin/
Executables added to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled.
settings.json
Default settings applied when the plugin is enabled.

A plugin that ships exactly one skill can put SKILL.md at the root and skip the skills/ directory entirely; it then takes its invocation name from the frontmatter name. Use the directory layout for anything that might grow.

claude --plugin-dir ./my-first-plugin

--plugin-dir loads a plugin straight from disk. That is the whole local development loop: edit, restart, try it. No marketplace, no install, no version number.

12.2 What a Plugin Can Carry

Each plugin component is one of the mechanisms from earlier sections. A few differences only appear once they are bundled.

Skills work exactly as in §8, with the plugin's name as a prefix: my-plugin/skills/review/SKILL.md becomes /my-plugin:review. Unlike personal and project skills, a plugin skill's frontmatter name does set the last part of the command, with the prefix staying in place. Plugin agents/ directories are also searched through subfolders, and there the subfolder becomes part of the name: agents/review/security.md in my-plugin registers as my-plugin:review:security.

Hooks live in hooks/hooks.json, with an optional top-level description, and are merged with your user and project hooks when the plugin is enabled. Use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} to refer to bundled scripts. It points at the installation directory, and that directory changes on every plugin update, so a hard-coded path breaks the first time anyone upgrades. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} points at a lasting directory that survives updates, which is where installed dependencies and caches belong.

MCP servers are defined in .mcp.json at the plugin root, or inline in plugin.json, and connect automatically when the plugin is enabled. §10.8's naming trap applies in full here. A tool from a server bundled in a plugin is named mcp__plugin_my-plugin_database-tools__query, not mcp__database-tools__query, and a permission rule or hook matcher written against the bare server key never fires.

An LSP server is the one plugin component with no standalone equivalent. LSP (Language Server Protocol) is the standard that editors use for code intelligence, and an LSP server is worth knowing about even if you never write one:

{
  "go": {
    "command": "gopls",
    "args": ["serve"],
    "extensionToLanguage": {
      ".go": "go"
    }
  }
}

Installing a code-intelligence plugin gives Claude the LSP tool. It reports type errors and warnings right after edits, jumps to a definition, and finds references. The LSP tool is the only built-in tool that a plugin can switch on. It is the same technology behind an IDE's code intelligence, and its effect on context is unusual: it reduces token use, because one symbol lookup replaces reading three files to find the same thing. The official marketplace ships ready-made ones for C/C++, C#, Go, Java, Kotlin, Lua, PHP, Python, Rust, Swift and TypeScript. Each needs the language server program installed separately, because the plugin configures it but does not install it.

Three fields are ignored in a plugin subagent, for security: hooks, mcpServers and permissionMode (§11.1). A plugin cannot grant its own agents a permission mode or attach hooks to them. If you need those, the agent file has to be copied into .claude/agents/ by the person installing it — which is exactly the friction the restriction is meant to create.

12.3 Installing and Living With Them

Two steps, and keeping them separate is the mental model:

/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official
/plugin install github@claude-plugins-official

Adding a marketplace registers a catalog; nothing is installed yet. Installing takes one plugin from it. The official Anthropic marketplace is added automatically the first time you start Claude Code interactively. If a network policy blocked that, the command above adds it by hand. /plugin opens the browser, which has a Discover tab.

enabledPlugins in .claude/settings.json declares the plugins a project uses. That is how a repository ships its own tooling, and it is the route that works in cloud sessions, where /plugin is not available.

Two practical details save confusion. First, /reload-plugins applies a change without a restart, and the install summary tells you when you need it. Second, plugin changes have a cache cost that depends on the component:

  • skills, commands, agents, hooks, monitors and themes are appended to the end, so the cache holds (§3.6);
  • a plugin providing MCP servers follows the MCP rules: safe for the cache when tools are deferred, a full invalidation when they are loaded into the prefix.

/reload-plugins warns and refuses when a reload would cause everything to be read again at full price; --force applies it anyway.

12.4 Scopes, and the Shortcut That Skips the Marketplace

Installing a plugin asks where it belongs. The answer uses the same four scopes as every other setting (§6.1):

Scope
Settings file
For
user
~/.claude/settings.json
Personal plugins in every project. The default.
project
.claude/settings.json
Team plugins, shared through version control.
local
.claude/settings.local.json
Project-specific plugins, kept out of git.
managed
Managed settings
Organisation plugins — read-only, update only (§15.6).

There is also a route that needs no marketplace and no install step at all. Use it when a personal skill grows too big to be a single file. Any folder under a skills directory that contains a .claude-plugin/plugin.json is loaded as a plugin named <name>@skills-dir at the next session. It is found where it is, not copied into the plugin cache, so editing the folder edits the plugin that is actually running.

<skills-dir>/foo/SKILL.md, no manifest
A plain skill named foo
<skills-dir>/foo/.claude-plugin/plugin.json
A plugin foo@skills-dir, which can bundle its own skills, agents, hooks and more
<plugin>/skills/bar/SKILL.md
A skill bar packaged inside a plugin

That is the cheapest possible upgrade path: a skill that needs a hook next to it becomes a plugin by adding one JSON file, with no distribution machinery at all.

Which skills directory the plugin sits in changes what it may do, and the difference is deliberate.

  • A personal-scope one in ~/.claude/skills/ has no restrictions: it is yours.
  • A project-scope one in .claude/skills/ arrives with the repository. So it loads only after you accept the workspace trust dialog (§5.6). Each of its MCP servers needs approval, its LSP servers start only after trust, and its background monitors do not load at all.

Trusting a parent folder is not enough, and neither is -p.

A project-scope @skills-dir plugin loads only from the .claude/skills/ of the directory you start Claude Code in. Unlike plain skills and commands, it does not walk up to the repository root — so launching from a subdirectory silently misses a plugin that lives at the top. Launch from the repository root, or run /reload-plugins after changing directories.

Editing works the way §8.2 describes for skills, and no further. A change to a SKILL.md takes effect immediately, while changes to hooks/, .mcp.json, agents/ and output-styles/ need /reload-plugins or a restart. There is no uninstall command; delete the folder, or:

claude plugin disable my-tool@skills-dir

12.5 Asking the User for Configuration

A plugin that needs an endpoint, a token or a directory has a bad option (telling people to edit settings.json by hand) and a good one. userConfig declares values that Claude Code asks for when the plugin is enabled:

{
  "userConfig": {
    "api_endpoint": {
      "type": "string",
      "title": "API endpoint",
      "description": "Your team's API endpoint"
    },
    "api_token": {
      "type": "string",
      "title": "API token",
      "description": "API authentication token",
      "sensitive": true
    }
  }
}

Each option takes a type (string, number, boolean, directory or file), plus a title and description for the dialog. Optionally it takes required, default, multiple, and min/max for numbers. sensitive: true masks the input and stores the value in secure storage rather than in settings.json. That field is what makes this the right mechanism for a token, not just a convenient one.

The values reach a plugin hook as ${user_config.*} substitutions, in exec form only (§9.3). Exec form means the command and its arguments are given as a list, with no shell in between. A shell-form plugin hook whose command refers to ${user_config.*} fails with an error instead of running. From a shell-form hook, read the $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY> environment variable instead, or add args to switch the hook to exec form. The restriction exists so a configured value is never re-read by a shell, the same reasoning that favours exec form for any path placeholder.

12.6 Distributing Your Own

A marketplace is a marketplace.json catalogue that lists plugins and where to find them, kept in a git repository:

mkdir -p my-marketplace/.claude-plugin
mkdir -p my-marketplace/plugins/quality-review-plugin/.claude-plugin
mkdir -p my-marketplace/plugins/quality-review-plugin/skills/quality-review

Users add it with /plugin marketplace add <owner>/<repo> and install individual plugins from it. /plugin marketplace update refreshes their local copy after you push. That is the whole distribution model, and its most useful property for a company is that it needs no registry and no publishing step: an internal git repository is a marketplace.

Three refinements exist for plugin distribution at scale.

  • A plugin dependency sets allowed version ranges, so one plugin can require another and refuse to load against a version it does not support. It is the same problem package managers solve, and it is why a plugin dependency is worth declaring rather than just documenting.
  • A plugin hint lets a plugin recommend itself from your CLI when it would be relevant. A plugin hint is how a plugin gets found by someone who did not know to look for it.
  • Plugin relevance is the organisation-wide version: plugin relevance settings let a company suggest its own plugins to its own people, so the recommendation comes from somewhere trusted rather than from a marketplace listing.

And claude plugin validate checks a plugin (or a plain directory such as .claude/agents) before anyone installs it. It is worth running in CI for a marketplace you publish.

Plugin distribution has one more property worth naming: because a marketplace is a git repository, distributing and reviewing are the same act. A plugin component changes through a pull request, and users get the change when they update.

Converting standalone configuration to a plugin is mostly moving files. .claude/skills/ becomes skills/, .claude/agents/ becomes agents/, and hooks from settings files become hooks/hooks.json. What changes is the naming (/deploy becomes /my-plugin:deploy) and the three subagent fields that stop applying. Check both before telling a team the plugin is a drop-in replacement.

12.7 When a Plugin Is the Right Answer

More than one repository
The clearest signal. A skill you have copied into three projects is a plugin whose absence you are paying for in every one of them.
More than one component
A skill plus its hook plus its MCP server. Distributing three files that must arrive together, and stay in step, is what a manifest is for.
It needs a version
Anything whose behaviour changing under someone would be a problem. The version field is the difference between a shared file and a release.
Not: one project's conventions
.claude/ in that project, committed. It already travels with the repository, which is the only place it applies.
Not: something still changing
Standalone until it settles. A plugin adds a namespace and an install step to every iteration.

The failure worth naming is the opposite of using plugins too little. A team that discovers plugins tends to build one big plugin containing everything, and it ages badly. A change to the deploy skill forces a new version, which reinstalls the review agent, the hooks and the MCP server for everyone. Several small plugins with clear boundaries beat one that does everything, for the same reason this is true of code libraries. And the marketplace makes many plugins no harder to distribute than one.

Exercises

Exercise 12.1 — Standalone or plugin? For each, decide and justify: (a) a /deploy skill that runs your team's release procedure for one service; (b) a security-review agent plus its PreToolUse hook, wanted by four teams; (c) a personal skill that formats your commit messages the way you like; (d) an LSP configuration for an in-house language used across the company.

Solution

(a) Standalone, in that service's .claude/skills/. It applies to exactly one repository and travels with it already. Making it a plugin adds a namespace, a manifest and an install step for a thing that would otherwise arrive by git clone. The signal to reconsider is a second service wanting the same procedure — at that point it has become case (b).

(b) A plugin, clearly. Four teams, two components that must arrive together and stay in step, and a hook whose behaviour changing unexpectedly would be a problem — every signal from §12.7 fires. Distribute through an internal marketplace and use the version field so a change reaches people when you decide rather than when they next clone.

One thing to check before promising a drop-in replacement: §12.2's restriction means the agent's hooks, mcpServers and permissionMode frontmatter fields are ignored when it ships in a plugin. If the standalone version relied on permissionMode: plan to keep the reviewer read-only, that must be re-expressed — as a tools allowlist on the agent, which is not ignored, or as permission rules in the plugin's settings.json.

(c) Standalone, in ~/.claude/skills/. It is yours, it applies everywhere you work, and nobody else wants it. A plugin would be a distribution mechanism with an audience of one.

(d) A plugin, and the one case where there is no alternative. LSP configuration has no standalone equivalent — .lsp.json is read at a plugin root and nowhere else. An in-house language across a company is also the ideal shape for one: install once, everyone gets type errors after edits and go-to-definition, and the context saving is real because a symbol lookup replaces reading files.

The test underneath all four: does this need to reach people who will not clone the repository it lives in? Yes → plugin. And separately: does the mechanism exist outside a plugin at all? LSP and bundled executables do not, which decides the question before preference does.

Exercise 12.2 — The plugin that installed nothing. A colleague builds a plugin with a skill, a hook and an MCP server. It installs without error, /plugin lists it as enabled, and none of the three works. The layout is below. Find every problem.

my-tools/
└── .claude-plugin/
    ├── plugin.json
    ├── skills/
    │   └── deploy/
    │       └── SKILL.md
    ├── hooks/
    │   └── hooks.json
    └── .mcp.json
Solution

One problem, repeated three times: everything is inside .claude-plugin/. Only plugin.json belongs there. skills/, hooks/ and .mcp.json all belong at the plugin root, one level up. The correct layout:

my-tools/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
├── skills/
│   └── deploy/
│       └── SKILL.md
├── hooks/
│   └── hooks.json
└── .mcp.json

Why it installs cleanly is the instructive part. The manifest is valid and in the right place, so the plugin is a plugin — it just contains no components, and a plugin with no components is not an error. Claude Code has nothing to complain about. This is the same class of silent failure as §9.11's un-firing hook and §10.2's typeless MCP entry: a configuration that is well-formed and inert.

How to catch it in under a minute:

/plugin shows the plugin enabled, so it is not the place to look. /hooks lists every configured hook with its source (§9.11), and a plugin whose hooks loaded shows a Plugin Hooks entry — its absence is decisive. /mcp lists servers with a plugin indicator. And typing /my-tools: in the command menu shows the plugin's skills, or does not.

claude plugin validate ./my-tools is the check to run before publishing anything, and it belongs in CI for a marketplace.

Two follow-ups once the layout is fixed, because the colleague will hit both. Any script referenced from the hook needs ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} rather than a relative or absolute path, because the installation directory changes on every plugin update. And the MCP server's tools are now named mcp__plugin_my-tools_<server>__<tool> — so any permission rule, hook matcher or subagent tools entry written against the bare server key silently matches nothing (§10.8).

The general lesson: a plugin fails by being empty, not by being wrong. So the first question when a plugin does nothing is never "is my hook script correct?" — it is "did the component load at all?", and /hooks, /mcp and the command menu answer that in three seconds each.

SECTION 13

Headless and the Agent SDK

Everything so far has assumed a person at a terminal, watching, approving and steering. That is where Claude Code works best. It is also a setup that can never do more than your own attention allows. The moment you want the same work done on every pull request, on a hundred files, or at three in the morning, you need the loop without the person. Running it that way, with no one at the keyboard, is called headless. The interesting question then becomes: what replaces the person's judgement?

There are three ways in, and underneath they are the same agent.

claude -p
The CLI in non-interactive mode. Reads stdin, writes stdout, exits with a status code. Composes with every other Unix tool you have, which is more of an advantage than it sounds.
TypeScript SDK
@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk. The loop as an async iterator, with typed messages, callbacks and in-process tools.
Python SDK
claude-agent-sdk. The same, with query() and ClaudeAgentOptions.

They are not three products. The SDKs (software development kits: libraries for using Claude Code from your own program) include a native Claude Code binary and control it. claude -p is that same binary run directly. All three have the same tools, the same agentic loop, the same context management and the same permission system from §5. What differs is how much of the loop your own code can reach into, and reaching in is the whole reason to prefer an SDK over a shell script.

13.1 claude -p: The Loop as a Unix Command

claude -p "Find and fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash"

That is the entire headless interface. Headless is what the rest of this section means by "without a person". The -p (or --print) flag makes the run non-interactive; --print is its long spelling, and the two are identical. It takes the prompt, does the work, prints a result, and exits with 0 on success and non-zero on failure, so a script can branch on the exit status. An invalid flag is reported on stderr before the run starts. A failure inside the run, such as missing authentication, is printed as the result on stdout. That distinction matters when you are deciding what to parse.

Non-interactive mode reads stdin (piped-in input), and that is where most of its value is:

cat build-error.txt | claude -p 'concisely explain the root cause of this build error' > output.txt

Piped stdin is capped at 10MB. Go over it and Claude Code exits with a clear error and a non-zero status. Larger input goes in a file whose path you give in the prompt.

Because it fits together with other tools like this, claude -p is a reasonable thing to put in package.json:

{
  "scripts": {
    "lint:claude": "git diff main | claude -p \"you are a typo linter. for each typo in this diff, report filename:line on one line and the issue on the next. return nothing else.\""
  }
}

Notice what piping the diff gives you: Claude needs no Bash permission at all to see the changes, because the data arrived on stdin instead of being fetched. That trick comes up again and again for locking down a headless run: hand it the data, not the ability to go and get the data.

Bare mode, and why it is the right default here

claude --bare -p "Summarize README.md" --allowedTools "Read"

--bare skips the automatic loading of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md. It starts faster and, far more importantly, it makes the run the same on every machine.

Without it, claude -p loads everything an interactive session would, including anything in the working directory or ~/.claude. §5.6 showed what that means in a repository you did not write. A -p session shows no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt, so a project's .claude/settings.json hooks run and its .mcp.json servers connect on the very first run. In CI it also means a teammate's personal hook can change what your pipeline does.

Bare mode gives Claude the Bash, file-read and file-edit tools and nothing else. You pass in whatever else you actually want:

System prompt additions
--append-system-prompt, --append-system-prompt-file
Settings
--settings <file-or-json>
MCP servers
--mcp-config <file-or-json>
Custom agents
--agents <json>
A plugin
--plugin-dir <path>, --plugin-url <url>

One consequence to plan for: bare mode never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain. Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, or supply an apiKeyHelper in the --settings JSON. Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry keep reading their own provider credentials as usual. The documentation says --bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and will become the -p default in a future release. That is a strong hint about how to write new automation today.

Two lifecycle details that bite in CI

Background tasks are killed at exit. A background Bash task, such as a dev server or a watch build, is ended about five seconds after Claude returns its final result and stdin closes. Background subagents and workflows are exempt, because their results are part of the output, so claude -p waits for them. That wait is capped at ten minutes by default (adjustable with CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS), so a stuck agent cannot hold the process open forever.

SIGTERM is not a clean stop. Killing a claude -p run with SIGTERM (the standard "please terminate" signal) exits with 143, leaves the current turn unfinished, and records no result for it.
