Claude Code ends the process tree of any running Bash command, runs SessionEnd hooks, and exits, without starting any new tool call or model request. To end the turn properly instead, send SIGINT (the Ctrl+C signal), or call the SDK's interrupt(), before stopping the process. A resumed session continues the turn SIGTERM left unfinished. That is either a nice recovery property or a surprise, depending on whether you expected it.

13.2 Output Formats: Getting Something Parseable

--output-format has three values, and your choice decides what kind of program you can write around it.

text
The default: plain prose. Fine for a human reading a log, useless for a program that needs a decision.
json
One object with the result, session ID and metadata. Including total_cost_usd and a per-model cost breakdown, so a caller can track spend per invocation without the dashboard.
stream-json
Newline-delimited JSON, one object per event. For anything that needs to react while the run is in progress.
claude -p "Summarize this project" --output-format json | jq -r '.result'

The cost figures need a caveat that §15 develops: they are client-side estimates, worked out on your machine, and can differ from your actual bill. They are excellent for comparisons (is this job twice as expensive as that one?), but should not be matched against an invoice.

For a result your program can act on rather than just read, combine json with a schema:

claude -p "Extract the main function names from auth.py" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"functions":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["functions"]}'

The structured value appears in structured_output, next to the usual metadata. An invalid schema is now a hard failure, Error: --json-schema is not a valid JSON Schema plus the validator's explanation. That is a real improvement on the older behaviour, which silently ignored the schema and returned unstructured text. Note that format keywords such as "format": "email" are accepted as annotations and not enforced, so validate anything you actually depend on.

This is the most useful thing in the section for building a gate. A pipeline step that reads .structured_output.blocking_issues | length is a real check. A pipeline step that searches prose for the word "problem" is a coin flip.

13.3 Reading the Stream

claude -p "Explain recursion" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages

Each line is one event. The last is a result message with the final text, cost and session details. To display tokens as they arrive:

claude -p "Write a poem" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | \
  jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'

Three event types earn their place in a serious integration.

system/init is the first event, and it is your configuration assertion point: the place to check that the configuration you expected really loaded. It reports the model, tools, MCP servers and loaded plugins. Most importantly, it has two error arrays that are left out entirely when empty:

plugins / plugin_errors
Plugins that loaded, and load-time failures with plugin, type and message. An affected plugin is demoted and absent from plugins.
mcp_servers / mcp_server_errors
Servers in the session, and --mcp-config entries skipped by validation — unknown_type, url_missing_type, invalid_config, reserved_name.
capabilities
Protocol behaviours this version implements. Feature-detect against this rather than comparing version strings, and ignore values you do not recognise.
A skipped MCP server does not fail the run. Claude Code validates each --mcp-config entry, skips the invalid ones, continues, and exits cleanly — and when stderr is captured by a CI runner rather than a terminal, it prints no warning either. A pipeline that assumed a database server was connected will produce confident output derived from nothing. Gate on mcp_server_errors being absent; the key's omission when empty is what makes that a one-line check.

Subagent messages appear as assistant and user messages whose parent_tool_use_id is the ID of the Agent tool call that started them; messages from the main conversation carry null there. By default only tool_use and tool_result blocks are sent. Pass --forward-subagent-text to also get subagent text and thinking, at every nesting depth, so you can rebuild the full tree by following the IDs.

The stream also has an input side. --input-format accepts stream-json as well as text, and --input-format stream-json is what turns a one-shot run into a conversation that a program drives. Your process writes messages in and reads events out, and the run keeps going instead of exiting after one turn.

system/api_retry fires before each failure that can be retried. It carries attempt, max_retries, retry_delay_ms, error_status and an error category: rate_limit, overloaded, billing_error, authentication_failed, max_output_tokens and the rest. This is how a long-running job tells "the API is busy" apart from "your card was declined". Both cause the same delay, and they are completely different problems.

13.4 Sessions Without a Terminal

Headless runs are stateless by default (each run starts from nothing), and most should stay that way. When you do need continuity:

claude -p "Review this codebase for performance issues"
claude -p "Now focus on the database queries" --continue
claude -p "Generate a summary of all issues found" --continue

--continue picks up the most recent conversation and skips background sessions. For anything running more than one conversation at a time, that is too fragile, so capture the ID instead:

session_id=$(claude -p "Start a review" --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id')
claude -p "Continue that review" --resume "$session_id"

The two commands do not need to run from the same directory: Claude Code finds a session by its ID in any project on the machine.

Skills work here too: /skill-name in the prompt string is expanded before the run. Built-in commands that only make sense in a terminal, such as /login, are unavailable. But /model, /effort, /fast and /rename take their value as an argument, and /config key=value changes a setting for that run.

Permission handling works differently in -p, and §5 gave the reason: there is nobody to ask. The built-in starting mode is Manual on every plan, so pass the mode you want.

claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"

claude -p "Look at my staged changes and create an appropriate commit" \
  --allowedTools "Bash(git diff *),Bash(git log *),Bash(git status *),Bash(git commit *)"

--allowedTools uses the permission-rule syntax from §5.2, wildcards and all. That includes the trap that the space before * matters: Bash(git diff*) would also match git diff-index. For a baseline instead of a list, use a mode. --permission-mode dontAsk denies anything not listed (the right way to fail in CI). acceptEdits writes files without asking. auto puts a classifier in the loop where a person would have been.

13.5 The SDK: When a Flag Is Not Enough

Everything above treats the agent as a black box you configure at launch. The Agent SDK lets you sit inside the loop, and that is the only reason to take on a dependency where a shell command would do. Everything the Agent SDK adds is about reaching into the loop, not around it.

npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk

pip install claude-agent-sdk

The TypeScript SDK and the Python SDK both include a native Claude Code binary, so most installs need nothing else. Two cases do not get one: a Python SDK install where pip falls back to the source distribution instead of a ready-built package for your platform (a wheel), and a TypeScript SDK install that skips optional dependencies (npm ci --omit=optional). Both are fixed by installing Claude Code natively. The Python SDK then finds it on PATH, and the TypeScript SDK takes a pathToClaudeCodeExecutable.

The loop is an async iterator over messages:

import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AssistantMessage, ResultMessage


async def main():
    async for message in query(
        prompt="Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix any issues you find.",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Glob"],
            permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        ),
    ):
        if isinstance(message, AssistantMessage):
            for block in message.content:
                if hasattr(block, "text"):
                    print(block.text)
                elif hasattr(block, "name"):
                    print(f"Tool: {block.name}")
        elif isinstance(message, ResultMessage):
            print(f"Done: {message.subtype}")


asyncio.run(main())

import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

for await (const message of query({
  prompt: "Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix any issues you find.",
  options: {
    allowedTools: ["Read", "Edit", "Glob"],
    permissionMode: "acceptEdits",
  },
})) {
  if (message.type === "assistant") {
    console.log(message);
  }
}

Note that the SDK reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment of the process that runs your agent, and does not load .env files. If you keep the key in one, load it yourself before calling the SDK. Third-party providers are switched on with their own variables: CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY=1, and CLAUDE_CODE_USE_ANTHROPIC_AWS=1 with ANTHROPIC_AWS_WORKSPACE_ID.

Session management works like the CLI. Capture the session ID from the result, resume by ID, or fork to try alternatives from a shared starting point, the same idea as §11.3's conversation fork, done from code. ClaudeSDKClient in Python and continue: true in TypeScript handle the common case automatically.

13.6 Custom Tools: Your Functions in the Loop

The SDK's signature feature is that you can give Claude functions from your own program, without running a separate MCP server process. A tool has four parts (name, description, input schema, handler), and it is registered through an SDK MCP server. An SDK MCP server runs in-process, inside your application, not as a separate process the way §10's servers do.

from typing import Any
from claude_agent_sdk import tool, create_sdk_mcp_server


@tool(
    "get_temperature",
    "Get the current temperature at a location",
    {"latitude": float, "longitude": float},
)
async def get_temperature(args: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    reading = await lookup_temperature(args["latitude"], args["longitude"])
    return {
        "content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"{reading:.1f} degrees Celsius"}],
        "structuredContent": {"celsius": reading},
    }


server = create_sdk_mcp_server(name="weather", tools=[get_temperature])

By the protocol's definition, an SDK MCP server is a full MCP server; from your side, it is just a table of functions. That is why an SDK MCP server's tools go through the same permission system as any other. In TypeScript the schema is always a Zod schema (Zod is a TypeScript validation library), and the handler's arguments get their types from it automatically. In Python it is a dict mapping names to types, converted to JSON Schema for you. A full JSON Schema dict is also accepted directly, for when you need enums, ranges, optional fields or nested objects.

The handler's return value has more shape than it first appears:

content (required)
Result blocks of type text, image, audio, resource or resource_link. What Claude reads.
structuredContent
The same result as machine-readable JSON, returned alongside. What your program reads.
isError: true
Signals a tool failure so Claude can react — and lets you compose the message rather than surfacing a raw exception.

Two annotations change how Claude uses a tool. readOnlyHint: true on a tool with no side effects lets Claude call it in parallel with others. That is a free speed-up for lookups, and a serious bug for anything that writes. And _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"] (§10.5) forces the approval prompt on every call, whatever the mode. In the SDK it reaches your canUseTool callback, because an SDK application is assumed to be able to show the prompt to a person.

The tools option is the other half. Passing an array that lists only the built-in tools you want removes the rest from Claude's context entirely: §5.1's bare-name deny, applied when the agent is constructed.

13.7 Control: Hooks, Rules and the Callback

The SDK checks permissions in six steps. Knowing the order is what lets you put a control in the right place.

1
Hooks
Run first. A hook can deny outright. A hook returning allow does not skip the deny and ask rules below — they are evaluated regardless.
2
Deny rules
Block even in bypassPermissions. Bare-name denies removed the tool before evaluation began, so only scoped rules are checked here.
3
Ask rules
Fall through to canUseTool for confirmation, even in bypassPermissions. Interaction-requiring tools land here too.
4
Permission mode
bypassPermissions approves what reaches it except critical-path removals; plan routes writes to your callback regardless of allow rules.
5
Allow rules
Approve. Never for an rm or rmdir on a critical path, which reaches the callback instead.
6
canUseTool
Everything unresolved. In dontAsk mode this step is skipped and the tool is denied.

The canUseTool permission callback is the piece with no CLI equivalent, and it is the reason to choose an SDK. The permission callback is the human in the loop, re-implemented as a function. Your application receives the tool name and its arguments, decides, and can rewrite the input on the way through. That is how you build an approval screen, an audit log that records every decision with its reason, a policy engine that asks your own service, or a Slack round trip that asks a person and waits until they answer.

SDK hooks are the same mechanism as §9's, delivered as callbacks (functions in your program) instead of separate processes. One difference is worth remembering: a PreToolUse callback hook that exceeds its timeout blocks the tool call, while a command hook that times out does not. The SDK's version is the stricter one, which is the right default when the hook is a function in your own process.

13.8 Structured Output, Cost and Observability

Four things a headless agent needs that an interactive session gets for free.

Structured output is the same idea as --json-schema, with types. TypeScript takes a Zod schema and Python a Pydantic model, and the result comes back typed, not as a dictionary you hope has the right shape. Use it whenever the output feeds a decision rather than a person. It is the difference between an agent that reports and an agent you can build on.

Session persistence matters because a deployed agent rarely lives in one process. The SDK gives you a session ID to resume by, forks a session to try alternatives and, where the default on-disk storage is wrong for your deployment, saves sessions to external storage of your own. Session persistence is what lets a stateless HTTP handler continue a conversation started an hour ago on a different machine.

Cost tracking is available per query, per step and per model. Cost tracking is the one to set up first, because it is the only one that tells you a deployed agent has started behaving differently. The result message carries the total. Per-step usage lets you find the expensive turn. The per-model breakdown matters as soon as subagents run on a different model from the main loop. Three practical notes:

  • read output tokens from the result message instead of adding them up yourself;
  • track costs on failed conversations too (a run that failed on turn nine still cost nine turns);
  • read cache tokens explicitly, because §3.7's caching changes what "input tokens" means.

Observability means OpenTelemetry (§15.4), and the SDK exports the same traces the CLI does. There is also a todo stream you can follow to show the agent's own plan in your interface. That is the cheapest possible progress indicator for a long run.

13.9 Deploying an Agent You Did Not Watch

An agent running unattended has every risk §5.9 warned about, and none of the protection a watching person provides. The documentation frames this as a threat model, and it is worth adopting.

Security boundaries
Name what is inside and outside. An agent that can reach production and an agent that can reach a replica are different systems, and the difference is a credential rather than a prompt.
Least privilege
The narrowest tool list and the narrowest token that does the job. Every capability you grant is one an injected instruction can use.
Defence in depth
No single control is the whole answer. A deny rule, a sandbox, a scoped token and an ephemeral container fail independently, which is the point.

The documentation calls this secure deployment, and its three headings above are all of it. SDK hosting is the practical companion: where the agent process actually runs, how many copies there are, and what each one can reach. Secure deployment and SDK hosting are the same decision seen from two ends: the hosting choice is what makes the security properties possible or not. The isolation options, from cheapest to strongest, are the sandbox runtime, containers, gVisor, virtual machines, and cloud deployments. It is the §5.8 choice, made once at deployment instead of per session. For a hosted agent, the practical baseline is:

  • a fresh, throwaway container per run;
  • a token allowed to do exactly the operations the agent needs;
  • outgoing network traffic limited to the hosts it must reach;
  • canUseTool logging every decision it makes.

One asymmetry is worth ending on, because it is easy to get backwards. In an interactive session, you are the last line of defence, and the configuration is a convenience. In a deployed agent, the configuration is the only line of defence, and nobody is there to notice that something looks wrong. Everything in §5 that felt like extra caution on your laptop is holding up the roof here.

Exercises

Exercise 13.1 — CLI or SDK? For each, choose claude -p, the SDK, or neither — and justify: (a) a package.json script that reviews the diff for typos; (b) a web app where users describe a change and watch Claude make it, approving each file write; (c) a nightly job that upgrades dependencies and opens a PR; (d) an internal tool that answers questions about your codebase, where every answer must cite files and be logged.

Solution

(a) claude -p. One prompt, one result, piped in and out. An SDK here is a dependency, a build step and a hundred lines to replicate what a pipe already does. The git diff main | claude -p ... form also means the script needs no Bash permission to see the changes.

(b) The SDK, and specifically for canUseTool. "Approving each file write" is the requirement, and it is precisely what has no CLI equivalent: the callback receives the tool name and arguments, your app renders them, the user decides, and the callback returns. stream-json would let you display the run but not gate it. Use stream-json only if you have a hard constraint against adding the SDK, and accept that you are then building the approval path out of subprocess plumbing.

(c) claude -p, with --bare and a schema. A nightly job wants determinism above all else, and bare mode is what stops a teammate's ~/.claude hook from changing what your pipeline does. Add --json-schema so the job can branch on a structured verdict — did the upgrade break anything, which packages were skipped — rather than grepping prose. The PR creation is a scoped gh invocation, not an agent capability.

(d) The SDK. Two requirements force it. "Every answer must cite files" wants structured output with a schema requiring a citations array, so an uncited answer is a schema violation rather than something a reviewer has to notice. "Must be logged" wants canUseTool and the message stream, which give you every tool call and every decision rather than a final result. Custom tools may also earn their place if the answers need to consult a service the codebase does not contain.

The dividing line: claude -p when you configure once and read a result; the SDK when you need to intervene, gate or record during the run. Everything else is preference.

Exercise 13.2 — The pipeline that lied. A nightly claude -p job summarises the previous day's production errors. It runs with --mcp-config pointing at a Sentry MCP server, exits 0 every night, and posts a summary to Slack. One morning someone notices the summaries have been generic for two weeks — plausible prose, no specific errors. Diagnose it and rewrite the job so it cannot happen again.

Solution

The diagnosis: the Sentry server stopped loading, and nothing said so. Claude Code validates each --mcp-config entry at startup, skips the entries that fail validation, and continues — the run exits cleanly, which is why the exit status has been 0 for two weeks. Claude, with no Sentry tools available, did the reasonable thing and wrote a summary from what it could infer, and prose is exactly the output format in which "I had no data" and "here is the data" look identical.

The likely trigger is mundane: a credential rotation left the URL or header unusable, or someone edited the config and left an entry with a url and no type — the single most common .mcp.json mistake (§10.2), and one whose only symptom is a skipped server. Worth noting that the startup warning does not help here: Claude Code prints it to stderr only when a terminal is attached, and a CI runner capturing stderr gets nothing.

The rewrite has three independent parts, and each one alone would have caught it.

One: assert on system/init. Switch to --output-format stream-json and fail the job if mcp_server_errors is present or if the Sentry server is missing from mcp_servers. The mcp_server_errors key is omitted entirely when empty, which makes this a one-line check:

claude --bare -p "$PROMPT" --mcp-config sentry.json \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose > run.jsonl

jq -e 'select(.type=="system" and .subtype=="init")
       | (has("mcp_server_errors") | not)
         and (.mcp_servers | map(.name) | index("sentry") != null)' run.jsonl > /dev/null

Two: make the output structured. --json-schema requiring an errors array with an event_id per entry turns "no data" into an empty array your job can test, instead of a paragraph. A summary with zero entries is then a fact the job can act on — post it, or alert on it if zero is implausible for a production system.

Three: --bare. The job should load nothing from the machine it happens to run on. It also forces the credential question into the open, since bare mode does not read OAuth or the keychain.

The general lesson, which is the point of the exercise. An agent's failure mode is not usually an error — it is a confident answer derived from less than you thought it had. Exit status tells you the process finished; it says nothing about whether the tools it needed were there. So an unattended agent needs two gates rather than one: a configuration assertion that the run had what it needed, and a schema that makes an empty result distinguishable from a full one. Neither is expensive, and the two weeks of plausible summaries is what it costs to have neither.

Exercise 13.3 — Design the approval path. You are building an internal tool where support engineers describe a data fix in English and an SDK agent implements it against a staging database, with a senior engineer approving anything that writes. Design it: which surface, how approval works, what the agent can reach, and what you record. Then name the control that does the most work, and say why it is not any of the ones you designed.

Solution

Surface: the Python or TypeScript SDK. Approval is the requirement and canUseTool is the mechanism; nothing else in this section can put a second human in the loop.

Approval path. The agent runs in your service. When it proposes a write, canUseTool fires, and the callback: renders the exact statement and its arguments into a review queue, notifies the senior engineer, blocks until an answer arrives, then returns allow or deny — with the deny reason passed back so the agent can adapt rather than retry blindly. Two design points matter more than the plumbing. Reads should not reach the callback at all: put Read, Grep and the read-only query tool in allowed_tools so the reviewer sees only what needs reviewing, because an approval queue that fires forty times per task trains people to click yes. And the callback should show the resolved statement, not the intent — "update 1 row in accounts where id = 4471" rather than "fix the account", since the whole value of the gate is that a person sees what will actually run.

What the agent can reach. A custom tool wrapping your database, not a shell with psql. The tool takes structured arguments and builds the statement itself, so the agent never composes raw SQL and the tool can refuse an unparameterised one. Mark the read tool readOnlyHint: true so lookups parallelise; leave the write tool without it. Pass a tools array containing only the built-ins you want, so everything else is out of Claude's context rather than merely denied. Add a deny rule on shell access outright — §5.1's bare-name deny, which removes the tool rather than refusing it.

What you record. Every canUseTool invocation with its arguments, the decision, the approver and the reason; the full message stream keyed by session ID; cost per run including failed ones; and the OTel trace. The rule to apply is that you should be able to answer "why did it do that?" three months later without the model, which means recording the inputs to each decision rather than a summary of the run.

The control that does the most work: the database credential. It is not in the list above because it is not part of the agent at all — and that is exactly why it is the strongest one. A connection scoped to the staging database, with no access to production and no DDL rights, bounds the worst case regardless of what the agent concluded, what the reviewer approved by reflex on a Friday afternoon, or whether an injected instruction (§5.9) persuaded it that the ticket said something else. Every control you designed is inside the system and can be reasoned around; the credential is enforced by a different system that has no idea a model is involved.

That is the §5.9 argument in its strongest form, and it generalises past this exercise: the best control on an agent is usually the one that is not aware it is an agent. Design the approval path anyway — it catches ordinary mistakes, which are far more common than adversarial ones — but do not let it be the only thing standing between a support ticket and your production data.

SECTION 14

Automation, CI and Code Review

Section 13 gave you an agent that runs without a person. This section is about where to put it.

That is a real question, not a formality. The same work (reviewing a diff, sorting out a failure, upgrading a dependency) can be started by many things:

  • a git event, such as a pull request being opened;
  • a schedule;
  • an incoming webhook (a web request another system sends when something happens);
  • a chat message;
  • a link in a runbook (a team's written how-to for operations).

Each choice decides who sees the result, which credentials the run has, who pays for it, and what happens when it goes wrong. Choose wrongly and you get automation that technically works and that nobody acts on.

There are six places to put it, and they differ in how they are built, not just in details:

GitHub Actions
Your CI, your infrastructure, your workflow file. Runs on any GitHub event, and @claude in a comment starts a session. Full control, and you maintain it.
Code Review
A managed service. Reviews every pull request with a fleet of agents on Anthropic infrastructure. No workflow to write, and correspondingly little to configure.
Routines
A saved configuration on cloud infrastructure, triggered by a schedule, an API call, or a GitHub event. Keeps working when your laptop is closed.
Scheduled tasks
Session-scoped — /loop and the cron tools, living in the current conversation. For polling something while you work.
Channels
Events pushed into a running session from an MCP server. The reactive option: CI pushes its failure to you rather than being polled.
Deep links
A URL that opens a session with a prompt pre-filled. Not automation at all — a starting point you can put in a runbook.

14.1 GitHub Actions

The Claude Code GitHub Action runs Claude inside your repository's workflows (GitHub's automated jobs). It does two things, and they are worth keeping apart.

@claude in a comment on a pull request or issue starts a session that analyses the code, makes changes and pushes commits. That is a conversational trigger: a person asks and Claude answers, right where the conversation is already happening.

A prompt on any GitHub event runs automatically: turn issues into pull requests, check something on every push, run a recurring task. That is scheduled work that uses a git event as its clock.

/install-github-app

The quick setup installs the GitHub App, sets up the secret used for authentication, and pushes a branch with the workflow files ready to merge. It needs admin access to the repository and the GitHub CLI signed in with gh auth login.

The credential is the part worth stopping on, because §13.9's argument applies directly. The app needs three permissions:

  • Contents read/write, so Claude can change files;
  • Issues read/write, so it can respond;
  • Pull requests read/write, so it can create pull requests and push.

That is a real grant, and it is the actual limit on what an automated run can do. Once a process holds a token, no permission rule in a workflow file restricts what that token can reach.

Authentication uses one of two secrets: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for a Claude API key, or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for a subscription token created with claude setup-token. In the workflow they map to the anthropic_api_key and claude_code_oauth_token inputs respectively. Mixing them up is the most common setup failure.

If you choose the review workflow, Claude posts each review on the pull request: an inline comment per finding, or one summary comment when it finds nothing. It skips some pull requests, such as drafts. GitLab CI/CD has its own equivalent with the same shape, and so does GitHub Enterprise Server for self-hosted GitHub. A GitLab pipeline gets the same @claude trigger and the same event-driven prompts, configured in GitLab's own pipeline file instead of a workflow file.

Two things to get right in any workflow you write. First, use --bare (§13.1), so the run does not load hooks, plugins or CLAUDE.md from whatever happens to be in the checkout. For a repository that accepts outside contributions, that is a matter of security, not tidiness. Second, give the run an exact allowlist, following §5.8's CI recipe: dontAsk mode plus --allowedTools denies anything not listed, instead of hanging on a prompt nobody will answer.

14.2 Code Review

Code Review is the managed alternative to writing that workflow yourself. It analyses pull requests and posts findings as inline comments on the lines where it found issues. Behind it, a group of specialised agents examines the diff against your whole codebase, looking for logic errors, security holes, broken edge cases and subtle regressions (things that used to work and now do not).

Two of its design decisions are worth understanding, because they are the difference between a review bot people read and one they mute.

A verification step filters candidates. Each agent looks for a different kind of issue. Then a separate step checks each candidate against how the code actually behaves, to remove false alarms. Results are de-duplicated and ranked before anything is posted. That is what "higher signal" means here, and it is why a review takes about twenty minutes, not thirty seconds.

Findings do not approve or block. They are tagged by severity and posted alongside your existing review process, which stays as it is:

🔴
Important
A bug that should be fixed before merging
🟡
Nit
A minor issue, worth fixing but not blocking
🟣
Pre-existing
A bug in the codebase that this PR did not introduce

That third severity is quietly the most interesting, because it is the finding a human reviewer almost never produces. A person's attention is on the diff, so a bug three lines above it is invisible. It is also the kind of finding most likely to be ignored, which is why labelling it separately, instead of mixing it with the diff's own problems, is the right call.

Reviews run when a pull request is opened, on every push, or by hand with @claude review as a top-level comment; @claude review always subscribes the pull request. Replying to an inline finding does nothing. To act on one, fix the code and push, and the next run closes the thread. Every comment comes with 👍 and 👎 attached, and the reaction counts tune the reviewer after the pull request is merged.

Two plugins sit next to it and solve related problems. security-guidance has Claude review its own code changes for vulnerabilities and fix them in the same session. It is the "shift-left" version: catching problems earlier, before a review exists to catch them. The Claude Security plugin scans a codebase for vulnerabilities and turns what it finds into patches for you to review. Both are installed like any plugin (§12.3). The security-guidance one is the more interesting of the two, because it works inside the loop rather than after it.

Adjust what it flags with a CLAUDE.md or REVIEW.md in the repository: what "important" means here, how many small style comments to allow, what never to report, what always to check. That file is all the configuration there is, and it is worth writing. A reviewer that flags your deliberate patterns is a reviewer people stop reading.

Code Review is a research preview for Team and Enterprise plans, and it is not available to organisations with Zero Data Retention enabled (§15.8). A managed service that analyses your code on someone else's servers is exactly what a Zero Data Retention policy rules out. On other plans, /code-review reviews a diff locally, and /code-review ultra (ultrareview) runs the same group of agents in a remote sandbox against your branch or a pull request. What ultrareview adds over a local review is that every finding is independently reproduced and verified before it is reported. That verification is the point: a review that only reports bugs it could reproduce is a much shorter and much more useful list.

14.3 Routines: Automation Without a Session

A routine is a saved Claude Code configuration (a prompt, one or more repositories, and a set of connectors) that runs on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure, or on your organisation's own self-hosted environment. It keeps working when your laptop is closed, which is what sets it apart from everything in §14.4.

Three trigger types:

Scheduled
Hourly, nightly, weekly, or once at a future time. Dependency audits, morning triage, a nightly sweep of a backlog.
API
Triggered by a call. Which makes a routine a building block for something else — your deploy pipeline can start one.
GitHub events
Reacting to repository activity, without a workflow file in the repository.

What decides between a routine and a GitHub Action is where the configuration lives. A workflow file is in the repository, reviewed like code, and versioned with it. A routine is a saved configuration outside any repository, which you can edit without a pull request and which can cover several repositories at once. The first is better for anything that should be reviewed; the second for day-to-day operational work.

One consequence worth knowing, because it produces a confusing failure: each routine run starts as a fresh remote session. So a skill that exists only in ~/.claude/skills/ on your machine is not there (§8.2). Commit it to the repository, ship it in a plugin declared in .claude/settings.json, or enable it for your claude.ai account.

14.4 Keeping a Session Working

Three mechanisms belong to a single session, and they solve a different problem from routines: making the session you already have keep going.

/loop re-runs a prompt at a fixed interval: check a deployment, watch over a pull request, look in on a long build. Cron tools schedule a single wake-up or a recurring one. Both are session-scoped: they live in the current conversation and stop when you start a new one. --resume does bring back any task that has not expired (a recurring task created within the last seven days, or a one-shot task whose time has not yet come).

/goal is the third, and it is different in kind, as §7.3 covered. It starts the next turn when the previous one finishes, not when a timer runs out, and it stops when a model confirms the condition. Use /loop for "check every five minutes"; use /goal for "keep going until this is true".

Channels reverse the whole arrangement. A channel is an MCP server that pushes events into your running session (a CI result, a monitoring alert, a chat message), so Claude reacts to something as it happens instead of finding out at the next check. Channels can work both ways: Claude reads the event and replies through the same channel. That is how the Telegram, Discord and iMessage bridges in the research preview work. Events arrive only while the session is open, so an always-on setup needs a background process or a terminal that stays open.

The choice between polling and pushing is the usual one. /loop costs a turn every interval whether anything happened or not, and its latency is half the interval on average. A channel costs nothing while idle and arrives immediately. Poll when the thing you are watching has no way to tell you; use a channel when it does.

14.5 Deep Links, Slack and Artifacts

Three mechanisms are about people. They are easy to overlook, because none of them is automation in the usual sense.

A deep link is a claude-cli:// URL that opens Claude Code in a new terminal window, with a working directory and a prompt already set. The prompt is populated but not sent until someone presses Enter. That is what makes it safe to put in the places a link normally goes:

An incident runbook
A step that opens the affected service's repository with a diagnostic prompt already typed.
A monitoring alert
A link from the alert to an investigation prompt for that specific metric.
A README
An onboarding prompt that opens the project the way a new teammate should start.

The first row is the underrated one. The expensive part of an incident is often the first ten minutes of working out where things are. A runbook step that opens the right repository with the right question already asked removes most of that, and costs you one URL to write.

Slack, through the Claude Tag integration, puts Claude Code where a team already talks. The Claude Tag makes it something you mention in a message, not an app you open. That matters for the same reason Code Review posts inline comments instead of writing to a log: automation nobody sees is automation nobody acts on. /install-slack-app handles the setup.

Artifacts publish a session's output as a live, interactive page on claude.ai. It is private by default, can be shared, and updates in place as the session continues. It is for cases where a terminal is the wrong medium: a migration plan for four teams to read, a dependency audit with a table nobody wants to scroll through in a terminal, a report people will come back to next week.

14.6 Cloud Sessions and Remote Control

There are two ways to move a session away from the terminal in front of you, and they are opposites.

Claude Code on the web runs at claude.ai/code, on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure or on your organisation's own self-hosted environment. Claude Code on the web is a full session, not just a viewer, which is what makes the next move possible. Sessions keep running when you close the browser, and you can follow them from the mobile app. --cloud creates or joins one from the CLI, and --teleport pulls a web session into your terminal. To teleport is to move the session, not copy it. That is the move that makes the two truly one product rather than two: start a task on your phone, and finish it at your desk with all your local tools.

Remote Control is the reverse: your machine, driven from a browser. The work runs and your files stay on your own machine; only the interface is somewhere else. It is the right choice when the work needs your local environment (credentials, a database, a device) and you are not at the keyboard.

The distinction to remember is where the code runs, not where you are sitting. A cloud session cannot touch your local database; a Remote Control session can do anything your machine can. Choosing between them is §5.8's isolation decision, made from the other end.

14.7 Choosing Where It Runs

Tied to a code change
GitHub Actions or Code Review. The event already exists, the audience is already looking, and the result lands next to the diff it is about.
Tied to the clock
A routine if it must run whether or not anyone is at a machine; /loop if it is about the session you are in right now.
Tied to an external event
A channel if a session is open and should react; a routine with an API trigger if it should run regardless.
Tied to a person
A deep link or Slack. The work needs someone's judgement to start, and the job of the automation is to remove the setup rather than the decision.
Tied to nothing yet
Run it by hand a few times first. Automation encodes a process, and encoding one you have not run is how you get a nightly job producing output nobody reads.

That last row is the practical advice worth ending on. Every mechanism here is cheap to set up, and none of them is cheap to maintain: a scheduled job that fails silently for two weeks (§13.2) costs more than the work it was doing. Run it manually until you know what the output should look like, then automate it with a check on the output, not just on the exit code.

Exercises

Exercise 14.1 — Place the automation. For each, choose a mechanism and justify it: (a) flag pull requests that change a public API without a version bump; (b) upgrade dependencies every Monday and open a PR; (c) when the staging deploy fails, have Claude read the logs and post a first diagnosis to the team's Slack channel; (d) give on-call engineers a one-click start for investigating a specific alert; (e) keep checking a slow migration you kicked off five minutes ago.

Solution

(a) A GitHub Action, or a Code Review instruction. The trigger is a code change, and the finding belongs on the diff. If you already run Code Review, this is a line in REVIEW.md — "always check that a change to api/v*/ carries a version bump" — which is far less machinery than a workflow. If you do not, a workflow with a targeted prompt and --json-schema output gives you a structured verdict a CI step can branch on (§13.2). A Stop hook would be wrong: it only fires in a session, and the property must hold for every PR including those a human wrote.

(b) A routine, on a schedule. It must run whether or not anyone is at a machine, which rules out /loop and scheduled tasks immediately — both are session-scoped. A GitHub Action on a cron schedule also works and is the better choice if you want the configuration reviewed in the repository. The routine wins when the job spans several repositories, since one routine can cover them where a workflow file cannot.

Whichever you pick, gate the output: a dependency upgrade that opens a PR should report what it upgraded and what it skipped in a structured form, so a failure to reach the registry is distinguishable from "nothing to upgrade" (§13.2).

(c) A routine with an API trigger, and Slack for the output. The deploy pipeline calls the routine on failure — that is what API triggers are for. A channel would be wrong here because it requires a session to already be open, and a staging failure at 3 a.m. has no session. Slack matters as much as the trigger: a diagnosis in a log nobody opens is not automation, and this is the §14.5 point in its plainest form.

(d) A deep link, in the alert itself. Not automation — the investigation needs a human's judgement to start — but it removes the expensive part, which is orientation. The alert links to a claude-cli:// URL carrying the right repository and a prompt naming the metric. The prompt is populated and not sent, so the engineer reads it, adjusts it, and presses Enter.

(e) Scheduled tasks, or /goal. Session-scoped is exactly right: you are here, the migration is running, and you want to know when it finishes. /loop at a sensible interval polls it; /goal the migration has completed and the row counts match is better if the completion condition is something Claude's output can demonstrate (§7.3). Neither should be a routine — the session ends and so should the checking.

The dividing question in all five: does this need to happen when nobody is present? Yes → cloud (routine or Action). No → session-scoped. And separately: who is the audience, and will the result reach them?

Exercise 14.2 — Review the workflow. A colleague adds this to a repository that accepts community pull requests. Name every problem, ordered by severity.

name: claude-triage
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  triage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          claude_args: --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"
Solution

One, and it is the serious one: Bash with no scoping, on untrusted code. --allowedTools "Bash" is the bare tool name, which permits every shell command. The workflow checks out a community pull request — arbitrary code from someone outside the project — and then hands Claude unrestricted shell in a runner holding ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and the workflow's GitHub token. A package.json postinstall script, or a prompt-injection payload in the PR description (§5.9), reaches both. Scope it: Bash(npm ci), Bash(npm test), and nothing else.

Two: no --bare. Without it, the run loads hooks from the checked-out branch's .claude/settings.json and connects its .mcp.json servers — and §5.6 is explicit that a -p session shows no trust dialog and no per-server approval, so a contributor can ship a hook that runs on the first invocation. --bare is the fix, and --setting-sources user plus --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' are the belt-and-braces version.

Three: acceptEdits on a triage job. Triage reads and reports; it has no reason to write files at all. acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands, which is capability granted for nothing. --permission-mode dontAsk with the exact allowlist is the correct shape for CI: anything unlisted is denied rather than prompted, so the job fails visibly instead of hanging.

Four: Edit in the allowlist, for the same reason. A job that cannot write cannot leave a surprise in the tree.

Five, and it is not in the file: the token. The workflow's permissions are not stated, so it inherits the repository default — which may be write. §13.9's point applies: no flag above constrains what a credential can do once a process holds it. Add an explicit permissions: block granting pull-requests: write and nothing else.

The corrected shape:

      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          claude_args: >-
            --bare --permission-mode dontAsk
            --allowedTools "Read" "Grep" "Glob" "Bash(npm ci)" "Bash(npm test)"

The general test, and the one worth carrying: ask what this job can do if it is fully persuaded by something in the branch it checked out. Under the original, the answer is "anything the runner can, with two credentials". Under the corrected version it is "read the repository, run two known commands, and comment" — which is bounded, boring and correct. That question is the same one §5.9 asks of a local session; the difference is that here nobody is watching, so the configuration is the only answer.

SECTION 15

Cost, Monitoring and Enterprise Operations

The previous fourteen sections were about making Claude Code work. This one is about what happens when it works and there are two hundred of you using it. Someone has to know what it costs, whether it is helping, what it is allowed to reach, and where the data goes.

Those questions arrive in a predictable order, and each needs different tools:

  1. A developer wonders why their session got expensive.
  2. A manager asks what the team is spending.
  3. A security review asks what data leaves the company.

This section takes them in that order.

15.1 What It Costs, and Why

Claude Code is charged by how many API tokens it uses. Across company deployments, the reported figures are about $13 per developer per active day and $150–250 per developer per month, with 90% of users below $30 per active day. The range is wide because cost depends on which model is used, how big the codebase is, and whether someone runs one session or six.

The advice that follows from those numbers is to start with a small pilot group and establish a baseline before wider rollout, using the tracking described below. An estimate taken from someone else's team is worth very little; a week of your own numbers is worth a lot.

/cost and /usage are the two commands here, and /usage is the one to use. /cost reports the running total for the session, while /usage shows that total broken down, plus what counts against your plan. Read the breakdown, not the single number.

/usage shows the current session:

Total cost: $0.55
Total duration (API): 6m 20s
Total duration (wall): 6h 33m 10s
Total code changes: 0 lines added, 0 lines removed

Usage by model:
  claude-sonnet-4-6: 1.2k input, 5.3k output, 940.0k cache read, 50.0k cache write ($0.55)

Read the breakdown and not the total, because it contains the whole argument of §3. 940k cache read against 50k cache write describes a session whose caching is working. The same session with those numbers reversed would cost several times as much for identical work. The input and output counts barely matter next to them.

The dollar figure is computed locally from token counts at standard list rates. It does not reflect promotional pricing or contracted discounts and may differ from your actual bill. It is excellent for comparison — is this job twice as expensive as that one — and should never be reconciled against an invoice. The Claude Console usage page is authoritative.

Totals reset when /clear starts a new session. Know that before you read a $0.00 total as good news.

On a paid plan, /usage also shows what counts against your limits, and three of its rows really help with diagnosis:

Attribution
Usage attributed to skills, subagents, plugins and individual MCP servers, each as a percentage. This is how you find out that one MCP server accounts for a third of your spend.
Behaviour flags
Long context or cache misses flagged when either accounts for 10% or more. A cache-miss flag is §3.6 telling you something is invalidating the prefix.
Loops
The heaviest /loop and scheduled tasks, with how often each fires, its total and per-run tokens, and when it last ran. A forgotten loop is a real and quiet cost.

d and w switch between 24 hours and 7 days. The figures come from the session history stored on this machine, so other devices and claude.ai are not included.

/insights answers a different question: how you work, rather than how much you used. It analyses your recent sessions on this machine and writes an HTML report on what you work on, where things got stuck (requests that were misunderstood, code that had bugs), and suggestions. It runs on any plan, and its tokens count against your usage like anything else.

15.2 Reducing It

Every lever here is something an earlier section already covered, and that is the point: cost is a consequence of context, not a separate subject.

Clear between tasks
Stale context costs tokens on every subsequent message. /rename before clearing so the session stays findable (§2.6). The single highest-value habit.
Compact with instructions
/compact Focus on code samples and API usage, or a standing Compact instructions section in CLAUDE.md so every automatic pass keeps what matters. Compact instructions in CLAUDE.md are the version that keeps working when you are not there to type one.
Choose the model deliberately
Sonnet for most coding, Opus for architecture and multi-step reasoning, model: haiku for simple subagents (§11.1). Picking once at the top of a session also avoids the cache cost of switching.
Prefer a CLI to an MCP server
gh, aws, gcloud add no per-tool listing at all (§10.10). Disable servers you are not using.
Install code intelligence
A "go to definition" replaces a grep plus reading three candidate files, and type errors arrive after edits without running a compiler (§12.2).
Preprocess with hooks
The biggest single lever nobody uses. A hook that greps a 10,000-line log for ERROR turns tens of thousands of tokens into hundreds — and hooks cost nothing in context themselves.

That last row deserves emphasis. The instinct, on seeing an expensive session, is to switch to a cheaper model, which lowers the price per token. Preprocessing lowers the number of tokens. That is usually the bigger factor, and it does not cost you capability. A PreToolUse hook that filters test output down to the failures is fifteen lines long, and it changes the cost of every debugging session after it.

A skill does the same for exploration. A "codebase-overview" skill describing the architecture, the key directories and the naming conventions gives Claude that context immediately, instead of spending tokens working it out again (§8.1).

15.3 Team and Organisation Spend

Where you see and limit spending depends entirely on how your organisation accesses Claude Code. Mixing up the three ways is a common cause of "we have no visibility":

Setup
Cap spend
Per-user reporting
Teams / Enterprise
Spend limits in admin settings
Spend report CSV; Enterprise Analytics API
Claude Console (API)
Workspace spend limits
Console dashboard; Claude Code Analytics API
Bedrock / Agent Platform / Foundry
Your cloud's budget controls
OpenTelemetry, or an LLM gateway

On Teams and Enterprise plans, each member's usage comes out of a per-seat allowance that resets on a rolling five-hour window and on a weekly one, shared with Claude chat and Cowork. The seat allowance is the default ceiling. To let people continue past it, you turn on usage credits and set spending limits at the organisation, group or member level. That is a really different model from paying per token, and it means "limiting spend" and "limiting usage" are two separate controls.

OpenTelemetry works on every setup. OpenTelemetry (OTel) is an open standard for sending metrics and logs to monitoring tools. It is the only option that streams token and cost metrics for each user into your own monitoring system, almost in real time. If the question is "what is happening right now?", it is the answer, however you pay.

15.4 Telemetry

export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1
export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp
export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Bearer your-token"
claude

Both exporters are optional; set up only what you need. To check that metrics arrive, look for claude_code.session.count, which is sent when a session starts. To check logs, submit a prompt and look for the claude_code.user_prompt event. If nothing arrives, run claude --debug and read the log for export errors.

There are eight OTel metrics, and the interesting thing about the list is that half of them are not about cost at all. Each OTel metric carries the standard attributes below, so any of them can be split by team, model or user:

claude_code.session.count
CLI sessions started
claude_code.token.usage
Tokens used
claude_code.cost.usage
Session cost, in USD
claude_code.lines_of_code.count
Lines modified
claude_code.pull_request.count
Pull requests created
claude_code.commit.count
Commits created
claude_code.code_edit_tool.decision
Code-editing tool permission decisions
claude_code.active_time.total
Total active time, in seconds

The last two are the ones worth building a dashboard around. code_edit_tool.decision is an approval-rate signal. If most edit decisions on a team are denials, the team's setup is fighting them, and no cost metric would show that. And active_time.total against cost.usage gives cost per active hour, the ratio that actually means something. Total spending rising because more people use the tool is a completely different situation from the same rise while usage stays flat.

Every export carries standard attributes: session.id, organization.id, user.account_uuid, user.email when signed in with OAuth, terminal.type, and whatever you set in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. That last one is how you split the data by department or team.id.

Events carry three attributes that metrics never do, because in metrics they would create an unlimited number of separate series. Each one solves a real problem.

  • prompt.id links a user prompt to every event that follows it, until the next prompt. It is the same value a hook receives (§9.5), so hook output and telemetry can be joined for a single prompt.
  • workflow.run_id rebuilds a dynamic workflow's whole run, including nested agents (§11.6).
  • workspace.host_paths records which directories a desktop session had.

Note one deliberate omission: Claude Code removes OTEL_* exporter variables from every subprocess it spawns, hooks included (§9.5), so a hook cannot accidentally send data into your pipeline.

Analytics is the other half. Its dashboard shows daily active users, sessions and contribution metrics, and can export to CSV. Telemetry answers "what is it costing?"; analytics answers "is anyone using it, and is it helping?".

15.5 Deployment and Gateways

Where the requests go is an organisational decision, and it has real consequences for the rest of this course.

Direct
The Claude API, with an API key or a subscription. Everything in this course works as written.
Cloud provider
Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, Claude Platform on AWS. Billing and data stay within an existing cloud relationship. Each names models differently — Amazon Bedrock takes an inference profile ARN where the Claude API takes a model alias — so a model value that works on one provider is not portable to another.
LLM gateway
Requests routed through infrastructure you run, for central key management, spend control and audit. An LLM gateway is the option that gives an organisation the most control and costs the most of the properties below.
Claude apps gateway
A managed gateway for Bedrock, AWS, Google Cloud and Foundry, with its own configuration, spend limits and deployment story.

A gateway is attractive for exactly the reasons people propose it: one place for keys, one place for limits, one place for logs. It is worth being explicit about what it costs, because these costs appear elsewhere in the course as puzzling symptoms:

Tool search may be off
A non-first-party ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL disables it, because most proxies do not forward tool_reference blocks — so MCP tool definitions load upfront and your context bill rises sharply (§10.9).
Caching depends on the gateway
The cache lives wherever requests are forwarded. A gateway that drops cache markers leaves a whole conversation billed as uncached input on every turn (§3.6).
Auto mode may be unavailable
Its model requirements are narrower on non-first-party providers (§5.5).
The window may be misjudged
Claude Code can assume the wrong context window for a gateway model alias, which moves the auto-compact threshold.

None of these is a reason not to run a gateway. They are reasons to measure before and after, because a gateway rollout that quietly doubles the cost of each turn looks exactly like Claude Code getting more expensive.

Next to the gateway question sit questions about the environment.

  • Network config covers proxies and certificates. Network config is where you make a company proxy that inspects encrypted (TLS) traffic work, instead of fighting it.
  • There is corporate launcher support, for companies that start tools through their own launcher.
  • Using dev containers gives everyone the same reproducible set of tools (§5.8).
  • A cloud environment hosts cloud sessions, and self-hosted environments serve organisations that want cloud sessions on servers they run themselves.

A cloud environment is configured once and inherited by every session sent to it, which is what makes routines (§14.3) reproducible.

15.6 Policy

Admin setup is where an organisation decides what to enforce, and managed settings are how that decision reaches developers' machines. Read the admin setup guide before choosing individual keys. The useful question is not "which settings exist?" but "which properties must hold whatever a developer does?", and that is a much shorter list. The mechanisms have appeared throughout this course, and are worth gathering in one place:

Permission rules
Not overridable downward. A managed deny survives --allowedTools (§5.6).
disableBypassPermissionsMode
Removes the mode entirely. disableAutoMode does the same for the classifier.
Sandbox enforcement
Managed sandbox.filesystem pins filesystem.disabled to managed settings, so developers cannot widen it (§5.7).
disableAllHooks
Only the managed level can disable managed hooks — an audit hook is not switchable off (§9.10).
availableModels
The lock that constrains /model, --model and the model key everywhere.
Managed MCP
Which servers are available, and which are not (§10.8).
Marketplace restrictions
Which plugin marketplaces may be added (§12.6).
disableWorkflows
Turns dynamic workflows off organisation-wide (§11.6).

Managed settings are delivered by a managed-settings.json file in a system directory, by an MDM policy, or as server-managed settings fetched from the claude.ai admin console. Server-managed settings are the only one of the three that reaches a cloud session. That makes them the right default for any organisation that uses cloud sessions at all. Managed settings changed through MDM or the console reach a running session on a schedule, not when saved (§6.3). That is why "the admin changed it and nothing happened" usually means "restart".

/status shows which managed source applies to a developer. It is the first thing to check when a policy seems not to be working. And the feature availability reference lists which features exist on which plan and provider. Check it before promising a team something their deployment does not have, because feature availability varies more than people expect: auto mode, tool search, Code Review, channels and workflows each have their own table.

15.7 Data

There are three documents, and the difference between them matters in a security review.

Data usage is the document that says what each provider stores and processes, and data usage really does differ by provider: a Bedrock deployment's data goes through AWS, not Anthropic.

Zero Data Retention (ZDR: nothing kept after a request is processed) is available for organisations that need it. It has a consequence worth knowing in advance: Code Review is not available with ZDR enabled (§14.2). That is the general shape of the trade-off. Managed services that analyse your code on someone else's servers are the first thing a retention policy removes, and it is better to find that out when choosing than when rolling out.

Legal and compliance covers the rest.

Two practical notes belong here rather than in a policy document. First, cleanupPeriodDays governs the retention sweep that deletes session transcripts, checkpoints and subagent transcripts after 30 days by default, and auto memory is excluded from it (§4.5), so memories stay until edited. Second, .claude/ holds application data with different lifetimes: some is cleaned up automatically, some is kept until you delete it, and some is stored as plain text. An organisation with a data policy should read that list rather than guess.

15.8 Troubleshooting

Troubleshooting Claude Code is unusual in one way: because broken configuration makes things worse without stopping them, the hardest part is usually noticing. Here are four resources, in the order to use them.

/doctor
A setup checkup that diagnoses installation and configuration problems and can fix them. It also proposes CLAUDE.md trims and estimates the skill-listing cost (§8.5). Run it first.
Debug your config
The wider walkthrough — /context, /status, settings precedence, and a clean-configuration test that isolates whether the problem is yours. Reach for debug your config when /doctor reports nothing and the behaviour is still wrong.
The error reference
The error reference lists every named error with its cause and fix. Claude Code's errors are unusually specific — Agent would be spawned with zero tools, headersHelper not run — and each is a search away from an answer.
--debug-file
The full log, which is where hook execution, matcher decisions and MCP connection detail actually live (§9.11).

The clean-configuration test is the one to remember, because it settles the most common question in one step. Run with --bare and --setting-sources user. If the problem disappears, it is in your configuration; if it stays, it is not. Two flags, and it saves an hour of switching settings files on and off one by one.

Exercises

Exercise 15.1 — Read the meter. A developer says their sessions have become expensive. /usage shows for the current session: 4.1k input, 12.3k output, 180k cache read, 620k cache write, on Opus. Diagnose it and give three changes in priority order.

Solution

The diagnosis is in the ratio: cache write is three and a half times cache read. A healthy session is the other way round by a wide margin — the §15.1 example shows 940k read against 50k write. Writes exceeding reads means the cached prefix is being rebuilt over and over, so almost every turn is paying to re-process the whole conversation instead of reading it back cheaply (§3.6). The behaviour flags row in /usage would flag this as cache misses, since it is well past 10% of usage.

What causes it, in likelihood order. Switching models or effort mid-session — each has its own cache, and with opusplan every plan-mode toggle is a model switch, so a developer cycling in and out of planning pays a full re-read each time. Repeated /compact, which invalidates the conversation layer by design. Or, in a gateway deployment, a proxy that drops cache markers, which leaves everything billed as uncached input (§15.5) — check whether ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set before blaming habits.

Three changes, in order.

One: pick model and effort once, at the top of the session. Free, immediate, and it addresses the most likely cause directly. If they are on opusplan, make that trade explicit — it is a good setting whose cost is invisible.

Two: /clear between tasks instead of /compact within one. Compaction rebuilds the prefix; clearing starts a short one. And /rewind beats /compact for abandoning a path, because it truncates to a prefix the cache already holds (§3.6).

Three: reconsider Opus. This is deliberately third. It reduces the price per token while the first two reduce how many tokens are processed at the expensive rate, which is the larger factor here — and switching model is the one change that costs capability. If the work genuinely needs Opus, keep it.

And check promptCacheTtl. On an API key the main conversation defaults to a five-minute TTL, so a developer who thinks between prompts pays a rebuild every time they pause. "promptCacheTtl": "1h" may be the single most effective line in the file for this person's working style.

The lesson: the cost total tells you there is a problem; the read-to-write ratio tells you which one. Look at the breakdown before changing anything.

Exercise 15.2 — Design the rollout. You are introducing Claude Code to 60 engineers at a company with an existing LLM gateway and a data-retention policy. Design the first three months: what you measure, what you enforce, what you deliberately leave open, and what you check before starting.

Solution

Before anything: check what the gateway costs you. §15.5's list is not a footnote here. Behind a non-first-party ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, tool search may be off — which loads every MCP tool definition upfront and raises the context bill on every request — caching depends on whether the gateway forwards markers, and auto mode may be unavailable. Run a two-person test through the gateway and directly, compare the cache read/write ratio and the /context breakdown, and find out. Discovering it after sixty people have onboarded means every cost number you gathered was measuring the gateway.

Also check feature-availability against the retention policy. If ZDR is on, Code Review is unavailable (§14.2), and a rollout plan built around automatic PR review needs to know that on day one rather than in month two.

Month one: five to eight people, measure everything, enforce almost nothing. Turn on OpenTelemetry from the start — it works on every setup and is the only near-real-time per-user source. Set OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES with team.id so the data is sliceable later. The baseline to establish is cost per active hour, from cost.usage against active_time.total, not total spend, because total spend will rise as adoption does and tells you nothing about efficiency.

Watch code_edit_tool.decision too. A high denial rate in the pilot means the permission setup is fighting people, and it is far cheaper to fix that now than after sixty people have each worked around it in their own local settings.

Month one, also: enforce the small number of things that are genuinely policy. A managed deny list for credentials and secrets, disableBypassPermissionsMode, and sandbox settings if the machines allow it. These are the ones no developer should need to think about, and putting them in managed settings from the start avoids the much harder conversation of taking capability away later.

Month two: widen to 20, and let the pilot's setup become the project's. By now the pilot has accumulated CLAUDE.md files, a few skills and a hook or two. Package what is shared into a plugin on an internal marketplace (§12.6) so the second cohort starts where the first finished rather than rediscovering it. This is the single biggest determinant of whether the wider rollout feels like the pilot did.

Month three: full rollout, with spend limits informed by real data. On Teams or Enterprise the seat allowance is already a ceiling; set usage-credit limits at group level using the pilot's distribution rather than a guess. Add the analytics dashboard for adoption, which answers a different question from telemetry — telemetry says what it costs, analytics says whether anyone is using it.

What to leave deliberately open, and why it matters. Model and effort choice, permission modes beyond the ones you locked, whether people use subagents or worktrees, and what goes in their personal settings. Every one of those is a productivity decision that varies by person and task, and enforcing them centrally buys a small amount of predictability for a large amount of friction. The rule from §6.6 generalises: put a policy at the widest scope where it is still true, and "everyone must use Sonnet" is not true.

The metric I would report upward is not spend. It is pull_request.count and commit.count against active_time.total — throughput per hour of use — with cost as a denominator rather than the headline. A rollout judged on cost alone optimises toward people not using it, which is the one outcome nobody wants.

SECTION 16

From Idea to Merged Change

Earlier sections taught the parts: how the loop works, how to steer it, what fills the window, and how to give it memory, limit it, verify it, extend it and run it unattended. This section is the whole path for one piece of work, from a sentence someone said in a meeting to a merged pull request. It is organised around a single claim: most of the value is decided before any code is written, and most of the risk is decided after the last line is.

The claim comes from how Claude Code fails. It rarely fails at writing a function. It fails in three other ways:

  • it solves a problem slightly different from the one you had;
  • it finishes something that only looks done;
  • it spreads past the edges of the task, changing things nobody asked for.

Each of those failures has a step in the workflow that exists to prevent it. Each step below is small, and each is justified by the failure it removes.

The prompts and recommendations are Anthropic's, from its best-practices guide and common-workflows guide, quoted where the wording is exact. The checks are this course's own addition, and the ones that can run do. The spec linter, the mutation check (deliberately breaking the code to see whether the tests notice) and the scope check below are real code with real printed output, in the same spirit as §17's history probes. The section ends with a small feature taken through the whole path, from failing tests (red) to passing ones (green).

16.1 The Whole Path, and the Failure Each Step Prevents

First, read the loop as a series of questions. Each question has an owner (who answers it) and an artefact (the thing the answer produces):

Step
The failure it prevents
The artefact it leaves
1
Challenge the request
Building the thing that was asked for instead of the thing that was needed
Answers to the questions nobody had asked
2
Write the spec
Every later step re-deriving the requirements, differently each time
SPEC.md
3
Plan, in plan mode
A well-made solution to the wrong problem
A plan you edited before it ran
4
Build one thin slice
A large change nobody can review and nothing has run against
A small change that works end to end
5
Tests worth trusting
Tests that pass whatever the code does
Tests that fail when the code is wrong
6
Review in a fresh context
The author grading its own work
Findings against the spec
7
Document the change
Knowledge that lives only in one session
Docs, changelog, and corrections turned into CLAUDE.md
8
Open the pull request
A reviewer reconstructing intent from a diff
A description with intent, evidence and risks

Two things follow from the table. First, no step is about typing code: the model does that, and the workflow surrounds it. Second, not every step is required for every task. §2.4 gave the rule for planning ("if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan"), and the same sense of proportion applies to the rest. A typo fix needs a check and a commit; a change that touches billing needs all eight steps. The skill this section teaches is knowing which of the eight the task in front of you deserves.

The steps also map onto tools you have already met, which is why this section can say little about mechanics. The spec and the plan use plan mode (§2.4) and fresh sessions (§2.6). The checks use §7. The review uses subagents (§11) and the bundled review command (§14.2). The record uses CLAUDE.md (§4). What is new here is the order, and the reasons for it.

16.2 Challenge the Request Before Any Code

The cheapest bug to fix is one in the requirements. The most expensive is one found after the feature ships. A request such as "add a way for users to export their data" hides a dozen decisions: which data, in what format, for whom, how large, how fast, what happens to deleted records, who is allowed to ask, and whether this is a feature or a legal obligation with a deadline. If you let it, Claude will make every one of those decisions silently, and each will look reasonable.

Interview mode: have Claude interview you

The best-practices guide has a specific technique for this, and it reverses the usual direction: have Claude interview you. It recommends starting from a minimal prompt and asking Claude to use its AskUserQuestion tool, and it gives this prompt:

I want to build [brief description]. Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool.

Ask about technical implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs. Don't ask obvious questions, dig into the hard parts I might not have considered.

Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.

Three parts of that prompt do the work. "Don't ask obvious questions, dig into the hard parts I might not have considered" points the model at the gaps, not at what you already know. "Keep interviewing until we've covered everything" makes the interview open-ended. It is a conversation, not a form, and the questions that matter tend to come in the third round, prompted by an answer in the first. And the last sentence gives it an artefact: the interview ends with a written spec, so the knowledge does not live and die in one conversation.

You do not have to use the interview format to get the benefit. The questions worth asking yourself before any feature form a short list; the interview is just a way of getting a model to ask them:

Who, and why now?
Who asked for it and what are they doing when they need it? A feature with no named user is a guess with a schedule.
What does done look like?
Concretely enough that two people would agree whether it was reached. If you cannot state it, you cannot verify it.
What is not included?
The things that are adjacent and tempting. Naming them is what stops the diff from sprawling.
What can go wrong?
Empty input, huge input, concurrent use, a failed dependency, a user who is not who they say. These become the edge cases in §16.6.
What already exists?
The pattern this should follow, the code it should reuse, the thing it must not break.

A useful test of an interview is what it changed. If you finish and nothing in your original idea moved, either the idea was unusually complete or the questions were too easy. Then it is worth running one more round with the instruction "what are the three assumptions in this request that are most likely to be wrong?" The answers are often the most valuable output of the whole session.

16.3 The Spec: the One Document the Rest of the Work Reads

The interview produces a spec, and the guide is specific about what makes one useful. In its words, a good spec is self-contained: it names the files and interfaces involved, lists what is excluded, and ends with an end-to-end verification that proves the feature works. It adds: "Time spent making the spec precise pays off more than time spent watching the implementation."

What a usable spec contains: goal, files, the out-of-scope list, an end-to-end verification step

That sentence is a specification for the specification, and it can be checked by a program. Four properties make a spec usable by a fresh session that has never seen the interview:

A goal in one paragraph
What the feature does and for whom, without a solution in it. If the goal names a library, it is a design in disguise.
The files and interfaces
