Run the experiments in this order, and do run them, because a wrong diagnosis is expensive in specific ways. Rewriting your CLAUDE.md because a session was polluted teaches Claude nothing it needed. Clearing a session because a hook has a lowercase matcher makes the problem come back in the next session exactly as before. And hunting through the code for a bug that is really a permission rule (Bash(rm *) does not block /bin/rm, because rules match the literal command text) can take an afternoon that one look at /permissions would have saved.

Configuration bugs are the ones Claude cannot debug for you by reasoning, because the fault is in what loaded, not in what was written. That is why the guide's first instruction is to inspect rather than guess.

17.7 Diagnose a Session, Recover a Session

Whichever kind it turns out to be, you diagnose it from evidence Claude Code will show you. The debugging guide lists the commands, and they line up with the questions in the order you should ask them:

/context
What is in the window? Everything occupying context by category: system prompt, tools, MCP tools, custom subagents with their source, memory files, skills, and messages. Run it first. If your CLAUDE.md is not listed, it did not load, and no amount of rewording will help.
/memory
Which memory files, from where? The locations across user and project scopes, and the auto memory folder.
/permissions, /hooks, /mcp, /skills
What rules, hooks, servers and skills are active? Each shows the resolved state, not what you meant to write.
/status
Which settings files are in effect? Including whether managed settings apply.
/doctor
Is the installation sound? Installation health, invalid settings files, duplicate subagent names, and checked-in CLAUDE.md content Claude can derive from the code, with proposed fixes.
/debug [issue]
What actually happened? Enables debug logging for the session and has Claude read the log and the settings paths to diagnose it.

Two more techniques come from the same guide. Test against a clean configuration when even --safe-mode leaves you unsure: point CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR at an empty directory, and launch from a directory with no .claude folder, .mcp.json or CLAUDE.md:

cd /tmp && CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=/tmp/claude-clean claude

If the problem disappears there, the cause is in your real ~/.claude or project .claude files, and you reintroduce them one at a time: bisect, for configuration. Two caveats from the guide: managed settings from your organisation still apply in a clean session, and you will be asked to log in again.

The other technique is to check the common causes before assuming a bug, because most configuration surprises are about location and syntax. The guide's table is worth reading once in full; these are the ones behind most cases:

A hook never fires
The matcher is an array instead of a string; or lowercase ("bash" instead of "Bash", since matching is case-sensitive); or the hook is in a standalone file rather than under "hooks" in settings.json. (§9.11)
A setting is ignored
The same key is set in settings.local.json, which overrides settings.json; or it was added to ~/.claude.json, which holds app state, not permissions, hooks or env. (§6.2)
A subdirectory CLAUDE.md is ignored
Subdirectory files load on demand, when Claude reads a file in that directory, not at session start. (§4.3)
A subagent ignores CLAUDE.md
The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip it, so restate the instruction in the delegating prompt. (§11.1)
A skill never triggers
It is in .claude/skills/name.md rather than .claude/skills/name/SKILL.md; or it has disable-model-invocation: true; or its description does not match how you phrase the request. (§8.5)
A project MCP server is missing
Its config is under .claude/ or under a servers key rather than mcpServers in a .mcp.json at the repository root; or its one-time approval prompt was dismissed. (§10.3)

Summarize from here, clear, and branch

When the problem is the session and not the setup, recovery has more options than "start over", and they differ in what they keep:

/rewind: restore code and conversation
Revert both to a chosen prompt. Right when a wrong turn also damaged files.
/rewind: restore conversation
Rewind the conversation but keep the code. Right when the code is good and the conversation went astray.
/rewind: restore code
Revert files, keep the conversation. Right when you want Claude to remember what failed.
/rewind: summarize from here
Compress from a chosen message onward into a summary, freeing context. A targeted /compact. Summarizing "doesn't change files on disk, and the original messages stay in the session transcript".
/clear
Empty context. The previous conversation is saved and can be resumed with /resume.
/branch, or claude --continue --fork-session
Try a different approach while keeping the original session intact.

Two rules from §2.5 carry over and matter most here. Checkpoints only track edits made through Claude's editing tools, so an rm or mv in a Bash command is not rewound. And subagent edits are usually not restored either, so git is the way back for those. The safe habit is the one from §17.5: commit after every green step. It makes every rewind decision cheap.

The best-practices guide gives a specific, counted trigger for clearing: after two failed corrections (its session guidance says "more than twice"), /clear and write a better initial prompt that includes what you learned. The rule exists because a failed approach stays in the window and competes with the fix, which §3.8 puts numbers on. The step people skip when clearing is carrying the knowledge across. What the session learned is exactly what a fresh one lacks, and asking for it costs one prompt:

Before I clear this session, write HANDOFF.md: the goal, what we tried and why
each attempt failed, what is known to be true, the next thing to try, and the
exact command that reproduces the failure. Do not include anything you are unsure of.

Again, the last sentence is the important one. A handoff written from a polluted context carries the pollution across, unless it is told to leave out what it is not sure of.

17.8 Large-Scale Change: Fan Out Across Files

The last case is the largest: a mechanical change that applies to hundreds of files, more than any single session can hold. Two mechanisms exist, and choosing between them comes down to who controls the loop.

/batch <instruction> is a bundled skill that organises the work for you. It "researches the codebase, decomposes the work into 5 to 30 independent units, and presents a plan". Once you approve, it "spawns one background subagent per unit in an isolated worktree", and each subagent "implements its unit, runs tests, and publishes its change". It needs a git repository (or a WorktreeCreate hook), and the documented example is /batch migrate src/ from JavaScript to TypeScript. The deciding property is the plan you approve first. The way the work is split up is where a migration goes wrong, and you see the split before any code changes.

Your own loop over claude -p gives you control of everything the skill decides: the unit of work, the check, the permissions, the retry policy and the record. The best-practices guide sketches it in four lines. It also gives the method that matters more than the loop itself: generate the list of files first and write it to a file, test the prompt on two or three files, refine it from what goes wrong, and only then run the rest. A prompt that fails on the fourth file will fail on two hundred, and at that scale every failure is a diff to review.

The guide's loop goes through the files with for file in $(cat files.txt). That splits on spaces, so it breaks on any path containing a space (the kind of bug ShellCheck reports as SC2013). Below is a version that survives real repositories, with the test setup needed to try it without spending anything. The stand-in for claude is a five-line script, so what is being tested is the loop:

import os, stat, subprocess, tempfile, textwrap

workdir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='fanout-')
bin_dir = os.path.join(workdir, 'bin')
os.makedirs(bin_dir)

# A stand-in for `claude -p`: it "migrates" a file, and FAILs on anything called legacy.
with open(os.path.join(bin_dir, 'claude'), 'w') as handle:
    handle.write('#!/bin/sh\ncase "$2" in *legacy*) echo FAIL; exit 0;; esac\necho OK\n')
os.chmod(os.path.join(bin_dir, 'claude'), stat.S_IRWXU)

FILES = ['src/app.py', 'src/legacy_report.py', 'src/util helpers.py', 'src/models.py', 'src/legacy_export.py', 'src/cli.py']
with open(os.path.join(workdir, 'files.txt'), 'w') as handle:
    handle.write('\n'.join(FILES) + '\n')

LOOP = textwrap.dedent('''
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -u
    ok=0; failed=()
    while IFS= read -r file; do
        result=$(claude -p "Migrate $file from Python 2 to Python 3. Return OK or FAIL." \\
                   --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(git commit *)" </dev/null)
        if [ "$result" = OK ]; then
            ok=$((ok + 1))
        else
            failed+=("$file")
        fi
    done < files.txt
    echo "migrated: $ok"
    echo "failed  : ${#failed[@]}"
    printf '  %s\\n' "${failed[@]}"
''').lstrip('\n')
with open(os.path.join(workdir, 'loop.sh'), 'w') as handle:
    handle.write(LOOP)

env = {**os.environ, 'PATH': bin_dir + os.pathsep + os.environ['PATH']}
syntax = subprocess.run(['bash', '-n', 'loop.sh'], cwd=workdir, capture_output=True, text=True)
print('bash -n loop.sh:', 'ok' if syntax.returncode == 0 else syntax.stderr.strip())
print(subprocess.run(['bash', 'loop.sh'], cwd=workdir, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout, end='')

bash -n loop.sh: ok
migrated: 4
failed  : 2
  src/legacy_report.py
  src/legacy_export.py

The loop handles the path with a space (src/util helpers.py) because it reads one line at a time instead of splitting a string. It also records failures instead of stopping at them, which makes the second pass possible: the list of failed files becomes the input to an improved prompt, and the loop runs again on those alone. The </dev/null matters: without it, claude -p can swallow the loop's own input, and the loop ends after the first file. The --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(git commit *)" is the guide's own restriction, and it is not optional at this scale. An unattended loop should be able to edit files and make commits and nothing else: §5's permission design applied to a batch.

Four disciplines separate a migration that lands from one that leaves a repository half-changed:

Make each unit independently verifiable. "Return OK or FAIL" is an agreement a script can count, but an OK is only the model's opinion. A stronger unit has its own check: run that file's tests after the change, and count only files whose check passed. Without that, you are counting confidence.

Make the unit idempotent. That is, safe to run more than once. A file that is already migrated must come back as OK without changing, because you will run the loop twice (once on three files to refine the prompt, and once on everything), and any interruption means a third run. If re-running a unit can break it, you cannot recover from a run that was killed.

Commit per unit. One commit per file turns a failure into git revert of one small thing, and turns "which of the two hundred changes broke the build?" into the bisect of §17.3.

Review a sample of the OKs, not only the FAILs. A loop that reports two hundred successes has told you what the model believed. Read ten of them.

Whether to use /batch or your own loop follows from those disciplines. Use /batch when the work splits cleanly into units, you want to review the plan up front, and the worktree isolation and per-unit tests it provides are what you would have built anyway. Write your own loop when you need a check the skill does not know about, a record you will act on afterwards, or narrower permissions than a subagent's defaults. Both use building blocks you have already met: subagents (§11.1), worktrees (§11.7), and the headless mode of §13.

Exercises

Exercise 17.1 — The first hour. You inherit a service with no tests and no documentation, and a deploy on Friday. Write the sequence of prompts and checks you would run in the first hour, with one mechanical cross-check for each claim Claude makes about the code.

Solution 
1. (plan mode)   Use a subagent to give me an overview of this repository: entry
                 points, main modules, data stores, external services. Report
                 file paths and line numbers and list what you could not determine.
   check:        run the citation checker of 17.2 over every path:line it gave;
                 run the inventory of 17.1 and compare (tests? size? TODO markers?).
2. (plan mode)   What are the key data models, and what does each of these terms
                 mean in this code: <the five words you did not recognise>?
   check:        grep each term; if it means two things, it needs two glossary entries.
3.               Trace what happens when <the request that matters on Friday>
                 reaches the service, step by step, with file and line for each.
   check:        follow two steps by hand in the code.
4.               Look through the git history of <the module Friday touches> and
                 summarize why it is the way it is.
   check:        git log --follow -p on the same file; read the two largest commits.
5. (a shell)     Hotspots and co-change (17.3): which files change most, and which
                 change together with the one you will touch?
6.               Write characterization tests for <the function Friday changes>
                 without changing it; comment anything that looks like a bug.
   check:        run them; read every recorded value yourself.

The order is the point. Steps 1 to 4 are questions, and every answer comes with something checkable: a location, a definition, a command. Steps 5 and 6 are what turns understanding into permission to change. Notice what is not in the first hour: any edit. The change is Friday's problem, and by then it has a safety net.

Exercise 17.2 — Which kind of broken? For each symptom, say which of the three kinds you suspect first, the one experiment that would confirm it, and what you would do if the experiment says otherwise. (a) Claude keeps changing the wrong file after you have corrected it three times. (b) A PreToolUse hook that blocks writes to migrations/ did nothing last night. (c) pytest fails on CI and passes on your machine, and Claude proposes three different fixes in a row. (d) Your CLAUDE.md says to use tabs, and the last three files Claude wrote use spaces.

Solution 
CASES = [
    ('(a) wrong file after three corrections', 'session',
     '/clear and re-ask with the file named; two failed corrections is the documented trigger',
     'if it repeats in a clean session, the instruction is ambiguous: name the file and the reason in CLAUDE.md'),
    ('(b) hook did nothing', 'configuration',
     '/hooks shows whether it is registered; then check matcher case and type (a string, "Write|Edit")',
     'if it is registered and matches, log its input and exit code (9.11)'),
    ('(c) CI-only failure, three different fixes', 'code (and an environment gap)',
     'reproduce it outside Claude in CI conditions; three different fixes means nobody has a hypothesis',
     'if it will not reproduce, the difference is the environment: diff versions, env vars, data'),
    ('(d) tabs instead of spaces despite CLAUDE.md', 'configuration',
     '/context: is CLAUDE.md in the window? If yes, is a longer or conflicting file competing with it?',
     'if it loaded and is short, a formatter hook enforces the rule; an instruction is a probability'),
]
for symptom, kind, experiment, otherwise in CASES:
    print(f'{symptom}\n    suspect   : {kind}\n    experiment: {experiment}\n    otherwise : {otherwise}\n')

(a) wrong file after three corrections
    suspect   : session
    experiment: /clear and re-ask with the file named; two failed corrections is the documented trigger
    otherwise : if it repeats in a clean session, the instruction is ambiguous: name the file and the reason in CLAUDE.md

(b) hook did nothing
    suspect   : configuration
    experiment: /hooks shows whether it is registered; then check matcher case and type (a string, "Write|Edit")
    otherwise : if it is registered and matches, log its input and exit code (9.11)

(c) CI-only failure, three different fixes
    suspect   : code (and an environment gap)
    experiment: reproduce it outside Claude in CI conditions; three different fixes means nobody has a hypothesis
    otherwise : if it will not reproduce, the difference is the environment: diff versions, env vars, data

(d) tabs instead of spaces despite CLAUDE.md
    suspect   : configuration
    experiment: /context: is CLAUDE.md in the window? If yes, is a longer or conflicting file competing with it?
    otherwise : if it loaded and is short, a formatter hook enforces the rule; an instruction is a probability

The lesson in (c) is that the three "fixes" are a symptom of the missing step 1 of the method: nobody reproduced the failure, so every fix is a guess. Claude produces plausible guesses cheaply, which makes the absence of a reproduction easy to miss. (d) is the reminder from §4.6 and §9 that an instruction is a probability and a hook is a guarantee: if tabs must be tabs, a formatter run by a hook makes it so regardless of what Claude decided.

Exercise 17.3 — Small steps. The refactoring loop of §17.5 stopped at step three. Explain what you do next: is step three simply wrong, or was the change it made intended? Show how you would record the decision either way, and what the four-step sequence looks like afterwards.

Solution 
def shipping_cost(kilos, zone, express=False):
    cost = 5.0
    if kilos > 2:
        cost = cost + (kilos - 2) * 1.5
    cost = cost * {'EU': 1.4, 'WORLD': 2.5}.get(zone, 1.0)
    if express:
        cost = cost + 12
    return round(cost, 2)

def step3(kilos, zone, express=False):
    cost = 5.0 + max(0, kilos - 2) * 1.5 + (12 if express else 0)
    return round(cost * {'EU': 1.4, 'WORLD': 2.5}.get(zone, 1.0), 2)

for zone in ('DOM', 'EU', 'WORLD'):
    old, new = shipping_cost(3, zone, True), step3(3, zone, True)
    print(f'{zone:<6} express, 3 kg: legacy {old:>6.2f}   step 3 {new:>6.2f}   difference {new - old:+.2f}')
print('the express fee is now multiplied by the zone rate; before, it was a flat 12')

DOM    express, 3 kg: legacy  18.50   step 3  18.50   difference +0.00
EU     express, 3 kg: legacy  21.10   step 3  25.90   difference +4.80
WORLD  express, 3 kg: legacy  28.25   step 3  46.25   difference +18.00
the express fee is now multiplied by the zone rate; before, it was a flat 12

Step three is not a refactor, it is a pricing change: it multiplies the express fee by the zone rate, so an express parcel to the world zone costs 18 more (the fee becomes 12 × 2.5 = 30 instead of a flat 12). The suite caught it. The next move is not to edit the golden value to make it pass. First find out whether the business meant it. If it did not, discard step three and keep the earlier structure; the sequence is then steps one, two and four, with four rewritten to apply the surcharge after the zone multiplier. If it did, land it as its own commit after the refactor, with the golden values updated in the same commit and a message that says "express surcharge now scales with zone (pricing change)", so that anyone bisecting a customer complaint about shipping costs finds a commit with a name that describes it.

Exercise 17.4 — Design the fan-out. You must convert 1,800 files from one logging library to another. Decide between /batch and your own loop, write the per-file check, the commit policy and the stopping rule, and say what evidence you want before approving the full run.

Solution 
failed_first_batch = 4
first_batch = 12
observed = failed_first_batch / first_batch
print(f'first batch: {failed_first_batch} of {first_batch} failed = {observed:.0%}')
for rate in (0.33, 0.10, 0.02):
    print(f'if the full run fails at {rate:>4.0%}: {int(1800 * rate):>4} files to triage by hand')
print('the number that decides whether to continue is the failure rate on the SECOND batch, after refining the prompt')

first batch: 4 of 12 failed = 33%
if the full run fails at  33%:  594 files to triage by hand
if the full run fails at  10%:  180 files to triage by hand
if the full run fails at   2%:   36 files to triage by hand
the number that decides whether to continue is the failure rate on the SECOND batch, after refining the prompt

Choose your own loop here, because the deciding requirement is a per-file check the skill cannot know about: after each file, run the tests for the module that file belongs to, and count it as done only if they pass and no other file changed. Commit once per file with the path in the message, so any single conversion reverts alone. Stop when the failure rate over the last 50 files exceeds a threshold you set before you started (5% is a reasonable opening figure), and treat the stop as information: something about the remaining files differs from the first batch. Before approving the full run you want three pieces of evidence: the prompt has been through at least two rounds of refinement on small batches; the failure rate on the second batch is much lower than on the first (the simulation shows why: a 33% rate on a batch of 12 predicts about 600 failures at scale); and you have read ten of the successful conversions in full. /batch would be the right choice if the conversion decomposed into a few dozen independent modules whose own test suites are the check, since the plan review and worktree isolation are then exactly what you would build.

SECTION 18

Capstone: A Repository from Cold Start to Production Setup

Seventeen sections taught mechanisms and methods, each correct on its own. This one applies them to a single repository, in the order a real project would actually do it. That is not the order the course taught them in: the course was organised by mechanism, and a real project is organised by whatever hurts next.

The repository is deliberately ordinary: orders, a Python service that is four years old, has 180,000 lines, a partially-honest test suite, three developers, and a monorepo layout with four packages. (A partially-honest test suite is one where some tests pass without really checking anything; a monorepo holds several packages in one repository.) It has no CLAUDE.md, no hooks, no skills and no permission rules. That is the state most repositories are in, and the interesting question is what to do first.

The idea running through what follows is the one §1.8 named: each layer adds distance between you and the work, and distance is only safe when there is something at the far end that can tell you whether the work is right. So verification comes early and extensions come late. Every single step is optional, but the order is not.

18.1 Day One: Find Out What Is True

Before configuring anything, find out what the repository is like to work in. Run three commands, then ask one question.

claude

/init

/init analyses the codebase and writes a starting CLAUDE.md: build commands, test instructions, conventions it found. Keep the commands and delete most of the rest (§4.1). What it can discover is what Claude could have discovered anyway, and every line costs tokens on every request, forever.

/context

This measurement decides several later steps. On orders it shows a system prompt, environment information, hardly any memory files, and, because nobody has configured anything, very little else. Note the number; you will compare against it in §18.9.

Then ask the question that tells you whether the loop can close at all:

How do I run the tests for packages/api, and how long do they take?

The answer on orders is the answer in most four-year-old repositories. There is a Makefile target. It needs a Postgres container. The container needs an env file nobody documented. And the full suite takes eleven minutes. That is the most important finding of day one, and it is not about Claude Code at all. Without a check Claude can run, nothing in §7 is available, and you are the verification loop.

So the first real piece of work is a fast check:

Write a make target `test-fast` that runs only packages/api unit tests with no
database, and prove it works. It should finish in under 30 seconds.

Eleven minutes is not a check; thirty seconds is. The slow suite still exists and still runs in CI. The fast one exists so the loop can keep turning.

18.2 CLAUDE.md, Written From Corrections

The temptation now is to write a complete CLAUDE.md. Resist it: a file written up front is a list of what you imagined would be needed. Instead, work normally for a week or two and write down every correction you type twice (§4.1).

On orders that produces about fifteen lines, and the interesting thing is how little of it you would have guessed:

# orders

## Commands
- `make test-fast` — unit tests, no database, ~25s. Run this after every change.
- `make test` — full suite, needs `docker compose up db`. Slow; CI runs it.
- `uv run ...` — never `pip`. The lockfile is `uv.lock`.

## Layout
- `packages/api` — FastAPI handlers. Thin; logic belongs in `packages/core`.
- `packages/core` — domain logic. No framework imports here.
- `packages/worker` — Celery tasks. Imports `core`, never `api`.
- `packages/admin` — internal tooling. Different conventions; see its own CLAUDE.md.

## Conventions
- Money is `Decimal`, never `float`. Cents as `int` at the storage boundary.
- `packages/core` raises domain exceptions; `packages/api` maps them to HTTP.
- Migrations are Alembic. Never edit an applied migration — add a new one.

<!-- The Decimal rule is here because it was violated three times in two weeks
     and each one reached staging. Do not delete it because it looks obvious. -->

Four things about that file are deliberate.

  • It starts with commands, because a Claude that cannot run the tests cannot verify anything.
  • The layout section states directional dependencies (which package may use which) instead of describing the folder tree, because the tree is easy to read and the direction is not.
  • The conventions are specific enough to check: "money is Decimal" rather than "be careful with money".
  • The HTML comment costs nothing in context (§4.3) while telling the next maintainer why a rule that looks obvious is actually essential.

packages/admin gets its own nested CLAUDE.md, which loads only when Claude reads files there (§4.3).

18.3 Permissions: The Boundary

Now limit what can happen. This goes in the committed .claude/settings.json, because it belongs to the project, not to whoever set it up (§6.6).

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(make test-fast)",
      "Bash(make lint)",
      "Bash(uv run *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Bash(git log *)",
      "Bash(git status *)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(git push *)",
      "Bash(alembic upgrade *)",
      "Bash(docker compose down *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(.env)",
      "Read(**/.env.*)",
      "Read(~/.aws/**)",
      "Edit(**/migrations/versions/**)",
      "Bash(psql *)"
    ]
  }
}

Each list answers a different question. Allow is the everyday commands: the ones every developer approves in their first hour anyway, so committing them turns six identical decisions into none. Note that Bash(uv run *) puts the * after the subcommand (§5.2); a wildcard before it would allow far more than intended.

Ask covers the three operations with consequences. An ask rule outranks every permission mode (§5.5), so this holds even for a teammate running in auto mode. That is exactly why it belongs in the committed file and not in anyone's local settings.

Deny carries two rules that are not obvious.

  • Edit(**/migrations/versions/**) protects migrations that have already been applied. Editing those causes schema drift (the database and the code quietly disagreeing) that nobody notices for a week. The rule says Edit, not Write, because a path rule on Write is accepted and never consulted (§5.4).
  • Bash(psql *) is there because orders developers have production credentials in their environment. The honest judgement is that no prompt should be the only thing standing between a persuaded model and that connection.

That last rule leads straight to the sandbox. On orders, developer machines hold AWS credentials and a production database URL, so:

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "filesystem": {
      "denyRead": ["~/.aws", "~/.ssh", "~/.config/gcloud"]
    },
    "network": {
      "allowedDomains": ["pypi.org", "*.pythonhosted.org", "github.com"]
    }
  }
}

This is the layer the deny rules cannot reach. A Read deny rule stops Claude's file tools and the shell commands Claude Code recognises. It does not stop a Python script that opens the file itself (§5.4). The sandbox binds every process, and the outgoing-traffic allowlist means a command that does read something cannot send it anywhere. That is the second half of §5.9's argument, and the half people skip.

18.4 Closing the Loop

With a fast check and a boundary in place, make the check automatic.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "if": "Edit(*.py)",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/format.sh",
            "args": [],
            "timeout": 30
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "SessionStart": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/orient.sh",
            "args": []
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/tests-must-pass.sh",
            "args": [],
            "timeout": 120
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Three hooks, and each one replaces an instruction that was only probably followed (§9.1).

#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/tests-must-pass.sh
input=$(cat)
[[ "$(jq -r '.stop_hook_active' <<<"$input")" == "true" ]] && exit 0
[[ "$(jq -r '.background_tasks | length' <<<"$input")" != "0" ]] && exit 0
if output=$(make test-fast 2>&1); then
  exit 0
fi
jq -nc --arg out "$(tail -n 30 <<<"$output")" \
  '{decision: "block", reason: ("test-fast is failing. Fix it before finishing:\n" + $out)}'

The stop_hook_active check prevents the infinite loop. The background_tasks check stops it firing while a generation step is still running (§9.8). And the block includes the last thirty lines of output, because a check that only says "tests failed" gives the next attempt nothing to work with (§7.2).

orient.sh prints the branch, the changed files and whether a migration is waiting to run. Those are facts that change, which is exactly what a SessionStart hook is for and what CLAUDE.md cannot express (§9.7). It matters more than it looks: it also re-runs after compaction, so a four-hour session still knows which branch it is on.

Trigger the Stop hook deliberately, once, before trusting it. A policy hook that fails to start produces one Failed with non-blocking status code notice and then silence (§9.5). A gate you have never seen fire is a gate you have no evidence about.

18.5 Skills: Moving the Procedures Out

By now CLAUDE.md has started to grow, and two things in it are procedures, not facts. Move them (§8.1).

---
name: new-endpoint
description: Adds a new API endpoint following this project's layering. Use when adding, changing or removing an endpoint in packages/api.
allowed-tools: Bash(uv run *) Bash(make test-fast)
---

Adding an endpoint touches four places, in this order:

1. **`packages/core`** — the operation, as a function taking and returning domain
   types. No FastAPI imports. Raise a domain exception on failure.
2. **`packages/core/tests`** — unit tests for it, including the failure paths.
3. **`packages/api/routes`** — the handler. Parse and validate, call core, map the
   domain exception to an HTTP status. Nothing else.
4. **`packages/api/tests`** — one test per status code the handler can return.

Then run `make test-fast` and confirm all four steps are present in the diff.
Do not add business logic to the handler; if it will not fit in core, say so and stop.

---
name: pre-pr
description: Reviews the current branch before opening a PR. Use when asked to review a branch, prepare a PR, or check whether changes are ready to push.
disable-model-invocation: true
context: fork
agent: Explore
allowed-tools: Bash(git diff *) Bash(git log *) Bash(make test-fast)
---

## The branch

- Diff: !`git diff origin/HEAD...HEAD`
- Commits: !`git log origin/HEAD..HEAD --oneline`
- Tests: !`make test-fast 2>&1 | tail -20`

## Your task

Report, in this order:

1. **Blocking.** A failing test, a secret in the diff, a `float` used for money,
   business logic in `packages/api`, an edited applied migration. Cite `file:line`.
2. **Worth a look.** Judgement calls, one sentence each.
3. **PR description.** Two or three sentences from the commits and the diff.

Say "nothing blocking" explicitly if section 1 is empty. Do not edit files.

The second skill does several things from §8 at once.

  • Dynamic context means it arrives with the diff, the commits and the test result already filled in, instead of spending three tool calls fetching them (§8.4).
  • context: fork with agent: Explore keeps all that text out of the main window and gives the reviewer read-only tools, so it cannot "helpfully" fix what it found (§8.7).
  • disable-model-invocation keeps it out of the skill-listing budget entirely, since you always type it yourself (§8.5).

The reference material is a 900-line description of the payment provider's API that matters only in packages/core/payments. It becomes a skill directory, with SKILL.md as the table of contents and the detail in a file next to it, plus paths: packages/core/payments/** so it only appears there.

18.6 Delegation and Parallelism

Two subagents earn their place on orders, for opposite reasons.

---
name: migration-auditor
description: Checks a database migration for reversibility and lock risk. Use proactively whenever a file under migrations/versions/ is created or changed.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: sonnet
---

You audit Alembic migrations for two properties and report on nothing else.

**Reversibility.** Every migration needs a `downgrade` that restores the prior
schema. A missing or incomplete one is a blocking finding.

**Lock risk.** On PostgreSQL, flag any `ALTER TABLE` that rewrites the table, any
`CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY`, and any `NOT NULL` added to a populated
column without a prior check constraint.

Report as `file:line — property — what to do instead`. Say "no findings" and stop.
Do not edit files.

The tools list here is enforcement, not advice (§11.1). This agent cannot write files at all. So "the reviewer helpfully fixed it, and now the diff contains changes nobody reviewed" becomes impossible, not just unlikely. The description is a routing rule and says when, which is why the agent is used without being asked.

The second is not a definition at all. When a change spans core and api, the right move is a fork (/subtask draft the API-layer tests for the change so far). A fresh subagent would need the whole conversation explained to it; a fork already has it, and shares the prompt cache (§11.3).

Worktrees arrive the first time two streams of work run at once (§11.7). Add .claude/worktrees/ to .gitignore, and add a .worktreeinclude that carries .env and the Docker override. Otherwise every new worktree starts with a broken environment, and people give up on the feature as too fiddly.

18.7 CI, and the Guarantee That Is Not Local

Everything so far is a fast feedback loop. None of it is a guarantee, for the reason §7.3's exercise ends on. A Stop hook does not fire when you interrupt a turn, and StopFailure fires instead of Stop when a turn dies on a rate limit. A session cut short ends with the check never run, and nothing reported about it.

So the same checks run in CI too. The local hooks exist to make CI failures rare, not to replace CI:

      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          claude_args: >-
            --bare --permission-mode dontAsk
            --allowedTools "Read" "Grep" "Glob" "Bash(make test-fast)"

The settings, one by one:

  • --bare, so the run does not load hooks, plugins or CLAUDE.md from the branch being checked (§13.1). For a repository taking outside contributions that is a matter of security, since a -p session shows no trust dialog (§5.6).
  • dontAsk, so anything not listed is denied instead of hanging on a prompt nobody will answer.
  • An exact allowlist with no Edit, because a triage job that cannot write cannot leave a surprise in the code.

And the permissions: block on the job grants pull-requests: write and nothing else, because §13.9's point is the one that survives every other control: no flag constrains what a credential can do once a process holds it.

18.8 The First Real Task, Through the Whole Path

Everything so far configured the repository. The real test of the configuration is the first piece of work done with it, so here is one, taken through the path of §16 and the inherited-code habits of §17. The task arrives as a sentence in a planning meeting: "customers should be able to get a partial refund on an order."

Challenge the request (§16.2). Before touching the repository, the interview asks what the sentence hides. Partial by amount, or by line item? Can an order be refunded twice, and how is the total capped? What happens to tax, and to a discount that applied to the whole order? Is the refund idempotent (safe to repeat) if the payment provider times out and the client retries? Find out which of these the business has already decided. The rest become open questions in the spec instead of guesses in the code. This is exactly the limit §18.9 names below, it cannot tell you the change was a good idea, and the interview is the step that can.

Read before writing (§17). packages/core has a refunds module that three people have edited and nobody fully owns, and the plan will change it. So before the plan is written, the session looks at what the history says about it:

git log --since='1 year ago' --name-only --format= -- packages | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

The answer (a short list of the most-changed files) is the hotspot list of §17.3. If refunds.py is on it, two more steps come before any change. First, a characterization test of today's full-refund behaviour (§17.4), so the refactor that partial refunds needs cannot change it unnoticed. Second, a co-change check, because a file that always changes together with ledger.py will need the same care.

Spec, plan and slice (§16.3 to §16.5). The spec names packages/core/refunds.py, the route in packages/api/routes/, and the migration for the refund record. It lists what is excluded (currency conversion, refunds to a different card). It ends with make test-fast plus one command that makes a partial refund against the test database and prints the new balance. The plan's first slice is the smallest behaviour that would embarrass you if wrong: a partial refund of a single-line order, capped at the amount paid. Not the route, not the migration, not refunds by line item.

Using what the setup provides. The configuration built in the earlier subsections now does its job without being mentioned:

The new-endpoint skill
Loads when the route is added and enforces the four-place layering, so the spec does not need to restate it.
The migration-auditor subagent
Runs when the refund migration is created and reports reversibility and lock risk, in its own context. This is the "second mind" of §16.7 already wired in for one class of change.
The Stop hook and make test-fast
Make the slice's check run before Claude may finish, so the first slice cannot be "done" while red.
The deny rules and sandbox
Mean an unattended session cannot touch the payment provider or the production database, whatever the refund code tries.

What the setup does not provide. Two steps are still yours. The first is the boundary cases: refunding exactly the amount paid, one cent over it, a refund after an earlier partial one, rounding on a line whose price includes tax. They come from the mutation habit of §16.6; a suite that only tests the middle would let the cap rule be deleted unnoticed. The second is the review against the spec (§16.7). It needs a different context from the one that wrote the code, so it runs as a fresh subagent against PLAN.md, with the instruction to report only findings that affect a requirement.

The pull request then carries what §16.9 asked for: the goal from the spec, the behaviour that changed, the exact commands and their output, the out-of-scope list, and the three places a reviewer should look hardest. On orders those are the cap rule, the rounding, and whether a retried refund is safe to repeat, and the description says so.

18.9 What It Adds Up To

Six weeks in, orders has a committed .claude/ directory containing a settings file with permissions, a sandbox policy and three hooks; a 15-line CLAUDE.md plus one nested file; three skills; and one subagent. That is about 200 lines of configuration, built up from friction people actually ran into rather than written in advance.

Run /context again and compare with §18.1. It has gone up by roughly two thousand tokens (CLAUDE.md, three skill descriptions, one agent description), against a 200,000-token window. That is the whole standing cost, because everything else loads only when needed or costs nothing at all: skill bodies when invoked, the reference material only in the payments directory, and hooks never.

What it bought, mapped back:

A loop that closes
make test-fast plus the Stop hook. Claude verifies its own work instead of you doing it (§7).
A boundary that holds
Deny rules plus the sandbox. Enforced by Claude Code and the kernel, not by instruction (§5).
Properties, not habits
Formatting and orientation happen every time, on turn one and turn ninety (§9).
Procedures that are cheap
Skills cost a description until used, so a 900-line reference is affordable (§8).
Volume kept out of the window
A read-only auditor and forks for side tasks (§11).
A guarantee outside the session
CI runs the same checks, bounded by a token that can only comment (§14).

What it still cannot do

Three things, stated plainly, because honest limits are more useful than a list of capabilities.

It cannot tell you the change was a good idea. Every check here verifies that the code does what it says. Whether the endpoint should exist, whether the schema is right, whether this is the fourth re-implementation of something in packages/admin: none of that can be checked by a program, and all of it is what review is for. An agent that passes every gate has shown correctness, not judgement.

It cannot survive an interrupted session. The Stop hook does not fire when you press Escape, or when a turn dies on an API error. CI is the answer; the local hook just gives you the same answer sooner.

It cannot stop a determined injection from doing what the credentials allow. The deny rules, the sandbox and the outgoing-traffic allowlist limit the damage; they do not make the session impossible to persuade. The strongest control on orders is not in .claude/ at all. It is that developer machines should not hold production database credentials. The second strongest is that CI's token can only comment. The best control on an agent is usually the one that is not aware it is an agent (§13.9).

The order, restated

If you take one thing from this section, take the sequence, not the files.

1
A check Claude can run. Everything else is worth less without it, and most repositories do not have a fast one.
2
CLAUDE.md, from corrections you actually typed. Not from imagination, and not from /init alone.
3
Permissions and the sandbox. Before any mechanism that increases autonomy.
4
Hooks for what must happen every time. Starting with the one that gates the finish.
5
Skills for the procedures that have grown out of CLAUDE.md.
6
Subagents, parallelism and CI — the mechanisms that add distance, once there is something at the far end that can check the work.

Each step is triggered by something you observed, not by a decision to adopt a feature: a repeated correction, a slow suite, a broken convention, a diff with a surprise in it. Configuration that arrives that way is configuration people keep. Configuration written up front from a course's table of contents is out of date within a month, which is a fitting last thing for a course to say about itself.

Exercises

Exercise 18.1 — The other repository. Your colleague's service is a 3,000-line Go CLI with excellent tests that run in four seconds, one developer, and no CI. Which of §18.9's six steps do you do, in what order, and which do you skip?

Solution

Step 1 is already done, and it is the biggest difference between the two repositories. A four-second test suite is the ideal check: fast enough to run after every edit, specific enough to point at the failure. Everything in §7 is available immediately, which is worth more than every other step combined.

Step 2 shrinks to about six lines. A 3,000-line single-package CLI has no layering to describe and no directional dependencies to state. What remains is the build command, the test command, and any convention that is genuinely non-obvious — error wrapping style, whether it uses a particular flag library. Writing more would be writing what Claude can read.

Step 3 is worth doing and is smaller. A single developer still benefits from Read denies on credentials and an ask on git push. The sandbox depends entirely on what is on the machine, not on the repository: if this developer has production credentials in their environment, turn it on; if the machine holds nothing interesting, the cost-benefit is genuinely marginal and the permission rules are enough.

Step 4 shrinks to one hook, and possibly none. gofmt on save is probably already in their editor, which makes a formatting hook redundant — and §7.6's advice applies: if Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it. A Stop hook running a four-second suite is nearly free and worth having.

Step 5: skip it. Three thousand lines has no procedures worth extracting, and a skill for a codebase you can read in an afternoon is machinery in search of a purpose.

Step 6: mostly skip, with one exception. One developer means no parallelism problem and no worktrees. But "no CI" is worth fixing regardless of Claude Code, and the argument is §18.7's: the local Stop hook does not fire on an interrupted session, so without CI there is no guarantee at all — only a fast feedback loop. A four-second test suite makes CI nearly free to add.

The general lesson: the configuration should be proportional to the friction, and the friction here is almost entirely absent. The orders setup exists because that repository is large, shared, slow to test and easy to break. Copying it here would produce 200 lines of configuration that never fires, for a repository where six lines of CLAUDE.md and one hook is the whole answer. The right amount of configuration is the amount your problems justify, and someone else's setup is evidence about their problems.

Exercise 18.2 — Six months later. The orders setup has been in place for six months. The team is now eight people, packages/admin has been extracted into its own repository, two developers have quietly added --dangerously-skip-permissions to their shell aliases, and the Stop hook has been failing to start for three weeks without anyone noticing. Diagnose what went wrong and describe the maintenance practice that would have prevented each.

Solution

Four failures, and only one is a bug.

The extracted repository left orphaned configuration. packages/admin's nested CLAUDE.md went with it, but the root file still describes a package that does not exist, and any skill or rule scoped to packages/admin/** now matches nothing. The prevention is treating .claude/ as code: a .claude change belongs in the same pull request as the structural change it follows, and a reviewer should ask about it. The specific failure — a paths pattern matching nothing — is silent (§4.4), which is why it survived six months.

The --dangerously-skip-permissions aliases are a symptom, not misconduct. Two people bypassed the permission system entirely, which means the allow list stopped matching how they work — probably new commands the team adopted that nobody added. The prevention is measurement: claude_code.code_edit_tool.decision in telemetry (§15.4) shows the denial rate, and a rising one is this exact signal arriving months earlier. The fix is to widen the allow list to the commands people actually run, not to lecture them.

There is a real risk underneath the sympathy, though. Those two developers are running with no permission checks at all, on machines that may hold production credentials, in a repository that now has eight contributors. If the boundary genuinely matters, disableBypassPermissionsMode in managed settings (§15.6) removes the mode — and that should follow the allow-list fix rather than replace it, or the two of them will find another workaround.

The Stop hook is the actual bug, and it is the most instructive. A hook that cannot start produces one Failed with non-blocking status code notice and then silence — the action proceeds (§9.5). Three weeks of turns ending with unrun tests, and nothing to notice. The likely cause is mundane: a path that moved, a dependency the script calls, a jq that is no longer installed. The prevention is a positive test: trigger the hook deliberately after any change to it, and confirm you see the block. §18.4 says this and it is the step people skip.

And the team grew from three to eight without the setup growing. A CLAUDE.md written from three people's corrections encodes three people's assumptions, and five newer developers have been discovering things the file does not say. The prevention is the same practice as writing it in the first place (§4.1): keep noting corrections that recur, especially from people who joined recently, because a new contributor's confusions are the most accurate available list of what the file is missing.

The practice that covers all four is one quarterly hour, and it is worth naming as a habit rather than a checklist: re-read the CLAUDE.md and delete what is stale; check that every paths pattern still matches something; trigger each policy hook once and watch it fire; and look at the denial rate. Every one of these failures is silent by design — Claude Code is deliberately built so that broken configuration degrades rather than halts (§9.11) — and silent failures need a scheduled check, because by definition nothing will tell you.

You started this course able to ask Claude Code to do things. You can now build the setup around it that makes four things true: the answers can be trusted, the limits are real, long sessions stay on track, and the whole arrangement is something a team shares rather than something you did once. More usefully, when you make a change to that setup, you can say which of those four it is buying.

What you can now do

  1. Reason from what Claude Code actually is. It is a model that writes text, plus a harness (the program around the model) that decides which of those requests become real actions. Every guarantee in the tool lives on the harness side of that line. The practical skill is knowing which side any given behaviour is on.
  2. Drive a session deliberately. Steer without interrupting, and interrupt when steering is too slow. Delegate the goal rather than dictating every step. Plan first when the change needs more than a sentence to describe. And clear early: a conversation still carrying two failed approaches does worse at the third attempt than a fresh one.
  3. Treat context as a budget. The context window is everything the model can see at once, and it is limited. You know what loads before you type, what fills the window, what survives compaction (the automatic summary made when the window is nearly full) and what does not, and why an instruction from turn two weighs less than a file read a minute ago. You also know the prefix rule: the start of the conversation is cached, so switching model is expensive at turn eighty and free at turn three.
  4. Make Claude know the project. CLAUDE.md for what is always true and short. Path-scoped rules for what is true in one directory. Auto memory for what Claude learned about you. And you know the honest limit of all three: they are context the model reads, not configuration the program enforces.
  5. Bound what it may do. Permission rules are checked deny first, then ask, then allow, and nothing overrides a deny rule. You know that the wildcard goes after the subcommand, that a single leading slash means "relative to the settings file's location" rather than the filesystem root, and that the sandbox layer (an operating-system fence) binds every process, not only the tools Claude Code recognises.
  6. Put settings where they belong. Five files, five audiences, and the ordering that catches everyone out: a team file committed to the repository overrides your personal one.
  7. Close the loop. Give Claude a check that returns a pass or a fail. Choose it so that the cheapest way to pass it is the result you actually wanted. Then enforce it at the level the situation deserves: in the prompt, across a session with /goal, deterministically with a Stop hook, or adversarially with a second model that did not do the work.
  8. Move procedures out of the window. Skills cost only their short description until they are used. Progressive disclosure goes one level further, keeping detail in supporting files that load only when needed. A skill's description works as a routing rule, telling Claude when to use it. And the listing budget silently drops descriptions when the team adds twenty more skills.
  9. Make things happen whether the model wanted them to or not. A hook has an event, a matcher and a handler. A hook blocks with exit 2, not exit 1. Its JSON output is thrown away if a shell profile printed a banner in front of it. And additionalContext is the quiet half: it puts facts into the window rather than blocking anything.
  10. Reach systems Claude Code cannot. MCP servers connect outside systems. You know their transports (how Claude Code talks to them) and scopes (who sees each one), that an entry with no type is read as a stdio server, why a token must never be committed to a shared .mcp.json, and how tool search makes ten servers affordable. Its absence explains a session that suddenly feels heavy.
  11. Buy a second context window. Subagents for volume. Forks for continuity and a shared cache. Background sessions for work you walk away from. Teams for genuine disagreement. Workflows when coordinating the work itself outgrows a conversation. And worktrees, which separate files rather than attention and combine with all five.
  12. Ship the setup. A plugin packages your setup so it travels. A marketplace needs no central registry. The manifest directory must contain only the manifest. And the naming of a plugin-bundled MCP tool can make a hook matcher silently miss it.
  13. Run it without a person. claude -p works as an ordinary Unix command. --bare makes runs reproducible. A schema for the output lets you tell an empty result from a full one. The system/init message lets you assert the configuration actually loaded. And canUseTool is the human approval step re-implemented as a function.
  14. Put automation where its audience is. It can start from a git event, a schedule, an API call, a pushed event, or a link in a runbook. And you have the discipline to run it by hand until you know what its output should look like.
  15. Know what it costs and why. The ratio of cache reads to cache writes is the first number to read. Preprocessing (trimming input before Claude sees it) is the lever that reduces tokens rather than their price. And telemetry's two most useful metrics are the ones that are not about money.
  16. Carry a piece of work from idea to merged change. Challenge the request before writing any code. Write a spec a fresh session can carry out. Plan in read-only mode and edit the plan. Build one thin slice. Test that the tests can fail. Review in a fresh context, and count as findings only those that affect a requirement. Open a pull request that shows evidence instead of reassurance.
  17. Work safely in code you did not write, and diagnose what goes wrong. Check Claude's orientation against facts. Ask for claims that carry citations. Read the history for hotspots and for the commit that broke things. Pin down current behaviour with tests before changing it. Tell three kinds of broken apart with one experiment each. And recover a session without losing what it learned.
  18. Take a repository from nothing to a production setup, in the order the problems arrive rather than the order a course teaches them.

The three sentences worth keeping

The model proposes; the harness disposes. Every safety property comes from that one fact. An instruction is a probability: Claude will usually follow it. A permission rule is a guarantee: the program enforces it. The whole craft of configuring this tool is knowing which of the two a requirement deserves, and moving it across the line when "usually" stops being good enough.

A check Claude can run is worth more than any amount of instruction about being careful. Without one, the loop ends at "looks done", and you are the verification step. With one, the loop finishes on its own, and every mechanism that adds distance between you and the work becomes safe. It is also the step most projects do not have, because the check has to be fast and most test suites are not.

Configuration should be proportional to the friction that produced it. Every good line in a .claude/ directory started as a problem: a correction someone typed twice, a convention that was broken, a diff with a surprise in it. Configuration built up that way is configuration people keep. Configuration written up front from a table of contents is out of date within a month.

Where to go next

Set up one real repository, in the order of §18. Not a demo: something you work in every day. The first step tells you the most. Find out whether there is a check Claude can run in under thirty seconds. If there is not, building one is the work. Everything after it is easier and less important.

Then leave it alone for a month and see what you correct twice. The most accurate list of what your setup is missing is the list of things you keep explaining again. It takes a few weeks of ordinary work to produce. Resist the urge to write the complete version now; it would be a list of what you imagined.

Re-derive what is version-dependent. This course names flags, defaults, limits and thresholds, and some of them will change. The four commands from the introduction (claude --help, /hooks, /status, /mcp) answer most "did this change?" questions in under a minute, and the reasoning behind each number in this course will outlive the number.

And read §7 again if you skipped it. It is the shortest path from "an agent that is impressive" to "an agent you can walk away from". It costs less to adopt than anything else in the course, and it is the section that makes every later one worth having.
